EDWARD HENBY SIEMS
Grand Master
Brother Edward Henry Siems, the 83rd Grand Master of Masons
in California, was born at Buena Park in Oregon County, California,
on December 7th, 1903.
He received his elementary schooling at Centralia Grammar School
in Orange County, later going through Anaheim Union High School
in the same county. After spending a year at the University of Southern
California, he attended the University of California at Berkeley, graduating from the college of Commerce in 1927.
Brother Siems was married to Pauline Baker at Berkeley on April
27th, 1933. The couple reside in Berkeley and have one child, Fred A.
Siems, aged 13.
The business experience of Brother Siems has been in the financial
world. After four years in the stock and bond business at Los Angeles
and Long Beach, he went to Oakland with the Key System Transit
Lines in 1931, becoming a director of the company in 1934. Since 1937
he has been the Secretary-T:t"easurer of the company.
His civic activities and affiliations are many and varied. He is a
member of the Rotary Club and Knights of the Round Table, the
Commonwealth Club of San Francisco, the Pacific Railway Club and
the Athens Athletic Club, of which he is a director. He has been a
member of the Oakland Junior Chamber of Commerce, of which he
was a director, the Senior Chamber of Commerce and the United States
Chamber of Commerce. He has interested himself in the Cub Scouts
and other boys' work. As an active member of the First Presbyterian
Church of Berkeley, he has given of his abilities by serving on its Board
of Trustees.
He has been devoted to the Masonic fraternity. He was initiated
in Buena Park Lodge No. 357 on Sept. 12, 1928, passed to the degree .

EDWARD HENRY SIEMS
Grand Master

of Fellowcraft on December 20, 1928, and was raised on February 14,

1929. After moving to the East Bay, he dimitted to Plymouth Lodge
No. 560 of Oakland on April 4, 1933. He became the Master of that
lodge in December, 1940, serving as such through the year 1941. During
1942 he was president of the East Bay Masters' and Wardens' Association. From 1941 to 1946 he was a member and vice-president of the
board of directors of the Masonic Clubhouse at Berkeley. He was
commissioned Inspector of the 34th Masonic District on April 18, 1943,
and served in that capacity until his election to the office of Senior
Grand Warden on October 18, 1946. As Senior Grand Warden and
as Deputy Grand Master from 1946 to 1948 he was a member of the
trustees of the Masonic Homes of California, taking an active interest
in the affairs of the Homes at Decoto and Covina.
On October 15th, 1948, Brother Siems was elected and installed as
Grand Master.
As Grand Master he had the unusual pleasure of having his brother,
Ted R. Siems, serve as Grand Sword Bearer, and he had the further
privilege of raising another brother, Charles John Siems, to the Sublime
Degree.
Throughout his year as Grand Master, Brother "Ed," as he is
familiarly and affectionately known to the great host of Masons who
greeted him in numbers throughout the length and breadth of the jurisdiction, took frequent occasion to "talk shop," reporting in his forthright and practical manner on what was currently happening among the
Masonic Craft in California and elsewhere. His travels as Grand Master
took him a total distance of over 41.000 miles, equivalent to nearly two
trips around the full circumference of the globe.
No Grand Master has ever been more approachable and no Grand
Master has ever given more abundantly of his time and efforts for the
Fraternity. No Grand Master has ever elicited more willing cooperation
from his Masonic brethren. No Grand Master has ever been more
cordially received and accepted as one 'of the Masonic workmen.

Masonry's Eternal Quest

.

Very Reverend W. PAUL REAGOR, Grand Chaplain
Impelled by a never satisfied restlessness man has ever been engaged in an eternal quest. It is not without signifkance that the very
genious of that quest has been incorporated within the framework of
the Masonic fraternity.
The truths and insights of masonry are taught by allegory and
symbol. At the very beginning this eternal quest is symbolized in the
query. "What do you seek?" At the opening of every meeting of a
lodge of free and accepted Masons this symbolism is further exemplified
in that beautiful ceremony wherein the substitute for the ancient
Master's word is brought from the west to the east. Then at the close
of the lodge it is again delivered from the east to the west, there to
remain deposited until called for at the opening of another session of
the lodge.
It is this search for the lost word, resting at the heart of masonry,
which is at once the source of its power in the lives of its members and
the secret of its continuing influence in society. Will you look with me
this morning in some of the directions toward which such a quest
takes us.
It is a quest which looks inward. Perhaps here is the primary·search
of man, that he might know and understand himself and through this
knowledge and understanding control and guide himself.
Any understanding insight into our own personalities and minds
reveals us as men and women of infinite capacities and possibilities. The
record of men who have "risen above themselves" is writ large upon the
pages of history. Great contributions have been made to the enduring
blessing of the race by men who have refused to be defeated by some
thunderbolt which had been hurled against them. All such achievements but illustrate the truth that more important than knowing himself
is the will to achieve this higher self.
The source of such a high determination arises not only within ourselves .but it is stimulated and encouraged by great acceptances and
ennobling fellowships.
It is at this point that we discover the secret of the hold that the
Masonic fraternity has upon the lives of men. "In whom do you put
your trust?" You know the answer. "What do you seek?" In darkness
you are seeking the light, and the light which you seek is that light
which will lead you not to more riches nor to more fame, but to a nobler
and more serviceable manhood. The obligation which you have just
taken binds you ever to seek those high ends in the fulfillment of your
own life.
In seeking such ends we do not travel alone. We share in a fellow-

10

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

ship which cuts across all social boundaries and reaches around the
world as a company of men who are engaged in the same quest. In
such fellowship we are mutually strengthened and encouraged. For
we shall never find the answer to that quest in the here and the now.
Who of us will say that he has realized his best self, or will ever stand
upon the pinnacle of his fullest possibilities. In pressing on we gather
and give encouragement and purpose within the framework of this
high fellowship. For such a fellowship must look and reach outward. ,
The "good society" has been the goal of men from the beginning of
time. High and low, master and slave, the proud and the humble, men
in all stations of life and in all areas of their contemporary social structure have longed and prayed for the time to come when every man would
sit under his "own vine and fig tree" in peace and security.
Yet I do not need to recount for you the record of the conflicts and
wars which have been the scourge of the race during all the centuries
of recorded history. Even within our own generation we have passed
through a period of two world-shaking cataclysms which have left our
civilization so shattered that even now, three years after the shooting
has stopped, we find our world still trembling on the brink of total
destruction.
Moreover, as man has traveled down through the centuries his
record has been one of increasing conquest. At first he lived in a small
flat world not much larger than he could see beyond his limited horizons.
The sky was an upturned bowl and the stars were just beyond his reach.
The heat of the sun frightened him, while the darkness of the night
left him in terror. The visitations of the elements and the ravages of
plague and pestilence were indications of hostile forces before which
man stood in cowering dread.
Indeed man has traveled a long distance from those early beginnings.
For today he lives in an immeasurable, unlimited universe, his night .
time illumined by stars which have been traveling through space lo
these millions of years. He has harnessed the energy of the sun, defied
the pull of this planet to· fly through the air, has plummeted to the
depths of the sea, exploring its mysteries and bringing forth its riches.
He has tamed the wild beasts to do his bidding and exploited the vast
storehouse of the natural world to bring forth no one knows how many
products to add to his delight, satisfaction and supposed peace. He has
conquered disease to such an extent that within our generation man's
life expectancy has increased by a quarter of a century. He has even
cracked the atom and thus almost discovered the mystery of creativity.
Yet in spite of such a phenomenal record of achievement and socalled progress we are living in a world torn to shreds by ill will and
bitterness. fear and suspicion, and we are daily undone by fratricidal
strife. Illustrations range from the individual to the international, from
the stories of murders and crimes of violence one reads in almost every

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

11

issue of the daily newspapers to the international wars which have
periodically engulfed the peoples of the world.
The answer is surprisingly simple. It is more than a matter of
organization, either political or economic. "Not by might nor by power
but by my Spirit, saith the Lord of Hosts." It goes beyond military
defense or diplomatic maneuver. "They that take the sword shall perish
by the sword." Surely the answer is to be found in that utterance one
discovers first on the pages of the New Testament, but quoted there ·
from one of the prophets: "He made of one blood all the nations of the
earth to dwell together in unity.''
We share in a fraternity dedicated to that high purpose. It is a
fellowship world-wide in scope and reaching across most of the artificial
barriers which men have erected between themselves. It transcends
race and creed and within its framework one finds that spirit of equality
and unity which became the source of the inspiration of the Constitution of these United States. Here is one fact we dare never forget.
Often meeting in our own temples, small in members, we are tempted to
feel isolated and far removed from the maelstrom of the world's tumultuous affairs. Yet whenever we meet and no matter under what circumstances, in groups large or small, we need ever to recall that we are a
part o~ that world-wide fellowship, craftsmen dedicated to the building
of a world of amity and good-wil!. of peace and brotherhood. That
js of the very essence of the purpose of Divinity, for did not the Master
pray, "Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.''
However, in all of this I see a grave danger and implicit temptation.
There is always the tendency just to solely enjoy our own fellowship in
such splendid isolation, letting "the rest of the world go by.'' It is so
cozy to be brotherly just to those who share in our own intimate fellowship and to be a brother only to those to whom we have sworn fealty.
Now, to care for our own is certainly the heart of our obligation. But
we dare not stop there. If we would make any effective contribution
toward the building of "One World" we are obligated as Masons to
throw that spirit of brotherhood so singularly ours creatively up against
the tensions and fears existing today between men and nations. Who
knows but we may have been called for just such a day as this?
The lines of our quest reach in and out and also up. Upon your
entrance into a Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons to receive the
degree of Entered Apprentice you put your trust in God. In all of
our supplications we address Him as the "Great Architect of the
Universe" and we pay homage to Him as our "Supreme Grand Master.''
He is the Guide of all our days.
Here is man's oldest and deepest search. The psalmist gathered
together this deep search in words which are always new when he

12

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

sang, "As the hart pantenth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul
after Thee, 0 God." And it was Augustine centuries later who pointe~
out that the "soul is restless and undone until it finds its rest in Thee.
If this upward quest would be brought to some noble fruition our
belief must grow into faith and trust. It is one thing to have belief in
God. That is an intellectual acceptance of Him as indeed the Supreme
Architect of the Universe. That is an intellectual recognition of that
Divine Creativity which is the source of all things both animate and
inanimate in our universe. It is an acceptance of those moral laws
which undergirds all of man's social and individual life. B1:1t such belief
does not carry us far enough.
There is available for all of mankind that added increment of
strength, that plus element in living through which comes lig~t for
darkened hours, guidance for perplexing days, comfort for experiences
of sorrow, forgiveness in the depth of sin, and strength for every weakness. Such a discovery is made when we move belief up into trust.
It is like a swimmer who throws himself back upon the water to float
when he would rest from the ardors of swimming.
It is not too much to say that the noblest of all achievements arises
from such trust. The founding fathers of this land were moved by such
a trust. They knew they were being led by the Di~ine Pro~idence as
they sought to lay the foundation for this democratic republic. Ev~ry
step of the way was made only after supplication for that light which
comes only from above.
.
.
A few Sunday evenings ago in listening to Edward Arnold m his
"Mr. President" show, he told the story of John Quincy Adams. All the
way through that story this sense of trust was so pervasive that one
found oneself living through those stirring days again.
May I bring this :meditation to a close with a personal illustration.
During the war a friend came to me one day with the request that ~ t~l~
with the president of the company for which he worked. He was killing
himself. His associates were concerned about him but none of them felt
they could talk with him. This he wanted me to do.
After thinking it over, I finally went to see him one afternoon about
four o'clock. He had been in his office then since five that morning. I
suggested at the beginning that I had come at the request of the men
with whom he worked. They were concerned and felt that he was
·
working too hard.
But then I added that I wasn't going to counsel him to take it easy.
He couldn't for weren't we in a war? But I did want to remind him of
that added strength that was available for all of those who learned to
trust.
I had hardly finished before he started in, first apologizing for not
coming to church and then revealing some of the intimate secrets of his
life, the values around which he built that life and the joy that was his

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

13

in the confidence that only a Divine Hand could have guided him in
preparation for this very hour. We finally left together about seven.
I reported the next day that they did not need to worry for I knew he
would carry through.
Such is trust, and he who has learned that high fellowship has indeed
learned the secret of all noble and victorious living.

MESSAGE OF THE GRAND MASTER

among the members in every section of our jurisdiction from the western
most outpost lodge on the Island of Kauai to El Centro No. 384 on
the southern border, and to North East Lodge No. 266 at Fort Bidwell
in the northeast corner of this great State. Minor differences of opinion
which always happen when two or more people get together were
usually solved by some sound thinking brother whispering good
counsel in the ears of all parties. In Masonic lodges there is no substitute for common sense and Masonic understanding.
The lodges, as far as I have knowledge, are in a strong financial
condition. Many have high-lighted the Masonic year by freeing their
Temples of debt and burning their mortgages. Several applications
for new lodge buildings are now being processed by the Committee on
Lodge Financing. It was my pleasure to convene Grand Lodge in
special communications on five separate occasions for the. pur~s.e of
laying cornerstones for Masonic Temples and other public bmldmgs.
The dates and places were as follows:
Dec. 21, 1948-New Hall of Justice, San Bernardino
Apr. 16, 1949-Masonic Temple, Van Nuys
May 7, 1949-0akland Main Public Library, Oakland
May 28, 1949-Masonic Temple, San Gabriel
Aug. 6, 1949-Granada Masonic Temple, Alhambra
On January 29. 1949, Grand Lodge was convened for the
purpose of dedicating the new Beverly Hills Masonic Temple.

One year ago this Grand Lodge elected me to the highest office
at its command, and now I stand before you to render the final report
of my stewardship. In doing so, I welcome you, one and all, to this the
1OOth Annual Communication of The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge
of Free and Accepted Masons of California.
As this week ends, it closes a year of intense activity. I have enjoyed
· every minute of it. It has been strenuous at times and to say that I have
appreciated the honor of becoming, by your sufferance, Grand Master
of this Great Jurisdiction, is a "masterpiece of understatement". How
successful this administration has been is left for you and time to judge.
I prayerfully submit for your thoughtful consideration this report
of the year's activity.
In entering on the new Masonic year, my successor will have under
his stewardship 601 lodges, 594 under charter and 7 now under dispensation. As of July 31, 1949, the aggregate membership was 190.543,
another all-time high. The net gain was 7,365. Growth of membership,
of course, is not our yardstick for measuring success, but rather indicates
the basic fact that more men are desirous of receiving those truths set
forth in our Masonic philosophy because of the favorable impression
they have of the craft and its members generally.
COOPERATION AND INFORMATION

A little over a year ago as I approached the res·ponsibility of Grand
Master, I felt that something was lacking in our Grand Lodge organizational set-up. There seemed to be pages missing in the administrative
book of continuity. There were so many matters of great importance
about which I knew so little. After some discussion with the elected
line officers I called a general conference of the elected Officers and
the principal Committee Chairmen. We met for two days of serious
discussions on matters Masonic. As a result of these discussions the
concensus was that many questions of policy were clarified, and it was
recommended that other such meetings be held. I was in accord with
the idea because of the benefits derived, but none were held as funds
had not been budgeted for the purpose. I recommend that should my
successor desire to hold such conferences, sufficient funds be appropriated for the necessary expense of travel and hotels.
CONDITION OF THE CRAFT

The Past Grand Masters, both living and dead, who have been
called to direct the activities of this Grand Jurisdiction have been men
of great mental stature and ability. Each has had outstanding attributes
of leadership which, combined with the cooperation of the Craft, has
made it fairly easy for your present administration to keep affairs
running smoothly. As far as I can detect, there is complete harmon}'.

TRAVEL AND VISITATIONS

Although I have consistently put in a full week's work at my office,
except for six weeks for extended travel, I have been able to measure

16

17

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

and lay out my work and time in accordance with our Masonic teachings
by dividing it into three parts (I cannot say equal), consisting of
service to God, our usual vocation and refreshment and repose. This
Great Jurisdiction, exclusive of Honolulu, covers over 155,000 square
miles, is 780 air miles north to south and 350 miles east to west at its
widest point and it is only with the generous cooperation of the brethren
that I have succeeded.
I have traveled approximately 20,000 miles by air ( 21 different trips
including Honolulu), 6,000 miles by rail and 15,000 miles by automobile.
My distant trips were on week-ends or holidays. Visitations within
125 miles of my home were scheduled for week nights, Monday through
Thursday. I am especially grateful to our Grand Tiler Alvin A. Horwege, who traveled with me on most of my local trips by automobile
( 73 in all). Special thanks are due two Past Masters of my own Lodge.
Plymouth No. 560, Brothers W. G. Thumann and Chas. K. Baxley,
who also accompanied me on many of these trips. These three brethren
were always ready and willing to take over the responsibility of driving
when requested. My thanks also to Brother William Rhodes Hervey, Jr.
as pilot and Mrs. Hervey as chief cook, for their generous hospitality
in taking me and other Grand Lodge Officers to San Diego and Catalina
Island on official visits on their very fine cabin cruiser the "Moana
Mele". Special orchids go to our Grand Secretary Lloyd E. Wilson for
filling in for me at Fort Bragg when I found myself snarled with "labor
pains" on June 21, 1949.
I was privileged to bring Masonic messages to approximately
45,000 Master Masons in person during the year, and to reach the
entire membership by the publication of one Grand Lodge Bulletin
in March.

K.L.X., Oakland. Letters, phone calls and general comment indicated
a rather wide listening audience.
The number of meetings, the hours spent, the miles traveled, and
the preparation time that went into each of them rather startled me
when the record was finally written. but all this seemed to fade into
obscurity when measured in terms of new friendships made and old
ones renewed. The courtesies extended, the genuine enthusiasm and
response of our brethren was the practical expression of brotherly love,
relief, truth, temperance, fortitude, prudence and justice exhibited by
them withersoever dispersed.

It is not possible to visit all 601 lodges or the 123 inspectorial districts, but through joint meetings and the combining of districts all but
one was within hailing distance of some scheduled meeting. I was
greatly honored and pleased on many occasions to learn that brethren
laid aside their working tools and drove 80 to 90 miles in each direction
to pay their respect to the office of Grand Master. In spite of these
several limitations I attended 152 meetings, divided almost equally
between official receptions and miscellaneous meetings such as De
Malay, Masonic social functions, luncheons, Masonic Clubs, Service
Clubs, Club -Houses at the University of California, Homes reception
at Decato, Breakfast meetings, Constitutions, Institutions, etc.
On the Monday following Grand Lodge, the East Bay Masters and
Wardens Association tendered me an official home-coming welcome,
attended by about 300 Masters and Past Masters of Alameda and
Contra Costa Counties. One interesting innovation was that portions
of the program were recorded and later re-broadcast over radio station

GRAND MASTERS CONFERENCE

In February I attended the Grand Masters Conference in the
Nation's Capital. accompanied by Deputy Grand Master Ellsworth
Meyer, the Grand Secretary Lloyd E. Wilson and P.G.M. William
B. Ogden, Chairman of Regional Ways and Means Committee, Region
X of the George Washington National Masonic Memorial Association.
This is not the time to report on all items of importance, but all who
have been privileged to attend these Conferences generally feel they
are tremendously worth while, and I strongly recommend that the practice established several years ago by this Grand Lodge of sending our
Deputy Grand Master, our Grand Secretary and the Grand Master to
the Conference be continued.
The Washington Conference in February is really a series of Masonic conferences for it includes the Conference of Grand Masters, the
Conference of Grand Secretaries, the annual meeting of the George
Washington National Masonic Memorial Association, and for
some Grand Jurisdictions the annual meeting of the Masonic Service
Association.
At the annual meeting of the George Washington National Masonic
Memorial Association your Grand Lodge was honored when the Grand
Master was asked to respond to the splendid address of welcome given

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
SPECIAL RELIEF

During the month of August, upon the urgent appeal for help by
Grand Master Repalda of Ecuador, I directed that $1,000 be transmitted
to them to assist the homeless and injured brethren whose property was
destroyed by the earthquake. There are approximately 2,000 Masons
in Ecuador, and the reports indicate such terrific destruction that I felt
the amount sent was little enough in comparison to the service it could
render. While action could have been delayed for official action by
this Grand Body, one cannot postpone hunger and suffering. The above
referred to amount was sent with our fraternal best wishes, with a request that they advise us if further assistance would be required.
GRAND LoDGE REGALIA

At the last Annual Communication there was appropriated $3,640
for the purchase of 26 sets of officers' regalia at $140.00 per set. With
the creation of the office of Asistant Grand Treasurer. one set was
ordered and delivered. The quality was excellent, it having been made
of prewar material. Shipping costs and other expense ran the price
slightly over $140.00. The manufacturer assured us that they had sufficient material of the same quality on hand to deliver 26 sets as required,
and the order was placed with assurance that delivery would be made
well in advance of our Centennial. October 9th, 1950. It developed that
the cost of the 26 sets would not exceed $4,095.00. It is therefore recommended that an additional amount of $455.00 be appropriated to cover
the increased cost of the new regalia.

INSPECTORIAL DISTRICTS

Pursuant. to authority under Section 53, some shifts were made in
Inspectorial Districts. With the addition of new lodges and others in
the making. I requested that a survey be made under the supervision of
the Ritual Committee, looking toward the further re-alignment of Districts. It is noted that some inspectors have as many as seven lodges.
Experience seems to indicate that four is a proper number, although
five is not too far out of line in metropolitan areas. Unfortunately, this
survey was not completed in time for me to take corrective action.
We have lost a number of our Inspectors through death and resignation. Section 53 provides,
"The Grand Master shall divide the Jurisdiction into Districts,
and shall appoint for each District an Inspector, who shall be a
Past Master of the Jurisdiction and (a resident of the District for
which he is appointed). and who shall, etc."
This last phrase has worked a hardship on the lodges for in some
cases it is almost impossible to find a man qualified and willing to take
over the responsibility of Inspector of the District. In some instances
an Inspector living in the Jurisdiction moves to the seashore or over
the hills to the country, thus disqualifying himself by virtue of residence. In some instances I find that the ordinances have been disregarded. It is, therefore, my recommendation that Section 53, 3rd line, be
amended by deleting the words "a resident of the District for which he
is appointed".
This amendment, if adopted, would be particularly helpful in rural
and mountainous areas where it is not practical to shift lodges within
Districts nor possible to find a Past Master qualified and willing to
carry the responsibility, but where a brother in a neighboring District
could be found who would be acceptable and who would serve.
MASONIC FUNERAL SERVICE

I have had a number of inquiries from Masters and clergymen as to
the proper interpretation of our Masonic law relating to others participating in conducting the funeral services for a departed brother. The
main problem seems to be "who is in charge of and who should conclude
the service?"

24

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

The law governing Masonic funeral services has not been materially
changed since it was first considered by Grand Lodge. S~bsequent
interpretations with the lapse of time have caused some confusion.
In 1891 Grand Lodge adopted a report of the Jurisprudence Committee which states in part.
"We do not understand this to mean that no service except the
Masonic burial service can be performed at the burial of one who
has requested Masonic burial. but only that the Lodge must, in the
procession, occupy the place of honor, and must have charge of
and conclude the service. Not infrequently the friends of the decedent desire services in the church of which he was a member or
attendant, and it is customary and proper in such cases for the
Lodge to accompany the body to the church and there assist in the
proper church services, and upon the conclusion of such services
to conduct the body to the place of burial. and there, in accordance
with Masonic usage, conclude the services and consign the body
to the grave."
In 1916 Grand Master Burnett ruled that the Lodge must conduct
and conclude services in the following words:
"In reply to a question whether a brotlier's dying request that
his funeral services be conducted by the Masons and Odd Fellows,
I held that the language. of Section 164 of the Constitution should
be construed as liberally as possible, but that it certainly means
nothing less than the whole service should be under the direction
of the Masonic LOdge: but that out of respect to the wishes of the
deceased, as a matter of courtesy to the other great fraternal organ~
ization, the Worshipful Master of the Lodge might properly request
the Odd Fellows to render their service or a part of it at the chapel.
it being understood that the Masonic Lodge shall "have charge of
and conclude the service."
May 10, 1949

It seems to me that under this regulation the Masters of our lodges
should find adequate latitude to carry out the wishes of the deceased
brother as well as the wishes of the bereaved family. I believe that the
reference in Section 647 report of the Jurisprudence Committee, last line,
namely,-"conclude the services and consign the body to the grave" is
no longer applicable in many instances and should be changed under
today's practices. Lodges rarely conduct graveside services. Statistics
show that in California not more than 50% of all funeral services are
graveside.
It is therefore my recommendation that Sections 647 and 648, Edicts
and Resolutions, be rescinded and that our lodges conduct Masonic
funerals in accordance with Section 266 of Ordinances.
Section 266 makes no mention of clergymen. Should it be the desire
of the family that the Minister of the deceased brother conclude the
service, give a eulogy or words of comfort,. or participate at the beginning of the service, the Master, the family of the deceased and the
Minister of his church should mutually decide the order of the service,
bearing in mind, of course, that our entire service must be given.

Grand Lodge sustained his ruling.
The problems that arise seem to be not because of conflict with the
ordinances but with the ruling of G. M. Burnett that the Masonic Lodge
"shall have charge of and conclude the service."
This ruling probably was in order and served the craft well when
it was declared but times have changed and I have difficulty to believe
that a Masonic Lodge has a right to dictate to clergymen or the bereaved
as to who should conclude the service. Nowhere in Section 266, Ross
Digest, is any mention made as to who should conclude the service. It
merely provides in part that * * * "No lodge shall attend any funeral
service or procession unless it is under the direction of the Grand Lodge,
the lodge itself or another Masonic lodge. The lodge conducting the
service shall assign such positions as may seem to it proper to other
. t'ies * * * ...

HOTEL EXPENSES FOR APPOINTED
GRAND LoDGE OFFICERS DURING GRAND LoDGE WEEK

The brethren honored by appointment as Grand Lodge Officers are
selected because of their contribution to Masonry in their respective
communities. In selecting appointees the Grand Mastei: should not first
be required to obtain a credit report to determine if the brother is financially able to accept the honor.
Our law provides that they be reimbursed for travel expense but not
hotel expense. In addition to travel and hotel expense the men who
accept the appointments usually have other expenses in connection with
their services during the year and payment of the hotel bill in addition
to travel expense during Grand Lodge Week would be a very small
recompense to them.
It is, therefore, my recommendation that each appointed Grand
Lodge line officer be allowed, in addition to his travel expense, hotel
expense for the period of Grand Lodge: it being understood that no
officer shall receive such reimbursement in more than one of those capacities as outlined in Sections 67 and 68 of Ordinances, and subject to
same audit as provided therein.
SuccESSION oP AGES

The Grand Master has been flattered many times, even to the extent
of being embarrassed as respects his age. Some overly enthusiastic
brethren have released to the press statements to the effect that I am
the youngest Grand Master this State has ever had. That is covering
too much territory. I will admit to the statement that I am the youngest
and oldest one this Grand Jurisdiction has had this Masonic year.

26

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

After some discussion with Brother Elbert W. Davis, Inspector of
the 33rd Masonic District, he developed the following information:
"The present Grand Master became 45 years of age less than two
months after his installation. In the light of statements made by various
brothers to the effect that Brother Siems is the youngest or one of the
youngest men ever to hold the office, the actual facts will be interesting.
Of the 83 Grand Masters who have served our Grand Lodge in its
nearly 100 years of existence, more than 30 of them were under the age
of 45 years at the time of election.
The youngest was Nathaniel G. Curtis, elected in 1857, who was
only 32 years of age. and who held the office for four terms. The next
youngest was Bro. Oscar Lawler, elected in 1908 at the age of 33 years. ·
then Charles L. Patton. elected in 1899 at 34. Two of our Grand
Masters were 35, three were 36, including Past Grand Master Dana R.
vVeller, now deceased. Three Grand Masters were 37 years of age.
Four were 39 years of age. including Bro. Francis V. Keesling, now
Grand Treasurer. Nineteen of the Grand Masters were 40 years or
younger, and it is interesting to note that during the Srst twenty-Sve
years of existence of our Grand Lodge, the average age of the Grand
Master was less than 40 years.
On the other hand, during its whole existence. the Grand Lodge has
'lected but six Grand Masters over the age of 60 years. All of these
men are living today, Past Grand Master James B. Gist ( 1933), Randolph V. Whiting ( 1934). James T. Fraser (1935). Leon 0. Whitsell
( 1938). William B. Ogden ( 1940) and Arthur W. Brouillet ( 1945).
The oldest of these was Brother Fraser who was elected Grand Master
at the age of 69. The only other one who was elected over the age of
65 years was Brother Gist."
MINIMUM DUES
At the last Annual Communication Section 251 of our Ordinances
was amended providing that minimum dues be increased from $9.00
to $12.00 per year. Constituent lodges affected by this amendment were
required to initiate legislation to amend their own by-laws pursuant to
Section 1 of Article 13 of the Uniform Code of By-Laws under Section
133 Ross Digest, to conform to provisions of said Section 251 as
amended.
"' ...-.,,.~
Two lodges refusing to take the necessary steps defeated the proposed resolution. In each case I issued the following order:
1. There shall be no meetings of the Lodge held during the
month of January except the January Stated Meeting and a meeting
which may be necessary for the purpose of conducting the funeral
of a Brother, and there shall be no Degrees conferred.
2. At the January Stated Meeting business must be restricted
to the disposition of the Minutes, the payment of necessary bills,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

27

and the introduction of a resolution to amend the By-Laws to increase dues to a minimum of at least $12.00 per year.
3. At the February Stated Meting business shall be restricted
to the disposition of the Minutes. the payment of necessary bills,
and to the adoption of the resolution to increase the dues.
4. No other meeting shall be held during February except for
the purpose of conducting a funeral, unless and until the Grand
Master lifts this restriction.
The lodges complied with the order and I lifted the re~trictions.

MASONIC CLUB WITHIN A LoDGE
Madera Lodge No. 280 F. & A. M. for permission to form a Masoni,
On May 20, 1949, I received inquiry and request for approval from
Club known as "Madera Masonic Club," it being the intent to limit the
membership of the club to members of Madera Lodge. It is my belief
that the lodge itself .should have direct supervision of all the activities
of its members insofar as Masonry is concerned and that the creation
' of a club within a lodge sooner or later results in the development of
cliques and possible disharmony. It is my further belief that a lodge
can sponsor any special activity in keeping with the dignity of Masonry
that a club could sponsor. I recommended against the formation of the
club.
In connection with formation of new lodges, I have insisted that
where the request for dispensation grew out of a Masonic Club that the
Club be dissolved prior to or at the time the new lodge was instituted.
MoRAL AND PHYSICAL QUALIFICATIONS
I was asked if a man 64 was considered too old to become a Master
Mason. I advised the lodge that the only regulations and restrictions
were those set forth in Sections 208 and 210, Ross Digest of Ordinances.
We have no law other than that the applicant for degrees of Masonry must be a man, etc., quoting Section 208. Some people I know
are old at Sfty while others are fairly young at seventy. An analysis
of applicants for degrees in the East Bay reveals that they range any-

28

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

where from twenty-one to sixty-five years of age. True, a man who has
waited until his sixty-fourth year has delayed becoming a Mason for a
long time and, in my judgment, should be very carefully investigat~d
as to his motives, but everything else being right the matter of years, in
my judgment, should not bar him. The true test should be "Is the applicant worthy and well qualified.''
SUSPENSION OF MASTER

.Under date of December 12, 1948, I received charges of un-Masonic

MISCELLANEOUS

During the year your Grand Master was asked on numerous occasions to interpret our Masonic Law. This, I was happy to do. The
answers given could not be considered as decisions and as such are not
individually listed in this report. The answers given were found within
the framework of legislation already in effect.
They included miscellaneous inquiries embracing expenditure of
funds as respects the general funds of the lodge or refreshment fund,
contribution by a lodge of its funds to the Homes Endowment fund,
solicitation of funds from lodges through sale of tickets, use of Masonic
emblem and titles in advertising commercial enterprises, solicitation of
funds by a lodge for account of a highly respected brother in distress,
use of commemorative paper aprons at the public unveiling of a plaque, ·
receiving application for degrees from one not able to qualify physically,
the question of renting Masonic Temples to undesirable tenants and
subversive groups, use of Masonic membership to sell certain types of
life insurance and many others.
Where the deed had been done I tried to weigh the motive behind
the act and governed myself accordingly, usually whispering good counsel into the ear of the erring brother. It was not my desire to penalize
any brother for misdirected enthusiasm unless our Masonic law was
deliberately circumvented. Such instances, I am happy to report were
rare.
DECISIONS

1. In January 1949, it was called to my attention that a father,
not a Past Master, was invited to act as installing officer on the occasion
when his son was being installed Master of the lodge. After the installation ceremony, but before the first stated meeting following installation, the Master-elect was cautioned that under the circumstances there

(

29

might be some doubt as to the legality of any business transactions of
the lodge, since he had not been installed by a Past Master or by his
predecessor in office. The Master-elect sought advice_ and was i~forme_d
that in my judgment his informant had whispered wise counsel mto his
ear, and, in order to correct the error, it was recommended that a second
installation ceremony be had prior to the January stated meeting. I was
informed that the retiring Master installed his successor in due and
ancient form.
2. I was asked if an application received from one who had
to rely on the use of a hearing aid and who couldn't hear without it,
could be accepted by a lodge. I ruled that it could not be received. Section 883 Ross Digest, Edicts and Resolutions.
3. Crocker Lodge No. 454, F. & A. M., asked for a definition
of "Total Revenue.'' The letter of inquiry reads in part as follows:
"The problem of determining the lawful, full amount of Lodge
Funds for Refreshment and Entertaining is assuming serious proportions in our Lodge and is causing an unfriendly feeling to grow
among certain groups of our more active members, which condition,
certainly should not exist in any Masonic Lodge. We are therefor,
enclosing a copy of our Receipts and Disbursements from Dec. 3,
1947 to Dec. 7, 1948 inclusive, and respectfully present the following facts, with the sincere hope that you, Most Worshipful Sir, as
presiding Grand Master, may advise a solution, or issue a Ruling.
"Crocker Lodge No. 454 F. & A. M. is the owner of a building
which contains our Lodge Rooms, Banquet Hall and Kitchen. We
also have as tenants a Drug Store, a Safeway Store, Butter and
Egg Store, Barber Shop and upstairs a suite of Doctor and Dental
Offices. The total cost or book value of the land, building, furniture and fixtures is $72,139.46 and as of Dec. 31, 1948, we owe a
balance of $4,167.37 on a building loan, which we are paying off
in monthly payments of $240.00.
"We also own $5,500.00 in U. S. Treasury G Bonds.
"Please note that our building receipts for the year 1948 totaled
$10,125.75."
Group A maintained the lodge is entitled to spend 20% of the total
income: that is, income from dues, application fees and gross income
from rentals, and supported their contention by quoting Section 630
Edicts and Resolutions.
Group B maintained that the 20% permissible for refreshment. and
fraternal intercourse should be based on dues, application fees and "net
profit" from the income from the building.
I ruled that I could not concur with the decision rendered by P.G.M.
Burnett in 1916, Section 630 Ross Digest, Edict sand Ordinances,
wherein he ruled that "total revenue" means "gross." Grand Master
Burnett apparently recognized the possible indulgence in extravagance

for social purposes and indicated that in that event it "should be brought
to the attention of the Grand Lodge that the needed change may be
effected." I believe that time has now come. I therefore ruled as follows:
"I have had for consideration your inquiry of December 31,
1948 regarding the definition of "total revenue" and the problem
with which your Lodge is confronted.
"I am not at all unfamiliar with Sections 159 and 630 of Ross
Digest but cannot concur with the decision rendered by P.G.M.
Burnett in 1916. Obviously, at that time it was the general rule
that single lodges were the owners of their temples. Since that
date we have many temples jointly owned not only by two or more
lodges but other bodies have joined in joint ownership. Even in
Masonry we have to be practical at times, and the ownership of
physical assets must be considered strictly on a business basis. It
is, therefore, your Grand Master's ruling that "total revenue" is
in effect "net revenue" as defined under present day modern accounting methods: that is, less all operating expenses such as taxes,
insurance, custodian, depreciation, etc."
4. During the time I was out of the State, Deputy Grand Master
Ellsworth Meyer ruled as follows:
"Your recent letter to the Grand Master was referred to me as
acting. Grand Master due to his absence from the State.
"You state that after initiation in 1925 an objection on moral
grounds was made to a certain Entered Apprentice, a committee
appointed, its report received and by vote of the lodge the Entered
Apprentice denied advancement. You further advise that he has
now made application for a waiver of jurisdiction in favor of.
Reseda Lodge No. 666 and you inquire as to the proper course to
pursue.
"Please be advised that in my opinion you should appoint a
committee to investigate the request in the same manner as is provided in cases clearly falling within Section 220 of the Ordinances
of the Grand Lodge. Of course So!-1thern California Lodge has
jurisdiction, but the committee should investigate the other phases
of the matter and report to the lodge, which will then decide
whether the waiver will be granted. It would seem logical that if
he is still objectionable that the waiver should be denied and if not
may be voted.
"If the waiver is granted you should advise the Master of
Reseda Lodge of the facts that it may determine whether it will
receive him in the further degrees.
"I do not for a moment infer that such is the attitude of any
member of your lodge, but it may be stated that it is not a proper
Masonic attitude that we don't want him, but if some other lodge

GRAND LoDGE OF CHINA

During the early part of this calendar year we received an urgent
request from certain Chinese brethren in China for the loan of our Book
of Ceremonies covering installation of Grand Lodge officers and other
printed forms which might be used by the Grand Lodge of China. Every
courtesy was extended to these brethren and I am happy to report that
the Grand Lodge of China came into existence on March 18, 1949. This
new Grand Lodge is operating under very trying conditions. The information available to us indicates that the brethren chosen as officers are
capable and imbued with the spirit that will result in a strong Grand
Lodge in the Far East. We tendered our fraternal best wishes and the
frate~nal_ greetings o~ this Grand Lodge at the time their Grand Lodge
was mstituted. Their response gave every evidence of their genuine
appreciation of our interest.
MASSACHUSETTS AND NEGRO FREEMASONRY

At the closing moments of the Annual Conference of Grand Masters
in February 1947, held in the Nation's Capital, there was read a pro·
posed report rendered by a special committee of Past Grand Masters
of_ the G~~nd Lodge of Massachusetts. This report while dealing directly
with legitimacy and regularity of Prince Hall Negro Freemasons, went
~uch further a~d broke down the well established and recognized principle of Exclusive Territorial Jurisdiction practiced and respected by
all Grand Jurisdictions in the United States.
M.W: John R. ~oore_. G~and Master in 1947, eloquently challenged
the propriety of their action m adopting the report and pleaded for reconsideration of their action. See 1947 Proceedings, pages 42 to 55
inclusive. The following year, M.W. Grand Master Chester H. Warl~w ( 1~48 Pro~eedings-pages 32 to 39 inclusive) after giving additional mformabon on the subject in his free and frank manner,
r~c~~mended that this Grand Jurisdiction stretch its patience to the
limit m the following words:
. "My Brethren, on this subject now before us I have spoken
freely and frankly and perhaps over-forcibly. We do not intend
offense. We seek clarity and clarification. We desire correction
of a~ important misstep in. Masonic progress. We do not suggest
to this Grand Lodge that it should take any action to interrupt or

33

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

disturb the peace and good fellowship which, except in this single
instance, has existed for nearly one hundred years between the ·
Grand Lodge of Massachusetts and the Grand Lodge of California.
Rather do we hope that these remarks may clear the minds, not only
of the Brethren of our two great Jurisdictions, but also may simplify
the issue for the leaders of the other Grand Jurisdictions of this
United States. We pray that some clear thinkers and some kind
friends in some of these Jurisdictions may whisper good counsel.
gently admonish Massachusetts of her error, and succeed in convincing her that she is following a false Messiah, not out of. but
into, a Masonic wilderness."
This proved to be a wise decision for much good and wise counsel
was whispered into the ears of our brethren from Massachusetts. . While
the subject was not formally on the program of the Grand Masters'
Conference in February 1949, it was discussed off the record by many
of the brethren in attendance. Your representatives were a particular
target since many were interested in the position this Grand Lodge
would take in October 1949. Since my two predecessors in office had so
ably laid the foundation of our position, and concurring in that position,
I felt obliged, recognizing full well that it would be received with
mingled feelings, to issue a "declaration of intent" at the closing session
of the Grand Masters Conference. The statement was to the effect
that our patience was rapidly running out. I further indicated that if the
situation remained the same in October I would have no alternative but
to recommend to this Grand Body that we join the Grand Lodge of
Texas and of Florida in severing fraternal relations with the Grand
Lodge of Massachusetts. The statement made at the Conference, as
was expected, was stricken from the record, but "even though the Judge
sustained the objection, I am confident the jury got the point."

Boston, May 11, 1949
To the Most Worshipful Grand Master of Masons in Massachusetts:
As requested by you on March ninth, your Committee has reconsidered the subject of Negro Freemasonry. lt ·has given careful and
sympathetic attention to the various comments of certain other Grand
Lodges relative to its earlier report of November 25, 1946 as approved
by the Grand Lodge on March 12, 1947 and has re-examined the ori~
ginal source material on which its earlier report was based, but we
believe it will serve no good purpose to re-open the discussion.
Misunderstanding and statements which we feel to be erroneous
have produced unfortunate events. The net result is producing disharmony in American Freemasonry whereas unity is what we need more
than anything else. Unity and harmony are vastly more important to the
Fraternity than debates about Negro Freemasonry.

Islands.

In my opinion the prcper way to cure this situation is to repeal
Sections 243a and 243b and adopt legislation permitting a Lodge in its
discretion to grant dimits to Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts.
This will also make it possible for Lodges to dear their records of
Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts who do not desire to proceed
further. It has long been desired, but no practical way has been found
under our present law to accomplish it.
I further recommend that some limitation be placed on Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts which will require them to present themselves for advancement within a given period of time under penalty of
not having the remaining fees returned to them. I am aware of Section
572. but to me this does not appear to meet the situation. It seems to me
that after a three year period an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft.
who has not advanced in that time, should be required to reapply to the
Lodge for the remaining Degrees and be subject to the same investigation and ballot as any other applicant.

It is a matter of great satisfaction to any Grand Master to know
that the regular and continuing programs of the Grand Lodge are administered by competent Boards and Committees.
The Masonic Homes, Clubhouses, Board of Control. Endowlll;ent
Board. and similar activities will all be reported on by the appropriate
directing body. I express my thanks to them for work well-done.
DEGREES BEYOND Jurusmcr10N

Last October we ~dopted Sections 243a and 243b as a means of
having Degrees conferred for Entered Apprentices a~d Fellow. Cr~fts
who had permanently removed from California. Wh1l~ ~he leg1sl~~on
was well intended and at the time seemed workable 1t 1s my opinion
that it has not proved satisfactory. The machinery is cumbers~me and
conflicts with the laws of other jurisdictions. We now have mne cases
of our own Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts residing elsewhere
who can never become Master Masons because of the requirements of
this Grand Lodge which conflict with the laws and practices of other
states.

CONCLUSION

Not so long ago you honored me by sentencing me to a year of hard
labor as your Grand Master. You are now about to grant me parole,
and I now earnestly implore you to grant me a full pardon for my
shortcomings. While ~he sentence was at hard labor, in truth the genuine pleasure of it all minimized the labor involved. The unfailing support and the tremendous help which was willingly given by every
member of the craft, the Grand Lodge officers, both elected and appointed, the Inspectors who responded to every call, and finally to the
Grand Lodge office staff for their most solicitous cooperation. The
Grand Secretary spoke for them all last year during the closing of
Grand Lodge for truly "my slightest whisper was responded to as
though it might have been a roaring command". May I also include my
own office staff, for without their complete cooperation many problems
which have been solved would now be resting in the file labeled "unfinished business".
To be a Mason is a great honor; to be appointed to serve the craft
in any capacity a privilege, but to be called to the high position of Grand
Master of more than 190,000 true and loyal brethren of this Grand
Jurisdiction is above the price of material worth. No predecessor has
ever appreciated it more than I have. In a few short days the gavel of
authority will be surrendered to other and worthier hands. I have every
confidence that your inexhaustible support to him and them will continue. Painfully conscious as I am, of my inability to adequately express
myself at a time like this, I shall solicit the aid of the poet in these words :

THIS AGREEMENT made in duplicate this last day of June, 1949,
by and between the STATE OF CALIFORNIA, acting through the
State Park Commission of the State of California, hereinafter designated State. and THE MOST WORSHIPFUL GRAND LODGE,
FREE AND ACCEPTED MASONS IN THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA. hereinafter designated Concessionaire (whether one or more
than one).
WHEREAS. the State has established a policy of perpetuating the
Town of Columbia as nearly as possible in its original condition as a
typical California goldmining town: and,
WHEREAS, said State has found that the foregoing policy can best
be carried out by having actual habitation and normal town life carried
on by certain of the present citizens now occupying premises in said
Town of Columbia; and,
WHEREAS, the State Park Commission has found that the property hereinafter described is situated in the old business section of the
Town of Columbia and is of sufficient historic significance to be· preserved as a building representative of the early mining days of said
community; and
WHEREAS. Concessionaire is prepared to erect and maintain a
replica of the original Masonic Hall at the Town of Columbia,
W1TNESSETH:
That State, pursuant to the authority and in accordance with Section
5003 of the Public Resources Code of the State of California, and in
consideration of (a) the payment by Concessionaire of the rental hereafter set forth; and ( b) the performance by Concessionaire of the
covenants, terms, and conditions hereunder agreed to be performed by
said Concessionaire, does hereby grant certain rights and privileges to
use all those certain premises situated in the Town of Columbia State
Park, unit of the California State Park System, located in the County
of Tuolumne, State of California, described as follows, to wit:
Lot 3 of Block 17 of the Townsite of Columbia, as per the
Official Map thereof.
together with all buildings and improvements thereon.

the following covenants and conditions, to wit:

Example No. I-The lectures are now given to the candidate when
he is in a confused state of mind and unable to derive the most from
them. Why not eliminate the giving. of the lecture after the First and
Third degrees until at the end of a Master's year and at that time have
the master assemble those candidates raised during his year and then
render a revised lecture that will cover the three degrees.
Example No. 2-Under present masonic law a Master is prohibited
from spending more than 20% of the Lodge's income for entertainment,
neither is a lodge permitted to support any endeavor that will bring
into the treasury funds for further entertainment purposes. With fewer
candidates and the amount required to cover dues remitted a master is
faced with a difficult problem of maintaining interest.
With full appreciation of the difficulties to be met in complying
with the above suggestions and yet believing their adoption will be
beneficial to masonry in meeting the changed conditions of today, I
ask that this be properly channeled so as to secure it's adoption.

REPORT OF GRAND TREASURER

Pursuant to recommendation and appropriate legislation, Past
Master Paul Pflueger was appointed and installed as Assistant Grand
Treasurer. It was the intent that the appointment of such officer should
be based on successful investment experience. That the recommendation
was sound has been demonstrated by the valuable services of Brother
Pflueger, based on his investment experience. He has been most interested and assiduous in making recommendations and in cooperation
with the Grand Treasurer, as this report will indicate.
At the annual communication in 1948 attention was invited to the
exceedingly large percentage of government bonds in portfolios, with the
observation that that situation could not be corrected even if desirable
without the amendment of the regulations governing investments. This
was followed by the comment in substance that circumstances may
develop the advisibility of extending the scope of qualified investments,
and that, if so, appropriate legislation should be considered. We have
now concluded that it is timely that consideratian be given to such extension of qualified investments by adopting what is designated "The
Prudent Man Rule" as related thereto. To that end there is appended
hereto as Exhibit No. 1 a monograph of pertinent facts prepared by
the Assistant Grand Treasurer, with the recommendation that the entire
tubject be considered by the Committee on Finances and the Committee
en Investment of Endowment Funds.
It is the Grand Treasurer's recommendation that the rule be adopted
and made applicable to all such funds as are now limited to federal,
county. state and municipal securities legal for savings banks. (Secs.
655 and 721 ).
Jn addition to the fact that such is a sound rule of investment, as has
been demonstrated by many so-called balanced funds, we should not
continue to be a cog in the machinery of government adapted, at least
at present, to the policy of maintaining low rates of interest by artiflcial
controls. Also, Gr~nd Lodge would be contributing to the business and
industrial welfare of the country by making funds available for productive use by successfully operated private enterprises.
Also, after mature consideration-a long time-I am of the opinion
that lodges should be allowed greater autonomy and not be circumscribed with unreasonable restrictions. To that end it is our recommendation that with respect to investments in securities, the Prudent Man
Rule be made applicable to lodges.
In relation to the recommendatioX:s herein made with respect to the
Prudent Man Rule, in these modern days all investors have access to
statistical and other departments of banks concerned with investments,
where impartial and sound advice may be obtained as a service available
to customers. After October 1, 1949, there will be no "legal for savings
bank" list in California, which in itself seems to make it incumbent on
Grand Lodge to clarify investment of funds by lodges.

For Fiscal Year Ending July 31, 1949
To the Brethren of Grand Lodge:
For your information, the Grand Treasurer describes the course of
funds received from all sources. Receipts from the several lodges are
deposited by the Grand Secretary to the credit of the Grand Treasurer
in the account maintained for that purpose with the American Trust
Company. In this account there is also deposited during the year s.uch
other items as bequests, proceeds of sales, etc. which are transmitted
directly to the Grand Secretary's office for the account of the Endowment Fund, the Masonic Homes or the Grand Lodge.
At the end of each month there is withdrawn from the above reservoir account, the total of amounts belonging to the Grand Lodge, the
Endowment Fund, the Masonic Homes General Fund or to any of the
14 special funds of the Masonic Homes in order that such items may be
deposited in the separate accounts of these funds.
Income from investments is received by the Anglo California National Bank under the existing custodial arrangements. Such receipts
together with collections on notes, proceeds of sales and other items
transmitted directly to the bank are deposited by it in the account of.
the particular fund involved.
For purposes of routine operation, money is transferred . from the
main accounts carried by the Grand Treasurer to "Operating Fund
Accounts" maintained under different signature arrangements. Appropriations and other special items (such as payments on contracts in
connection with homes construction ) are paid by means of checks drawn
by the Grand Treasurer on the proper accounts.
The magnitude of these transactions is indicated by the figures of
total income and disbursements tabulated in the auditor's "Consolidated
Statement,"The extent of these transactions is evidenced by the fact that
it involves 14 commercial accounts and 13 savings accounts, maintained
in the American Trust Company, Anglo California National Bank,
Bank of America, Bank of California. Central Bank of Oakland. Covina
National Bank, Crocker First National Bank. Security First National
Bank of Los Angeles, and Wells Fargo Bank and Union Trust Company.
The Grand Treasurer has endeavored from time to time, in cooperation with the Grand Secretary, to arrange the respective reports
so that "He who runs may read." It will be the endeavor this year to
further clarify the reports so that reconciliation will be less complicated.
In accordance with recommendation at the previous annual communication, expenditures by the Grand Secretary from the revolving fund
are subject to current monthly audit by professional auditors.

The Prudent Man Rule
The Prudent Man Rule was first laid down at the 1830 sitting of the
Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, and was at that time known as
the "Massachusetts Trustees' Investment Rule."
The original state, Massachusetts, promulgated the rule by court
decision, and subsequently many other states passed statutes embodying
the rule. In passing such statutes practically all have followed the
original 1830 decision of Mr. Justice Putnam, the sum and substance of
which is as follows (and which has been embodied in the Model
Prudent-Man Investment Statute prepared by the Committee on Fiduciary Legislation of the American Bankers Associati~n Trust Division):
The Model Prudent-Man Investment Statute
1.
"Section 1. In acquiring, investing, reinvesting, exchanging,
2.
retaining, selling and managing property for the benefit of
3.
another, a fiduciary shall exercise the judgment and care
i.
under the circumstances then prevailing, which men of
prudence,
5.
discrefion and intelligence exercise in the management of
their
own affairs, not in regard to speculation but in regard to the
6.
7.
permanent disposition of their funds, considering the probable
8.
income as well as the probable safety of their capital. Within
9.
the limitations of the foregoing standard, a fiduciary is
·

to ac::quire and retain every kind of property real. personal or
10.

but not

cretion and intelligence acquire or retain for their own
account.

( 1ic. time and without regard to its stability for original purchase.
(Note-the foregoing addition to Section 1 is included for consideration
of those states which desire particular treatment of the retention of

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

The following comments are taken from a bulletin of the Trust Divis·
ion, American Bankers Association, "The Prudent-Man Rule for Trust
Investment," in which the Model Statute is set forth. This booklet is
the work of the Committee on Fiduciary Legislation of the Trust Division and was largely contrived and written by Mayo Adams Shattuck.
Mr. Shattuck is a member of the Boston Bar, former President Massachusetts Bar Association, State Board of Bar Examiners, Massachusetts
Annotator for the Restatement of Trusts, and a widely known author
and lecturer on fiduciary subjects.

"It is to be observed that the model statute embraces all aspects of
fiduciary administration. It is not limited to the act of investment; it
most certainly is not designed merely to allow the purchase of corporate
bonds, debentures, preferred and common stocks. It seeks to bring into
the law of any jurisdiction in which it is enacted the elasticand beneficent
rule which obtains in states which follow Massachusetts. It imposes
an objective standard and it uses the precise language of Mr. Justice
Putman in Harvard College v. Amory, 1830. The heart of Harvard
College v. Amory lies in its next to last paragraph, viz.: 'Trustees are
justly and uniformly considered favorably, and it is of great importance
to bereaved families and orphans, that they should not be held to make
good, losses in the depreciation of stocks or the failure of the capital
itself, which they held in trust. provided they conduct themselves honestly and discreetly and carefully, according to the existing circumstances, in the discharge of their trusts. If this were held otherwise, no
prudent man would run the hazard of losses which might happen without any neglect or breach of good faith.'
"The aim of the model statute is to mold the law so that prudent
men will be freed from all manner of artificial shackles and liabilities in
the administration of the property of others. It is eminently fitting and
practically necessary that trustees be held (a) to the strictest possible
standard of fidelity; and ( b) the fairest and most fruitful, not the strictest, possible standard of care".
In that original decision the sentence is also included: "Do what
you will, the capital is at hazard."
'

"This is the so-called Massachusetts Trustees' Rule: observe that
it expresses a two·fold objective; a consideration of the probable income, as well as the probable safety of the capital. It should not be
supposed that it is right to emphasize one of these objections at the
expense of the other, particularly if the one selected for emphasis is
the precise one which the founder of a trust would have expected to be
of lesser importance. The income is important, safety, even if there be
such a thing, is not everything.''

I. INVESTMENT SCOPE GENERALLY
From Trusts and Estates, February, 1949, page 74.
"The latest report of the Comptroller of Currency shows that 24%
of the total investments of $15,449,506,445 of living and court trusts
administered by national banks alone is in equities.
"The actual amount doubtless exceeds this substantially, since many
trust equity investments are reported on original received valuations
or even on nominal or $1 per share valuations for no par stock".
"In addition the trust departmens of state banks and trust companies
administer more trust funds than do national banks, and follow similar
investment practices. In some Prudent-Man Rule states, like Massachusetts, the proportion of investments in equities is about 50% and
even outside the Prudent-Man Rule states, a large percentage of trust
instruments under which trustees now operate give discretion to invest
in stocks as well as bonds or other legals."

"Now, in another accounting proceeding brought by Central Hanover Bank & Trust Co., the Court of Appeals has not only upheld the
constitutionality of the law but has also sustained the Surrogate's jurisdiction over common funds in which living trusts are participants.
"Except for a possible appeal to the United States Supreme Court
on the due process question the major legal problems of common trust
funds have now been resolved and the way is open to their efficient
and extensive operation. Maintenance of such funds by 64 banks in 22
states has demonstrated their investment and operating advantages,
both to beneficiaries and trustee.
"Since the present decision was handed down on June 2, a poll indicates that a number of New York trust institutions, which had deferred
action pending a final decision, are soon to inaugurate common funds
of the discretionary type. Of ten of the larger City banks not already
operating funds, four expect to start by the fall while only two do not
anticipate the need for their establishment. It was also pointed out that
the latest quarterly accounting date in the year has a tax accounting
advantage as the date for starting a fund.
"Several upstate banks also anticipate the creation of funds in the
near future, and this decision may well give impetus to establishment
of common trust funds elsewhere.''

II. "CAN INVEST IN STOCKS"
From Trusts and Estates, July, 1949.
"For the first time District of Columbia fiduciaries accountable to
the District Court will be permitted to invest in preferred and common
stocks, according to a recent announcement by Chief Judge Bolitha J.
Laws. The recommendation for this liberalization of Local Civil Rule
23 governing trust investments was made by Register of Wills Theodore Cogswell, who with the assistance of Standard & Poor' s will
compile the list of equities to be added to the legal bond investments.
"Only stocks listed on the New York (Stock and Curb), Washington or Philadelphia-Baltimore Stock Exchanges will be eligible, and
no more than 40% of the total value of a trust fund may be invested
therein, with a maximum of 10% in any one corporation."
Ill. "COMMON TRUST ISSUE RESOLVED"
From Trusts and Estates, July, 1949.
"The question of due process in giving notice of accountings to
beneficiaries of common trust funds, raised by a 1947 Surrogate's
Court decision, has now been settled by the favorable ruling of the New
York Court of Appeals, that State's highest tribunal.
"The Monroe County Surrogate's holdings would have imposed ·a
heavy burden of expense on trusts by requiring personal service and
special guardians for all beneficiaries non sui juris. In declaring unconstitutional New York's statute providing for service by publication
and appointment of one special guardian for income beneficiaries and
one for principal, this case had been a major deterrent to establishment
of new funds, in view of the basic issue raised.

IV.

Excerpts from "CURRENT PROCEDURES EMPLOYED BY
INVESTMENT MANAGERS OF ENDOWMENT FUNDS
OF EDUCATIONAL, RELIGIOUS, FRATERNAL AND
PHILANTHROPIC ORGANIZATION" by Henry J. Simonson, Jr., President National Securities & Research Corporation
(Aug. 1949)
"The following report is based upon a survey tqat was made to
determine the present investment procedures, methods, and types of
securities used by the managers of the investments of institutional
funds. Spcial inquiry was made as to the use of any type of formula
plan in timing changes in the percentages of the value of the respective
funds that are invested in bonds and in stocks from time to time.
"The educational, religious, fraternal and philanthropic organizations contacts all have sizable funds-the minimum amount of any one
fund being in excess of $2 million, the maximum amount over $200
million, and the aggregate of all funds in excess of $3 billions. Data
was· received from over 100 such institutions, and the following represents a factual summary of the information received.
"MANAGEMENT RESPONSIBILITY. Of the institutions reporting, the majority indicated that the management of their funds is
delegated by the Board of Directors (or Governors) to an executive
committee, investment committee or finance committee. A number of
the institutions employ independent investment counsel firms or use the

62

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

services of banks or trust companies as investment advisors. In other
instances, the Board of Governors or Board of Directors make investment management decisions without outside professional aid. It appears,
except where the value of the funds is high in the millions, that little or
no full time office staff of investment analysts and statisticians is
maintained.
"TYPE OF INVESTMENTS. Twelve per cent of the reporting
institutions stated that their investment funds are confined exclusively
to government, state, municipal, and high-grade corporate bonds. Of
this group, it is apparent that a number, seeking greater income (where
permitted by law to do so) are considering the adoption of a more liberal
policy that would provide for investments of a certain portion of their
funds in high grade preferred and common stocks.
"Of the institutions reporting that their investments are in both
bonds and stocks, the percentage varies from 50% to 80% in bonds,
with an average of about 60%. Although a number of the institutions
have a small percentage of their funds in medium grade bonds, the
great majority favor governments and high-grade corporates.
"Preferred stocks of the better grade represent from 15% to 20%
of portfolio assets and except for relatively small amounts held in
cash for current needs, the remainder of the assets are invested in
high-grade income producing equities.
"It is apparent that institutional policies and objectives vary to
such a wide degree that the most desirable percentages to be invested
in bonds or stocks at various levels during cyclical movements of stock
prices would necessarily be so different as to require individual formula
plans in a great many instances. Certain institutions with a more liberal
policy as to funds being invested in equities could have a narrower range
for changes based upon equity price fluctuations than those of the more
conservative funds. Nevertheless the idea of changing the weightings
of portfolios as to bonds and stocks appears to be an outstanding
consideration of most institutions except those, of course, that are required to limit portfolios exclusively to bonds."
