Statement read by Herbert Hoover at the Hearing Before San Jose
.
Superior Court, February 10, 1936.
"The trustees of Stanford University. in consequence ~f cert~m
financial policies, are now confronted with a grave prob~em m the. mvestments of the University endowment. That problem .1s the. ~oss1ble
protection of the endowment by investment of the fu~ds m. equities such
as common stocks and real estate instead of exclusively 1n bonds and
mortgages as hitherto. The trustees of sister universities ~ver the country are many of them already taking action to. protect. t~e1r endowments
by investments of at least part of their funds mto equities. The trustees
of Stanford are in need of some clarification of these powers to make
such investments.
"The problem has only recently arisen. For fifty years both prudence and wisdom have caused the trustees to invest the endowment
now amounting to some $24,000,000 in seasoned bonds and first mortgages. Not only has the original endowment been maintained intact but

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

65

entirely aside from new gifts the trustees have by wise investment increased the capital. Common stocks or real estate or other equities have
not been purchased because of the greater risks involved.
"The devaluation of the dollar, the widespread bank credit inflation
and the possible menace of currency inflation are the new factors with
which the trustees must deal. The theory of the devaluation of the
dollar is that it will increase prices of commodities. thus causing a rise
in the cost of living and necessitating an increase of salaries. The theory
also implies a transfer of values from the bond holder to the common
stock holder. The practical effect should be to increase the cost of operating the institution. In such case. if our income is to remain fixed, we
shall need either to employ less faculty or reduce the range of instruction or reduce the number of students.
"The bank credit inflation is a factor independent of devaluation
and has already caused a large drop in interest rates. More than twothirds of our investments are subject to call or mature in the next five
years. and if these interest rates continue we shall probably lose about
one-fourth of our endowment income. This would again necessitate
reducing the service which our institution gives to youth, even were
devaluation not in action.
"The question of currency inflation is one of constant discussion in
government and the press. and while not at the moment more than a
menace. it is one which cautious trusteeship should be in position to
meet. The record of similar institutions in Europe under currency inflation is before us, where their endowments are largely wiped out.
"Experience in similar occ~sions shows that common stocks and real
estate and other equities ultimately rise in value somewhat in proportion to the increase of devaluation or inflation. While common stocks,
real estate and other equities are subject to risk, yet this may be the
lesser risk than bonds and mortgages.
"The gravity of the matter is clear when we remember that Stanford
has trained over 15,000 yo.uth, a ·large part of them without means of
their own, and that a community of nearly ten thousand people are
largely dependent upon the institution.
"Whatever view we take of the situation, the trustees should have
the freedom to protect the endowment as best they can."

MEMORANDUM OPINION-IN THE SUPERIOR COURT OF
THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA, IN AND FOR THE COUNTY
OF SANTA CLARA- In the Matter of the Petition of The Board of
Trustees of the Leland Stanford University for a determination and
confirmation of its powers with respect to the investment of Trust
Funds.
"Petitioner herein seeks a judicial determination of its powers of
investment of trust funds, particularly with respect to the investment

66

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

of such funds in debentures and shares of stock in corporations. The
proceeding is authorized by the provisions of Act 8701 , approved Febru·
ary 10, 1903 (Stat. 1903, p. 9).
. .
.
"These two questions are presented for determination here.
.
"1st: Are the petitioners forbidden by the express terms of the
trust, as now in force. to invest any of the trust funds in debentures or
stocks of corporations?
"2nd : If not so expressly forbidden. is the making ~f such inves~·
ments inhibited by anything in the nature of the trust itself'. or their
obligations or responsibilities as trustees of the trust properties?
"A careful examination of the grants. amendments and acts, bearing
upon these trusts, fails to disclose any definite pro~ibition of such in·
vestments; and I am of the opinion that the first question may confidently
be answered in the negative.
"The second question is approached with somewhat less confidence.
"While the general rule, laid down in this state. as well as in ~ost
other jurisdictions, with relation to the obligation of a trustee, requir~s
that he exercise only the same measure of diligence that a man of ordi.
nary prudence would be expected to exercise in the care of his own
property under the same circumstances, it would s.eem, on careful con·
sideration, that this statement fails to take into account the element of
speculation. A man of ordinary prudence might well be expected to
speculate, at times, with his own property. Indeed. most men do so.
But a trustee, by the very nature of his obligation, is inhibited from subjecting the trust fund to the risks of specula~ve enterpris~s. Because
of this principle, and perhaps stimulated by divers regulations enacted
for the guidance of investments by banks a~d other st~te·c?ntrolled
institutions. a wide-spread belief has grown m the public mmd . .t?at
trust funds may not properly be invested in other than public securities,
or well secured bonds, notes and mortgages. This view was examined
and discarded by the learned justice who wrote the opinion in Harvard
College, et all vs. Amory, more than an hundred years ago. A~d events
occurring in the financial world, during the present generation, ha~e
afforded many striking examples of the wisdom of Justice Putnam s
comments in that famous case. It may be conceded that in normal times,
a bond or secured obligation has a greater quality of security for invest·
ment than private corporation stocks or debentures. and is less subject
to fluctuation in value; but it is likewise true, as we have had recent
occasion to observe. that there are conditions under which even public
securities. as well as secured obligations of other kinds. suffer serious
depression in value. In such instances both income a~d capital a~e
jeopardized or lost. Experience has also shown us that investments m
shares of private corporations may. and often do, afford a greater meas·
ure of safety, combined with a larger income yield, than investments
in public securities or bonds in the same period. It would. therefore

·~

67

seem to be an unreasonable rule. to require a possibly unsafe invest·
ment. with little return. and exclude a safer, or equally safe one, pro·
ducing a greater return. And, particularly is this true of a trust whose
essential purpose would be defeated, if. the income from the trust funds
be withdrawn or substantially curtailed.
"A heavy burden of responsibility rests upon trustees, in the ad·
JDinistration of the trust funds. They are charged with the exercise of
the highest degree of good faith: while they are required to exercise
only the same degree of care, in investment, that a man of ordinary
prudence would be expected to exercise in the management of his own
property. under similar circumstances. they are, at the same time, forbidden to enter into any transactions wherein the element of speculation
is obviously present: and, finally, they are charged with the duty of so
managing the trust property as to accomplish, insofar as the same is
possible, the primary purposes for which the trust was created. Some
trusts are concerned principally with the integrity of the corpus of the
trust property-the income therefrom being of a secondary considera·
tion. It would be safe to say that a great majority of existing trusts are
of that character. But there are trusts whose existence depends upon
the income derived from the trust property, without which income the
real purpose of the trust would fail. Stanford University is one of the
latter character. The trust there created was for the primary purpose of,
not only establishing a school of higher education, but of maintaining
and continuously operating the same. The trust funds came into the
hands of the trustees for those purposes. Unless these funds can be made
to earn sufficient income to carry on the operation of the school, there
would be a total failure of the trust itself. The preservation of the corpus,
intact, without sufficient income, would be idle and meaningless. Vacant
study halls and a deserted campus would not constitute a university.
It is the duty of these trustees to maintain the corpus of the trust prop·
erties intact. if they can do so, without suspending or seriously curtailing
the operation of the university; but, in the final analysis, it is their
primary duty to see to it that the educational work is carried on as de·
signed by the founders of the trust.
·
"In the case of In Re: Buhl's Estate, 178, N . W. 651, the Court, in
dealing with a trust, which was one of that character wherein the pres·
ervation of the corpus was the primary consideration, and the income a
secondary one, held that the trustees might properly make an investment
of trust funds in dividend-paying stock and interest-paying bonds of
a private corporation, when such corporation has acquired. by reason
of its property and the prudent management of its affairs for a consid·
erable period of time, such a reputation for permanence and stability as
to command universal confidence. The Court there, in a modified form,
followed the Massachusetts rule, first laid down in the Harvard College
case. cited supra. If this measure of the power of the trustees be the
proper one in the case of such a class of trusts-and so it seems to be--

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

68

69

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

there should be no hesitancy in applying it to the character of trust here
under consideration. And this would appear to apply with greater
reason in times when depressed monetary values and defaulted or
repudiated public commitments have raised grave dou~ts in t~~ minds
of prudent business men of the ultimate safety of public securities. To
quote from Justice Putnam, in the Harvard College ca~e, . .
" 'There is one consideration much in favor of investing in the
stock of private corporations. They are amenable to the law. The
stockholder may pursue them, and compel them or their officers to
do justice. But the government can only be supplicated.'
"The examination of many other authorities and opinions, whose
citation need not be made here, has served to confirm these views on
the subject in hand.
"I am of the opinion that the petitioners may lawfully and properly
make investment from trust funds coming to their hands, in bonds,
debentures and shares of stock of private corporations which are wellmanaged, and have enjoyed for a considerable period of time such a
reputation for permanence and stability that they comman.d th~ gene~al
confidence of careful and intelligent investors: and may likewise so invest in other generally recognized forms of investment providing and
adequate rate of interest and affording reasonable assuranc~ of stable
values. This is not intended to exclude other powers of investment
heretofore exercised or decreed to them.
"The Court's decree will be entered in accordance herewith.''
(Signed) WM. F. JAMES
Presiding Judge
Dated Feb. 25, 1936

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
I have the honor to present to you herewith my Eighth Annual
Report as your Grand Secretary.
We have again been fortunate in having the complete cooperation
of the Secretaries of the Lodges and of the staff with the result that a
very satisfactory year's work has been accomplished.
GENERAL OFFICES

At the last Communication of Grand Lodge we requested and received an appropriation of $5,000.00 for the purpose of rearranging,
remodelling and redecorating the Grand Lodge Offices. Plans were
prepared and submitted to the Grand Master. With his approval we
undertook the work during the past summer, and it is now completed
and operating efficiently. The total cost was $4,894.05.
DUPLICATE CHARTER

Georgetown Lodge No. 25 lost its original charter in a disastrous
flre and requested the issuance of a duplicate. The Grand Master ap·
proved this, and at his direction we had an exact.duplicate of the early
charter engrossed. This made it possible to have reproductions made
so that we are now in a position to issue actual duplicates of early
charters in other cases of disaster.
We cannot again too strongly urge that every Lodge have its
original charter photostated.
ENDOWMENT FUND OVERPAYMENT

A.F.E. Irwin Lodge No. 645 in remitting contributions received for
the Endowment Fund forwarded $170.00 in excess of contributions
collected. The Lodge did not immediately detect the error, and it was
not until after the close of the flscal year that the Lodge called it to the
attention of the Grand Secretary and requested a return of the excess
payment.
The Grand Secretary is of the opinion that he has no authority to
withdraw funds from the Endowment Fund for the purpose of correcting
the error. He does, however, believe the money should be returned to
the Lodge, and he, therefore, asks the authority of Grand Lodge to
reimburse the Lodge in the amount of $170.00 during the 1:Urrent fiscal
year.

WESTCHESTER LODGE U. D.

Westchester Lodge U. D. was instituted June 18, 1949, just six
weeks before the close of the fiscal year. Due to its brief existence I
recommended to the Grand Master that the Lodge be not required to
pay the per capita tax, which recommen·dation was approved by him.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge.
Free and Accepted Masons of California:
Again, it becomes my privilege to account to the Grand Lodge for the
activities of the Grand Lecturer and the Ritual Committee for the
Masonic year just closing.
Masonry continues to be on the march and our jurisdiction is now
at its peak, both in total membership and in the number of Lodges on its
roster.
Reports furnished by 11 9 of our 123 Inspectors indicate that the
Lodges are prosperous and busy. The officer material is predominately
on the favorable side, both in ritualistic perfection and in administrative
ability.
During the course of the year, the Inspectors have conducted innum~
erable schools of instruction and have traveled thousands of miles in the
pursuit of their duties.
The number of new Lodges in process of formation has added an
additional activity to the Inspectors involved. Under our law, they are
required to certify to the ritualistic ability of each set of proposed
officers. This means, in many cases, that the entire group must be
coached and taught until they become proficient. At times this may run
into several months of constant attention.
There is now a uniformity in all the work of the Lodges and a pride
in its exactness which excites the admiration, not only of our own
brethren, but also of those from other jurisdictions who happen to
visit us. This is the result of having made the language of our work
into a grammatical. connected, consistent and complete text; and further,
perhaps more, the result is due to the faithfulness and energy of the
Inspectors of the various districts who, by reason of their annual visits
to the Grand Lodge and the schools of instruction, are able to keep
the correct work fresh in their own memories and carry it home to their
Lodges. By this means the most remote districts away off in the recesses
of our rugged mountains and mining regions are enabled to share equally
with the brethren of our great plains and fertile valleys the knowledge
and beauties of our ritual.
The paragraph above was taken from the 1904 report of Grand
Lecturer William H. Edwards. It was true then and it is more so today.
Our inspectors have a long record of faithful performance and the words
reported by Brother Edwards are as deserving at this moment .as they
were in the years of long ago.
During the past year, the Inspectors have met with their Assistant

the functions of an Inspector.

RITUAL COMMITTEE

During the year, the Ritual Committee has been in regular communication by mail and at each of the division meetings at least four members
were in attendance. In addition to completely reviewing the ritual at
these gatherings, other matters of import were studied and clarified.
Our final meeting was held on August 6th and 7th at which time the
ritual was again reviewed. The following matters were also discussed.
ASSISTANT GRAND TREASURER

The creation of the office of Assistant Grand Treasurer requires the
adoption of new language for the Grand Lodge Opening, Closing and
Installation Ceremonies. In preparing the language to cover this office,
we have followed the existing ritual. We are cognizant of the fact that
a Committee on Grand Lodge Ritual will present a report later at this
communication. Whatever recommendation which they may make can
be covered in a supplemental report.
OPENING AND CLOSING CEREMONY

We recommend first that the Assistant Grand Treasurer be seated
on the right of the Grand Master next to the Grand Treasurer similar
to the arrangement of the Assistant Grand Secretary and the Grand
Secretary. Also that he take his 'place in the procession according to

MONITOR AND OFFICERS' MANUAL

The Monitor and Officers' Manual as now used provides for a
ritual to cover the Reception of Grand Lodge Officers. On page 59
provision is made for all Grand Lodge Officers with the exception of
Inspectors who are entitled to "Grand Honors" on their official visits.
We recommend that at the next printing of the Monitor and
Officers' Manual. the following language be inserted on Page 59 immediately following the language now in brackets relating to the use of
the phrase "Of the Grand Lodge of California."
'*' Inspectors
The Worshipful ............................ ,
Inspector of the ....................... .
Masonic District, desires admission.
CONCLUSION

During the early part of this year, it was necessary for me to curtail
my activities due to illness. I reluctantly had to cancel some of my
engagements which had been arranged prior to my indisposition. I
regret exceedingly any inconvenience which I may have caused by the
upsetting of plans. I missed greatly the opportunity to participate in
the very enjoyable Masonic gatherings which I had been accustomed
to attend.
During this period, our ritualistic activities did not suffer because
of the very fine cooperation of the Assistant Grand Lecturers who have
carried on in very excellent style. It is comforting to know that here in
California we have four capable Assistant Grand Lecturers who are
uniform in ritual and in complete harmony with the Grand Lecturer.
Each of them is well equipped and qualified to act for the Grand Lecturer. It is a tribute to the far sighted brethren who conceived our
present plan of administering the important work of ritualistic instruction. In particular, we should be thankful that Past Grand Master
James B. Gist had the determination to put into operation the divisional
method of instruction and supervision during his year as Grand Master.
I express my heartfelt thanks to my associates on the Ritual Committee, to our M.W. Grand Master, to the V.W. Grand Secretary and
his fine staff and to all who have made this position so enjoyable and
pleasant.
Respectfully submitted,
ARTHUR M. WARREN

Grand Lecturer
Adopted.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LoDGES

Past Grand Master Hervey made a partial report for the Committee
on Policy and General Purposes.
Your Committee has had under consideration the various applications for recognition of foreign Grand Lodges and it is prepared at this
time to report as to the following:
GRAND LoDGE OF LowER CALIFORNIA

The Grand Lodge of Lower California, of which Ricardo C. Salazar, Avenida Mexico No. 120, Tijuana, Lower California, is the Grand
Master and Alfonso Gomez Pereyra is Grand Secretary, and whose
headquarters are at Tijuana, Lower California.
_This Grand Lodge was constituted on January 5th, 1933 by symbolic Lodges Precursora No. 33 of Mexicali, Ignacio Zaragoza No. 24
of Tijuana and Occidental No. 226 of Ensenada, all in Lower California, all three being dependents of the Grand Lodge Valle de Mexico
and now, after sixteen years of regular Masonic life, they have under
their jurisdiction twelve subordinate Lodges, with a total membership
·
of 700.
The Grand Lodge meets three times a year at Tiajuana, a city with
a population of from 40,000 to 50,000 people and the Lodges have drawn
their membership from the leaders in the community. The Grand Master
is an industrialist and the manager-owner of the Telephone Company
'
Light & Power and Ice Company plant.
We. have examined the constitution of this Grand Lodge and find
its purposes and practices conform to the requirements and standards
set up by us for the recognition of foreign powers. This Grand Lodge
has been recognized by 7 Provincial Grand Lodges of Canada, by the
Grand Lodges of England, Ireland and Scotland, 7 Grand Lodges in
Australia, 19 Grand Lodges in the United States, by practically all the
recognized Grand Lodges in Central and South America and by all the
regular Grand Lodges of the Republic of Mexico.
Your Committee is of the opinion that this Grand Lodge should be
recognized by the Grand Lodge of California and we recommend that
such recognition be given to it.
GRAND LoDGE OF NUEVO LEON

The Grand Lodge of the State of Nuevo Leon, whose address is
Apertado 30 Monterrey, Nuavo Leon.
This Grand Lodge was duly and regularly constituted on June 24th,
1905 and is an independent, self-governing body with entire and undisputed jurisdiction over the symbolic Lodges within its jurisdiction,

90

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

which is embraced within the political boundaries of the State of Nuevo
Leon, Mexico, and is sovereign and supreme in all its territory.

"CALIFORNIA'S CENTENNIALS RECALL EARLY
MASONIC HISTORY"
JOSEPH R. KNOWLAND, SR., Grand Orator

It has 46 active Symbolic Lodges, with an aggregate membership
of 3170. The present Grand Master is M. W. Eutimio Cisneros and
Esteban Leal Villareal is Grand Secretary. The ritual of the Grand
Lodge is fundamentally in accord with the ancient landmarks, customs
and usages of the Craft, which involve Monotheism, the Three Great
Lights on the Altar while at labor, secrecy, the Symbolism of the Operative Art, the division into three symbolic degrees, the legend of the
Third Degree. It makes Masons of men only, it is non-sectarian, nonpolitical and its dominant purposes are charitable, benevolent and educational.
The regularity of the Grand Lodge can be traced back directly to
the Grand Lodge of England, via the Grand Lodge "Unida Mexicana"
of the State of Vera Cruz and the Grand Lodge of Cuba.

It holds fraternal community with the Grand Lodges of Texas,
Oklahoma, Louisiana, Arizona, Kentucky, New Hampshire and Massachusetts and with the York Grand Lodge of Mexico.
Your Committee is of the opinion that this Grand Lodge would be
justifled in recognizing the Grand Lodge of the State of Nuevo Leon
and so recommends.
By separate action each of the above recommendations was unanimously adopted.
Brother Hervey reported that study was being continued relative to

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Past Grand Masters. Grand Lodge
Officers, Distinguished Guests and Members of Grand Lodge:
I have deemed it to be most appropriate at a time when this state is
commemorating one of the three years of outstanding historical events,
that I should recall early Masonic history associated with California's
centennials. In 1947, through legislative mandate and the appointment
of a state-wide centennials commission, · California pledged itself to
fittingly celebrate the gold discovery in 1948, gold rush days in 1949,
and in 1950 the admission of this territory to statehood. At the request
of Governor Earl Warren, I accepted the chairmanship of the Centennials Commission.
During 1948 there was officially commemorated at Coloma the gold
discovery by James W. Marshall-a history-making event with ramifications that were far-reaching in their effect upon state and national
history. Speciflcally, the added gold supply enabled this government
to finance the unfortunate and prolonged struggle between the states.
This historic rush across the plains, with its attendant hazards, emphasized the necessity for the building of a transcontinental railroad, while
those argonauts who came by water and crossed the fever-infested
isthmus, or rounded the treacherous Cape Horn, accelerated the movement which eventually resulted in the construction of the Panama Canal.
The present year, 1949, recalls the stirring gold rush days and the
establishment of stable government for California through the drafting
of a constitution at Monterey. This highly dramatic gathering at Colton
Hall, originally constructed as a school house and public meeting place,
was last month most successfully commemorated. During a nine day
period, with record crowds in attendance, a most colorful pageant with
a cast of 700 was presented, entitled "Beginners of Statehood.'' Impressive ceremonies were also held at Colton Hall.
There were forty-eight delegates in the Constitutional Convention,
hailing from fourteen states, with seven native Californians.
In recalling the history of this memorable gathering it is most noteworthy that it was called during the height of the gold rush excitement
when the quest for riches was the objective of most arrivals. Sixteen
of the delegates, about one-third, had come west following the discovery
of gold by Marshall. All of these forty-eight participants, those who
came recently and the earlier arrivals, obviously must have been inspired
by .the thought that in life there are things more precious than goldlove of country, support of constitutional government and maintenance
of law and order.

This assemblage organized on September 3, 1849, and at the conclusion of their work on October 13th, presented a constitution that
reflected high credit upon their deliberations and no doubt expedited in
Congress the admission of California as the 31st state in the American
Union.
It was a gathering that obviously was attractive to Masons. As yet
no Grand Lodge had been established in California. The few Masonic
Lodges existed by virtue of charters from other states. Regardless of
these conditions, there were nine members of the Craft sitting as delegates, active and influential and wielding an influence far beyond their
numerical strength. They worked generaJly in unison and the record
shows them to have been sound on vital issues. It is significant that
Robert Semple, a Mason, was chosen as chairman. Semple was a tall
Kentuckian, standing six feet eight, and clad in buckskin, his head
adorned by a fox skin cap. He was editor of California's first newspaper,
"The Californian," and was generally credited with being "Ready with
his pen, quick at the type case and true with his rifle."
Among this close working group of nine Masons, four were lawyers,
one of these, Elisha 0. Crosby, I knew when I was a boy in Alameda,
where he officiated as Justice of the Peace.
Thirty-seven years after the constitution was drafted he returned
to Colton Hall and was the last delegate to speak in that historic
convention building. The occasion was the fortieth anniversary of the
raising of the American Flag at Monterey by Commodore John Drake
Sloat, who, by the way, was also a member of the Fraternity.
'
On that historic occasion, Judge Crosby in closing his remarks,
his voice trembling with emotion, said, "Well do I remember that last
day of the sitting, and how we clasped hands as we separated, many of
us for the last time on earth." Then he dramatically uttered this admonition: "In the name of those departed, and the little band that yet
remains, I ask you to take your place to preserve the good we did in
this first step to found a constitutional government in California."
Today, after the passing of a full century since the constitution was
drafted, these words should stimulate all California Masons and good
citizens to continue to be zealous in upholding .and preserving constitutional government.
The other lawyers in the convention were Lansford W. Hastings,
Jamesue Hall Jones and Myron Norton, the latter a member of Stevenson's New York Regiment which was brought to California in 1847.
Jones, 25 years of age, was the youngest of the group.
Jacob D. Hoppe and Abel Stearns were merchants. Rodman M. Price
was a :United States Navy purser who served with Commodore Sloat
and was later governor of New Jersey, while ·Pierre Sansevain was
said to be a viticulturist. Although a Mason, he was not a citizen of
the United States. The average age of this Masonic group was 35

-

93

years. These Masons vigorously championed a public school system
which the convention provided. Chairman Robert Semple stepped from
his chair to raise his voice and lead the successful battle for a cause
which still has the militant support of Masonry in California and
throughout the country.
In the pre-American occupation period and before the gold discovery
a sizable group of the early settlers were sea-faring men while others
were members of those early parties which had crossed the continent
for adventure and colonization. Among these were a number of Masons.
In this group was Peter Lassen whose party brought the first Masonic
Charter and organized Western Star Lodge at Benton City near where
was later located Leland Stanford Ranch. After a short time the Lodge
was removed to Shasta City and when the Grand Lodge of California
was formed in 1850, became Western Star Lodge No. 2.
On May 10, 1948, this lodge celebrated its hundredth anniv:ersary
and many Masons journeyed to this historic town. During Western
Star's centennial over fifty other California Lodges came to Shasta and
the visitors were thrilled, particularly the candidates, as degrees were
conferred in the ancient Lodge Hall. An outstanding event was on the
night that Grand Master Morris E. Ewing of Missouri, the Grand
Lodge of which state, a hundred years before had granted the charter,
came out for a special meeting and presented a bronze plaque to the
lodge. On this eventful night, Grand Master Siems made an official visit.
On May 10 of this year, 1949, at a special session called to fittingly
close the historic year, and with the Lodge Hall crowded, the impressive
ceremony was held by depositing a metal coffer, or casket. This was
sealed after being filled with various documents and mementoes to be
inspected when another full century has passed.
Other members of the craft included in this impressive list were:
Benjamin D. Wilson, known as Don Benito, who came to California
in 1841 and settled on a ranch near the present site of Riverside. He
became mayor of Los Angeles in 1851, and was honored by having Mt.
Wilson named for him.
Colonel Jonathan D. Stevenson of the New York regi~ent which
bore his name was elected as the first Grand Master. when a California
Grand Lodge was organized, and he became the first Grand Master.
John W. Geary, elected first alcalde, or mayor, of San Francisco,
has a most brilliant war record in both the Mexican and Civil Wars, and
was later governor of Pennsylvania.
William Heath Davis, author of "Sixty Years in California"; Kit
Carson, after whom Kit Carson Pass was named, noted scout who
guided General Fremont and other early exploring parties; George C.
Y.ount. for whom Yountville in Napa County was later named; John
Bidwell, an associate of Captain John A. Sutter of Sutter's Fort and
intimately associated with early California history; Pearson B. Redding,

a peak and fort bearing his name; Thomas Fallon who first raised the
American Flag at San Jose, following Sloat's action at Monterey. When
Fallon heard that war had broken out between Mexico and United
States, he recruited a small company of Americans at Santa Cruz,
crossed the. Santa Cruz Mountains and raised the flag on July 13, 1846,

William B. Ide, another California Mason, headed the famous Bear
Flag Party, raised the emblem, since adopted as the California State
Flag, at Sonoma on June 14, 1846, and issued a fiery proclamation as the
head of that party. Later, Ide held many important positions in Colusa
County. The Native Sons of the Golden West yesterday dedicated
a monument in Colusa County to his memory. Sam Kelsey and Henry
Fowler were also members of that famous party.
Abel Stearns, who has already been mentioned as one of the delegates to the Constitutional Convention, was among the first Americans
to settle in California, arriving in 1829 and locating in Los Angeles.
He shipped to Philadelphia Mint in 1842 first gold mined in California. This was found near San Fernando Mission in Los Angeles
County and obtained by Stearns in exchange for merchandise.
Another Mason whose name was associated with early gold discovery and who might have become famous in California history was
Charles R. Bennett whose tombstone in the Masonic Cemetery at Salem,
Oregon, declares him to be the "Discoverer of gold in California."
Bennett came to California with Fremont in 1845. One day while
watering the animals on the American River, El Dorado County, he saw
yellow metal in the water, and as he had had experience in the gold
mines of Georgia, he recognized it to be gold. It was taken to Fremont's
tent, and ordered to be tested by the medical corps. Fremont, informed
that the find was gold, but realizing he was on foreign soil, suggested
they forget the incident.
Bennett also claims to have been with Marshall when gold was discovered at Coloma and contended he was the first to pick up a piece
of the precious metal, informing Marshall it was gold. Whether there
is truth in these statements of Bennett, the fact remains that the man
who gave the discovery to the world which started the great rush of
argonauts westward was James W. Marshall, and to him belongs the
credit.
In all of California history, the most tragic record of hardship, suffering and of heroism is found in the story of the Donner Party. It is
truly epical. Over a century has elapsed since the tragedy. Forty-two
men, women and children lost their lives in the most spectacular catastrophe to befall any group of emigrants' bound for California. In the
party of ninety-three, were 34 children ranging in age from one to fourteen years. Time does not permit a recital of the whole story, but the
part played by Masons is upon this occasion appropriate.

In nearly all the emigrant parties there was a common tie binding
those who belonged to the craft. In the long and trying days during the
haz~dous treks across the plains, or protracted sea voyages .with their
immment dangers, Masons somehow became known to each other and
the families likewise seemed to be aware of the ties that bound certain
individuals.
There were three members of the fraternity who apparently assumed
a certain leadershi.p in the Donner .party. They were William Heill'}'
Eddy, James Frazier Reed, and William McCutchen.
After word reached the outside world that the party was snowbound near Truckee, and starvation and exposure were taking their
toll. several attempts were made to send relief from Sacramento and
San Francisco, Acquilla Glover was a member of one of the first
~onner relief parties which successfully crossed the mountains to bring
aid, and fi?ally reached the snow-bound and starving survivors. It
was Glover s duty to get Mrs. Reed and children ready for the hazardous return trip across the snow-clad Sierra Nevada Mountains.
The relief party had not proceeded more than two miles on the
return trip when it became apparent that the two Reed children were
too small to continue. Recognizing this fact it became Glover's duty
to i~form the moth.er that they must go back to camp. The thought of
lea~mg these. two httle ones with others at such a trying time was a test
which was difficult for any mother to face with unanimity. Worn down
by famine and suffering, the ordeal was doubly severe. Then a thought
Bashed through the mother's mind. "Are you a Mason?" she asked of
Glover. He replied that he was. Placing her hand upon his shoulders
and looking searchingly into his eyes, she asked, "Will you, on your
word as a Master ~.ason, come back for these children, if I leave them
here as you request? There was only one answer for any red-blooded
man and a loyal Mason to give and unhesitatingly he replied, "I willl"
The sorrowing mother, caressing the two little children, started out
on the hazardous journey with firm step and with that confidence which
comes with complete trustfulness.
Little Patty Reed, the daughter, was then eight years old and her
brother, Tommy, younger. The little girl at the parting set an example
to those older for her self-control and fortitude. As the men were taking
her back to camp, controlling her emotions, her voice displaying firmness
she sai~ as she took To~my by the hand, "I am going back to take car~
of my httle brother, but I never expect to see mother again." I knew
Patty years later and talked with her many times after she had become
Mrs. Martha Jane Reed Lewis. She was probably the last survivor and
passed away in 1923.

In early California history, during and following the gold rush days,
there were a galaxy of men, members of the craft, who displayed remarkable traits of character, who were early builders, while a .substantial
number occupied positions of high honor. Time will permit only the
mention of a few.
Jonathan Trumbull Warner, a six-foot-three Connecticut Yankee,
acquired and built up the now famous Warner's Ranch. This landmark
figured prominently in the conquest of California. The famous Butterfield Overland Mail Co. established a stage station there in 1858.
Josiah Belden, one of the public-spirited citizens of San Jose,
who put up the money to supply a state house which burned in later
years, was chosen the city's first mayor.
In the early mining days, William Morris Stewart was a member of
Nevada Lodge of Nevada City, and was later United States Senator
from the state of Nevada. Governor Bigler of California in 1854 appointed Stewart to fill the place of Attorney General during the incumbent's temporary absence from the state. Stewart became a great mining
expert. He secured, while senator, Mark Twain a job as clerk in the
upper house.
A California senator also came out of Nevada Lodge in the person of
Aaron A. Sargent. He was appointed Grand Orator of the order but
senatorial duties prevented his acceptance after he had been elected to
that office. He had previously served as a member of the national House
of Representatives and minister plenipotentiary to Germany.
.
The famous James G. Fair was made a Mason at Bear Mountain
Lodge No. 76 when he was installed as Senior Deacon.
Edwin Markham, author of "The Man With the Hoe," was a member of Acacia Lodge No. 92, in El Dorado County. He was one of the
great contributors to the literary fame of California.
Among the notable members of Henry Clay Lodge of Sutter Creek,
was Alvinza Hayward, miner, banker and millionaire and a great California builder. Hayward was a most enthusiastic Mason and remained
active until his death. He never forgot his fellow members and was
known for his generosity.
From the smallest lodges sometimes come the biggest men. John W.
Mackay, nationally known as one of the big four of Comstock Silver
fame, was a member of Forest Lodge, Forest City, Sierra County.
He has always been reputed as one of the most democratic individuals
and one with great loyalty to friends.

97

Gravel Lodge No. 69 of Camptonville erected a monument in honor
of a noted Californian, Lester Allen Pelton, inventor of the Pelton
waterwheel, who joined the lodge in 1869.
In the heydey of early mining, Lodges were started in many of the
communities which have now become ghost towns. For instance, there
were Masonic Lodges in Illinoistown, and in both Alpha and Omega,
Orleans Flat, Moore's Flat, North Bloomfield, Brandy City, Red Dog,
Spanish Flat, Coloma, where gold was discovered, and Elizabethtown,
now all memories. Then there were Drytown and Fiddletown, Rough
and Ready, and I might continue.
In these early mining towns, fire was a great and continuing hazard.
Few of the Lodges escaped, particularly at a time when insurance was
little known. Some of the Lodges burned at least five times and in many
cases, early records were destroyed. Mariposa Lodge, for instance,
operated under a five mile roving charter. The Lodge had two disastrous fires and many times they had to meet in the hills back of the
town under a tree and elsewhere, the home of a member or in the
county courthouse.
The story of historic Rough and Ready is interesting. It was wiped
out by fire three times and in 1850 the town seceded from the Union
because a Yankee trimmed a Southerner in a mining deal. It was decided
to secede and a call to organize a new state in which no yankees would
be allowed to live. The State of Rough and Ready was the result.
Finally, the new state was dissolved by its organizers in order to
participate in a 4th of July celebration.
Typical of the fate of other early California communities after mining
operations had slackened, and devastating fires taken their toll, Columbia, in Tuolumne County, was fast becoming a ghost town. This "Gem
of the Southern Mines," and once mentioned as a state capital, was taken
over as a state park in 1947 with impressive ceremonies led by Past
Grand Master and Governor Earl Warren and the Park Commission.
All that was left of the Masonic meeting place, Columbia Lodge
No. 28, was an excavation above which had stood a dignified but small
hall within the sacred walls of which early California history was made.
Out of this lodge came a Grand Master, William Abraham Davies,
who was also elected Grand Commander of the Knights Templar. After
consolidation with Tuolumne Lodge No. 8 at Sonora the property was
sold to a mining man who desired to test out the ground as other lots
in the vicinity had yielded paying ore, but this venture failed to pay the
expenses of the effort.
The movement of the Grand Lodge to rebuild the old hall at Columbia is most praiseworthy and has caused much favorable comment
throughout the state. In the years to come when possibly all these

A century ago California was confronted with many problems as it
passed through the transition period, when permanent government was
being established, and law and order gradually maintained, all marking
the beginnings of a great state. Then our population was small, for
when the first legislature convened in San Jose in December, 1849, it
was less than 100,000, while today it is fast approaching the ten million
four hundred thousand mark.
Great national problems face us today as we assume the responsibilities as citizens of one of the largest states in the American Union.
Our obligations as Masons and American citizens never weighed more
heavily upon us. One hundred years ago the country was heeding admonitions of the Father of our Country to "Avoid entangling foreign
alliances." Today we must all admit Washington's words of caution
have probably of necessity been almost entirely disregarded. The red
menace has put us in Europe to the very limit of our financial resources.
If I interpret the general thinking it appears to be that we cannot afford
to disregard the plight of those sixteen world areas now under
red pressure, and must show a willingness to aid in rehabilitating and
pcouraging them that they may eventually become self-supporting and
pemain self-governed. The noble effort may fail, but our willingness to
help should, on the other hand, increase our prestige throughout the
world, and America can feel that it has at least tried.
These.California Centennial years should be inspiring as they recall
the splendid courage of the early builders of this Fraternity as they
strove to spread the tenets of Masonry throughout the then ever. changing mining regions and into a new territory. While these efforts
were difficult and the obstacles encountered were at times most discouraging, these pioneers were not deterred in their fraternal activities, but
found time to simultaneously assume the role of good citizens and
render valuable service in establishing constitutional government for
California when conditions were most chaotic.
With the passing of a century we today find our problems are growing with the years. We must watch and seek to curb those forces within
our own boundaries, and from without, insidiously striving to undermine
our ancient institutions. May this group, and others, stand as bulwarks
against the propaganda and teachings of those who seek to belittle and
to destroy, to cast aspersions upon what our forefathers, many of them

Thirtieth Annual Observance of Public Schools Week
To the M. W. Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
A report from the Committee on Public Schools Week has more than
once commenced by calling attention to the continued growth of the
Observance in public favor; and more than once it has been said of a
particular observance that it was the most successful ever held.
That was not strange in the early days of the movement before Public Schools Week had received the recognition accorded it in recent
years. But it does seem surprising, and certainly very gratifying to this
Committee, that we are warranted by the reports from the lodges in
describing our latest observance in the very words used of an earlier one:
"It was bigger and better in every way than the most successful of past
years-'bigger and better from every point of view-in attendance at the
evening 'open house' programs, in the number of visitors to the schools,
in the type of programs presented, in the generous support of the newspapers and broadcasting stations, and in the enthusiastic cooperation
given by the groups which join with us in the annual observance."

A motion by Past Grand Master Arthur S. Crites prevailed requesting the Grand Orator to de!iv~r a. copy of the oration to the Grand
Secretary for printing and d1stnbut1on to the Lodges.

There can be no question, of course, that the cooperation received by
Grand Lodge and the constituent lodges from the other organizations
contributed materially to the success achieved. But it is likewise true
that the Masonic Fraternity continues to be the mainstay of the
movement.
-

This is not said boastfully, but as the mere statement of a fact that is
everywhere evident. There are many communities in which a very successful observance was held where the only assistance received by the
lodge was that given by the school people. In fact in some of these communities, the Masonic Lodge is the only organization or association of
any sort or kind. Indeed it would not be too much to say that we believe
that there are only a few communities in which there would be an observance of Public Schools Week were it not for the part played by the
lodges.

Dear Mr. Adams:
Long before coming to California I heard many favorable reports
about the success of Public Schools Week as conceived and promoted
by the Masonic Order of California. After having observed the Week's
activities at close range I can sincerely say the reports were not in the
least overdrawn.
In the Los Angeles School District, during the week of April 25 to
29, more than a quarter million citizens visited our schools and observed
the educational program in action. Many Masonic Lodges held special
meetings devoted exclusively to discussions of the public schools and
their problems.
It is highly commendable that the Grand Lodge has encouraged
many other community groups to participate in Public Schools Week.
So widespread has the participation become in Los Angeles that practically all civic organizations take notice of the event and representatives
of the press and radio besiege us for news stories describing the school
activities which are planned for the Week. To the Masonic Order in
this area we school people, and the citizens generally, owe a debt of
gratitude for such solid support of the system of Public Education.

Again we thank the Masonic Order of this State for its consistent
and intelligent support of our public schools.
Yours sincerely,

The announcements of Public Schools Week made by the State
Heads of the cooperating org~nizations are of especial value. Not only
do they awaken the interest of their members in the local observances
but they serve another purpose. These announcements are obtained b;
our Director of Publicity and with the Proclamation of the Grand Master
and the Proclamation issued by the Governor furnish the stories sent
out by this Committee to the State press--metropolitan and ruralduring the six weeks immediately preceding the beginning of the
observance.
These stories are always well received; but the response this year was
particularly gratifying. There were extensive quotations from all of
them by editors and publishers throughout the State; (lnd there were
several newspapers which carried in full Grand Master Siems's proclamation and that issued by Governor Warren and also a statement which
had been issued by the Superintendent of Public Instruction. Excerpts
from both proclamations appear in much of the local publicity. Repeatedly quoted in urging visits to the schools was this excerpt from the
Governor's proclamation:
"It is not sufficient for one merely to pay his school taxes and
consider that he has done his part. It is the responsibility of each
citizen to maintain a continuing and active inter-est in our public
schools and in the type of education they provide."
In addition to the proclamations issued each year by the Grand
Master and by the Governor, there have been, for many years, proclamations issued by the Mayors, or other civic heads, of many of our
communities. But never before were there so many as were issued this
year. It would seem as though the Mayor, or some authorized official,
or body, in every city and town in California issued a proclamation

104

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

recognizinig Public Schools Week and calling on the people to give it
their support by visiting a school or in some way joining in the observance. In at least two instances there was a joint proclamation by Mayors
of adjoining communities.
These local proclamations are excellent publicity for the local observance. The story is frequently illustrated by a photograph showing the
official seated at his desk signing the document; with a group behind him
in which are representatives of the school people and of the Committee of
Arrangements. Two instances of this reported this year are here mentioned: although in one the official was not the Mayor of a city, but the
Governor of the Territory of Hawaii.
A newspaper clipping attached to a report from one of the largest
of our cities shows the Mayor signing the proclamation, and standing
behind, looking over his shoulder, the City School Superintendent on his
right, and on the other side a Past Grand Master who is referred to in
the caption as "a leader in the movement to have the first week set aside
thirty years ago when Masonic Groups sponsored the program." Incidentally all three men are Masons.
Attached to the joint report from the five lodges on Oahu, T. H.
is a clipping which shows Governor Stainback again this year signing a
proclamation while grouped behind him and looking on are, among
others, the Superintendent of the Department of Public Instruction and
the Chairman of the Masonic Committee sponsoring the observance;
and with them a prominent member of Grand Lodge who is one of the
leaders among the Island brethren.
One reason, perhaps, for the great amount of publicity given the
observance this year was a recognition of the fact that, as was set forth
in an editorial, it was never more appropriate; because there has never
been greater need for that sound and sterling American citizenship of
the type which our public schools, with the proper teaching can inculcate
in American youth.
In this connection it is interesting to note the attention given the
observance itself as distinct from the news report of a particular program.
Illustrative of this are the following comments which are a few of the
many which might be quoted:
"The Masonic Lodge was the founder of Public Schools Week
some 29 years ago. It is one of the many worth-while projects spon. sored by the Order.''

105

"This is Public Schools Week; and it is one of the few of the
many 'weeks' seeking publicity that is really worth while.''
"Public Schools Week is the parent's opportunity to find out
where, how and with whom their children are growing up. It is an
invitation to get acquainted and pull together for the best interests
of the rising generation.''
"Almost every week in the year has been appropriated for one
or more special purpose.... There is Baby Week and Fire Week
and this week and that week and every type of week imaginable.
But none is more important, or deserves more attention than Public
Schools Week."
"Among the special 'weeks' of the year, few, if any, are more
worthy of recognition than Public Schools Week which will be
observed next week-April 25-30."
"Of all the varied 'weeks' as they come along none is endorsed
with higher and more patriotic purpose than Public Schools Week,

"The Thirtieth Annual Public Schools Week celebrated and

And here is one which perhaps should be more valued than any of
the others, because it is so evident that the praise given the observance
is not occasioned by any Masonic bias in its favor. There is no reference to Masons or Masonry in the editorial; and it is the Parent-Teacher
Association which is given the credit for "backing the annual week.''
Incidentally the word "public" is also not to be found in the entire
editorial and the week is described as " Annual Schools Week." We
quote only the beginning of the editorial and that portion giving well deserved praise to the Parent-Teacher Association:

"There is approaching another 'week' as such periods are named
in proclamations and in observance.
"This one will not call for parades and open celebration; neither

"But it is all-important, perhaps of supreme importance as

Helpful indeed was the Parent-Teacher Association not only in that
community. but elsewhere as well. Without depreciating. in the slightest degree, the contributions made by other organizations. we can not
forebear saying that it appears from the reports that in some communities that association was the only organized unit actively cooperating
with the local lodge.

It is impossible to account with certainty for such a successful observance as was held this year. The only thing that is certain is that
success does not · just happen: but is the result of the zeal, interest and
intelligence with which the arrangements are made and carried out.

107

The publicity given this year's observance exceeded even that reteived last year. Not only was it in its entirety greater in volume, but
there were more editorials and more of those special articles of a sort
ordinarily found only in educational journals. There were also more
potographs and cartoons-some illustrating news stories and others
on the editorial· pages with editorials concerning the Observance and
urging the people to visit the schools.
The limitations of this report do not permit the extended reference
that should be made to the very valuable service thus rendered the cause
of public education. But we make mention of three instances typical of
m.any. The first is of a newspaper which published a series of articles,
pne appearing each day during the week, discussing the problem "Why
Children Fail In School." In another newspaper there was each day
during the week an editorial on an educational topic, or on a local situation affecting the schools, written by one of six editors. These were
"guest editors" invited by the Publisher to write the editorials in the
hope that it would, as he said, "stimulate some thinking and arouse more
interest in the public schools."
The third of the references we make is to a somewhat unusual.
but very effective contribution of newspaper publicity. In a city in which
Public Schools Week is always enthusiastically, and very intelligently,
observed, a newspaper published a special illustrated section of four
pages devoted entirely to Public Schools Week, and the local schools.
We fear that the condensation we must make may not do justice to it,
but lack of space forbids the detailed description it so well deserves.
Except for an article on "Public Schools Week Saluted By Community," and giving the local program for the week, and also one explaining a "New Crowding Threat Seen For High Schools," the entire section is composed of pictures. These are photographs of the pupils of the
schools in various situations and constitute a picture story which is both
informative and thought provoking.

We wish it were practicable to report in detail the manner in which
the arrangements for some of the local observances were made-the
meetings of the Committee, and of the sub-committees-the discussions
of suggested programs, and the type finally agreed upon-the suggestions with respect to window exhibits, what they should be and where
to be displayed-the contacts to be made with the service clubs-how
the visitors to the schools should be taken care of-and the many other
details which spell the difference between success and failure. But lack
of space forbids.

The first page tells the story, in pictures, of "Shirley's Day At
School." She is shown leaving home and then joining other children on
their way to school while a policeman holds back the traffic; and then in
successive pictures Shirley is shown availing herself of the offerings of
the school. including the cafeteria and the hobby class, and in the last
picture having a skinned knee, resulting from a slight accident on the
1>layground, being cared for by the school nurse.

Above and beyond everything else, the success of this year's, as of
past years'. success was primarily due to the zealous and especially valuable cooperation of the school people and to the cordial support of the
newspapers and the broadcasting stations.

The second page shows high school students "learning to be good
ltitizens" and "to understand and appreciate American Democracy."
The last of the nine pictures on that page shows how "democracy can be
learned on the playground as well as in the classroom."

108

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

On the third page is shown in pictures "the vocational, and the avocational, training" offered by the evening High School. And on the last
page are pictures evidencing the "new crowding threat" and the reasons
urged for the building of a new high school. With the pictures 'is a map
of the school district, and there is also a graph illustrating the expected
enrollment trend and the capacity of the existing high schools. The
rapid increase in births since the beginning of the war as aifecting school
population is shown in two photographs--one of a tiny baby in the
nurse's arms and the other of "that tiny baby now in the fifth grade and
who by 1953 will be entering high school."
There was here a real service to the community (and perhaps to
other communities) as well as evidence of an enthusiastic cooperation in
the observance of Public Schools Week. It is but typical, however of
that fine cooperation which the newspapers of California-both metropolitan and rural-always give to the observance of Public Schools
Week: and also of the valuable service they thus render their respective
communities.
The broadcasting stations were no less generous in their support
than were the newspapers: and no less valuable was the service they
rendered. There was hardly one report from a community in which
there is a station which did not make special mention of the extent of
of radio participation in the program.
The net-work systems were no less cooperative than were the small
independent stations. Again this year, in addition to "spot announce#
ments" and newscasts, there were broadcasts of addresses, plays,
chorals, glee club renderings, panels and round-table discussions: and
there were several programs broadcast from classroms. It would seem
that each year radio plays a larger part in the observance of Public
Schools Week.
The newspapers and the broadcasting stations are not the only
sources of publicity made use of by the committees in charge of a local
observance. Last year there was reported as a novelty the use of lapel
ribbons on which was printed "Visit Your Schools." This year there
were several reports of the use of this form of publicity. The ribbons
were worn by clerks in the stores, by delivery men and by attendants in
service stations during the week prior to the opening of the observance.
A variation reported this year was a ribbon, to be worn during the week.
The inscription had been changed from "Visit Your Schools" to "I Have
Visited a School-Have You7" They were obtainable only at the schools
where they were given to all visitors.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

109

Another way of attracting visits to the schools or to the evening
programs is through the use of store windows for school exhibits-the
most attractive being the "live" or "action" exhibits.
There was this year in one community a combination of the ribbon
idea with a store exhibit which had for its focal point a "little red school
house" bulging with children. Poised overhead was a stork in flight with
a diaper of babies suspended from its beak. With the exhibit was a placard telling the number of babies born in that city each year with the enrollment in 1939 and in the current year and the anticipated 1959 enrollment. A picture of the school house (without the children and without
the stork) was printed on a "souvenir bookmark" with the inscription
"The Little Red Schoolhouse has grown up--and is now bursting at the
seams." This was printed by the schools and was distributed at luncheons and dinners immediately preceding, and during the week.
A very clever distribution of exhibits-"action" and "still" was reported from a community in which the arrangements had been made in a
manner which practically insured a successful observance. A typewriter
shop had students from the commercial classes demonstrating phases of
instruction in the commercial field. "Art in action" was the display in a
paint store: the "Health Program" was displayed in the window of a
pharmacy, and "Thrift in the Schools" in a Bank window. In other
windows demonstrations were given in weaving, painting, ceramics and
cartoon drawing: and there was a display of 500 text books in current
use in the elementary grammar and high schools. A Title Guaranty
Company had a series of photographs of new school construction and of
a new school swimming pool which had just been completed.
In a community from which came an extremely interesting report of a
very successful observance, the class from the Print Shop contributed a
very clever stunt at an open house affair. Each visitor on leaving was
presented with a facsimile of a special edition of the "Print Shop
Gazette" with his name in a head line reading "John Doe (but the real
name of the visitor) is greeted in attending Open House." Inside information is that as the visitors signed the "Open House" register on
their arrival their names would be rushed to the linotype, the line cast
with the individual's name in the heading which was then locked up in a
form and imprinted in the blank space on the already printed page.
As has been indicated there were this year an unusually large number
of programs calculated to convey information with respect to what the
schools are doing, and how it is being done, rather than to provide entertainment. We wish we could describe some of these such as the "Backto-School" and "Showing Mom and Dad" and those where the teachers,
and some times the students, explained in detail the modern methods of

Of course, as there always are, there were parades and pageants and

these were "The Days of '49," "Golden California," "California Yesterday and Today," "California's Golden Age," "Olden, Golden California" and many others too numerous to mention. They told the story
in whole or in part of the growth of the State from the Mission period
down through the gold rush and covered wagon days: and of course
there were elaborate costumes with incidental music and dancing. They
carried out one of the purposes of the Week in that they tended to focus
the attention of the public on the schools.
Themes of the sort mentioned were not the only ones around which
observances were built. Among others deemed worthy of mention were
"The Public School-Defender of Democracy," "The Public Schools
Are Your Schools," "Know Your Schools-Their Work and Their
Needs": and one which seemed to strike public fancy because frequently
editorialized-"The Lamp of Freedom-the Public School." One commentator said of it, "a very good slogan since more than ever we are
realizing that the public school, whether rural or urban, is a fertile field
for the germination of the seeds of democracy."
Again this year liberal use was made of "forums" and "panels" of
various sorts to convey to the public information with respect to the
schools. The subjects apparently most frequently discussed were the
crowded conditions of the schools and the urgent need for more classrooms, and pending bond issue elections.
Akin to the forum and panel discussions, was what must have been
ari exceedingly interesting program in the form of a "quiz" presented' at
a club luncheon meeting to show the wide range of information possessed
by our modern youth. The "quiz master" was the Superintendent of
Schools who propounded the questions to a .group of high school students
who had no previous knowledge of what they were to be asked. In fact
some of the questions came from the audience.
There will naturally be differences of opinion as to which of the purposes of Public Schools Week is, in itself, the most important. But one
might hazard the opinion that the most important thing Public Schools
Week is doing-indeed has done-is to bring about that close contact

These gatherings, sometimes in the form of luncheons, are a development of the "Pre-Week Dinner" inaugurated many years ago, and still
given each year in a city in which there are three lodges. The officers of
these lodges are the hosts and the Mayor of the City, the members of
the Board of Education, the Superintendent of Schools and the Principals of the schools, with a few others, are the guests.
Among the gatherings reported this year were some in which the
roles of host and guest were reversed. In more than one instance it was
the school people who wanted to show their appreciation of what was
being accomplished by the observance of Public Schools Week: and
they gave a dinner, or luncheon, for the friends of the school who had
been active in making its observance a success. On at least one occasion
it was the Parent-Teacher Association that was host.
So valuable do we believe this sort of thing to be, that we here repeat
what was said last year of a dinner in which the hosts were the members
of the joint committee of the Masonic lodges joining in the observance,
and the guests were ninety principals and teachers of the schools in the
area; and the announced purpose of which was "to provide an expression
of appreciation for the contribution of our public schools to the welfare
and development of the community:"
"That this 'appreciation banquet' served its avowed purpose,
there can be no doubt. But something more than this must have
been effected. Affairs of this sort are a recognition of not only the
worth of our teachers, as such, but also of their high place in the
civic life of the community: and incidentally of their social status.
They tend to make the profession attractive to those young people
who now seem disinclined to prepare themselves for it."
That was only a surmise; but that it is a fact was evidenced this year
by several letters, or excerpts from them constituting parts of reports
received from the lodges. We mention only a few: One was a letter
to the master of a lodge from the Surperintendent of Schools who
wrote. "On behalf of our public schools I want to express appreciation
for the very fine dinner and program given by your lodge in honor of
the school people in this valley. We put a high premium on your
interest in us as a group and hope that we will conti!}ue to merit your
confidence." And in another community it was a teacher who wrote the

nity." And another master reported the receipt of a letter from the Prin..

teachers, "It is my feeling that
Lodge is evidencing strong leadership in teacher recognition which can only lead to better teaching and
better schools.''
The feeling of that Principal is, we think, that of the school people

week's activities was the feeling that teachers and administrators were
being appreciated as never before and were being encouraged to go on
and continue the fine work they are now doing."
Expressions such as these would seem to warrant the opinion expressed in a Bulletin of Suggestions issued by the State Department of
Education even before Public Schools Week had attained its present
proportions.
After detailing "some of the more important purposes which can be

"Public Schools Week has proved highly effective as a public
relations enterprise.... It has contributed to the accomplishment of
all the foregoing purposes. No other single institution or agency
has contributed more to the understanding of public education in
California and to the high esteem held by citizens for their schools.''
We close this report with a quotation from an editorial in a newspaper published in a city which is justly proud of its fine educational

school standards. Its biggest goal is to foster an interest in educa.-

A study of the above figures, commencing with 1940, indicates a
balance between income and expenditures which continued through
1941. Beginning with 1942, income began to rise and maintenance cost
actually decreased. Since 1946 costs have risen sharply, due principally
to the withdrawal of price controls and a rapid rise in wages and salaries.
The cost of labor and materials, food, etcetera, is a part of the total
economic structure, and not subject to the control of your Board. In
1949, the maintenance cost will be seen to have exceeded income by a
' little more than $80,000.00.
The surplus and reserves built up during the years of high income
have been spent in the building operations at both Homes. The Covina
properties have been brought to a high state of rehabilitation and replacement of equipment, at a cost of approximately $225,000.00. The
rehabilitation, reconstruction and new construction at Decato, most of
which has been completed, will approximate $750,000.00. The Board
believes that Grand Lodge approves the action of the Board in the
expenditure of these reserves, rather than making an assessment upon
the Lodges to accomplish the result. At the request of the Board, Grand
Lodge relieved the Lodges entirely of a per capita tax during the
"good" years. It is our hope and expectation that we will be able to
operate during this current year within the funds at our disposal. We
do not, however, feel that it is safe to enter the year commencing August
1, 1950 without additional income, and we therefore recommend that
an additional 50c per capita be levied for the maintenance of the Masonic Homes.
VISITATIONS TO COVINA

Visitations by lodges to the Home for Children at Covina have
reached such proportions and present so many problems that your board
must take action by way of limiting them. Almost without exception
from two to twelve lodges visit the home each Sunday of the year.
During , May 1949 lodge visitations were responsible for 1,812
visitors in addition to the regular number of friends and relatives of the
children. Each group requires the assignment of guides and the result
has been that some children must make as high as eight tours of the
grounds on a single Sunday. Most visitors find one tour to be sufficiently
extensive to be tiring and it is not reasonable to permit such demands to
be placed upon the children on their day of rest.
These visitations at present eliminate any possibility of rest or recreation on Sundays. They introduce other problems also. Request is always
made that the visitors refrain from tipping their guides and that if they
feel moved to make a donation that they make it for all the children.
Little heed is paid to this request and it is the rule rather than the exception to slip the guide a dollar or two. Each child receives his needs
and spending money from the home and tips received on the side are

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

pocketed and encourage a breaking of rules and regulations necessary
to the welfare of all. This practice also contributes toward eliminating
any sense of service or friendship in guiding groups and leads toward
the placing of a pecuniary value upon lodge visitations.
Unfortunately many lodges do not notify the Superintendent that
they are coming and the flrst knowledge of the visit is the arrival of
forty or fifty visitors. Not infrequently the lodge plans to have a picnic
lunch in a public park in Covina and as there is a limit upon the number
using the city's park for such purpose, problems of public relations with
the municipal authorities are introduced.
The Board of Trustees appreciates the continuing interest of lodges
evidenced by the visitations, but is confident that members of the craft
share the opinion that the home is maintained flrst and foremost for
the children and not as an exhibition. It is therefore necessary to order
that after November l, 1949 group visitations by lodges or other
organizations will be permitted only on the flrst and third Sunday of
each month. No change is ordered as to the existing rules governing
single visitations of relatives of the children.

To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
Brethren: I present, herewith, the Superintendent's report of the Masonic Home at Decato for the year ending July 31, 1949.
At the beginning of the year 180 women and 121 men were comfortably housed in the Home. During the year 21 women were admitted at
an average age of 79.54 and 28 men, average age 75.96. During the same
period we lost by death 29 women, average age 80.31, and 25 . men,
average age 73.8, leaving at the end of the year 172 women and 123
men. the average age for women 78.81 and for men 77.95, a total of 295.
Included in this number are 12 married couples.
Our records indicate that 1596 members, their wives or widows,
have been admitted to the Home; 582 women, 1014 men passed away
and 81 men and women were withdrawn. The records further indicate
that 656 are buried in the Home Plot and 859 were returned to their
Lodges for burial, since the Home was dedicated in 1898.
The health condition of the residents of the Home during the year
has been good. However, due to the inflrmatives common to old age, the
east wing on the fourth floor and the hospital facilities have been constantly taxed. Miss Esther G. Payne is still rendering valuable service
in these departments.
Many enjoyable parties and programs have been planned and presented during the year by members of the Home. These functions are
enjoyed immensely by the residents and tend to create a closer bond
between them, and a very desirable atmosphere in the Home. These activities are under the supervision of Mrs. Lotd, who lends much toward
their success. All departments in the Home are completely staffed and
operating satisfactorily.
We have practiced, throughout the year, every economy consistent
with maintaining a high standard, however, our operating cost is still
mounting. This condtion. I am sure you will agree, is general and will
continue until the general economic conditions throughout the country
become stabilized.
There has been no change in the lease of the farm land. Receipts
from that portion reserved for the Home's use are as follows:·

HEALTH PROGRAM:

Through an intensive health program stressing prevention, we are
happy to report we have had no serious health problems. Five appendectomies, two cases of fractures and minor surgery are recorded. Physical
examinations made at regular intervals by Dr. W. P. Magan and
associates, give a complete record of the growth of the child, with immunization against smallpox, diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis but a
small part of our prevention program. Additional nourishment and rest,
vitamin supplement, together with careful control of menu planning,
making certain of dietary values; are contributing factors to our enjoying good health this past year. The encouragement of children and
the acceptance by them, to attend the daily clinic, learning to assume
their responsibility in helping the nurses and doctors keep them in good
health, is very gratifying. Periodic eye examinations, securing glasses
prescribed, insures our children of the best possible care. Three children
are receiving special orthodontia treatment by Dr. T. W. Paul and
Dr. Ellwood Laine. Our visiting dentists treated sixty-eight cases
during the year. The daily average of bed patients for the year was 1.5,
while on the other hand, visits to the nurse at the Home clinic averaged
16.9 per day, for the year. We are deeply gratful to our doctors and
nurses for their untiring devotion to the health of the children in this
growing stage.
FARM AND GROUNDS:

This year an intensive program has been carried forth on our farm
and grounds. New lawns, many beautiful flowers and shrubs have been
planted thus enhancing the beauty. On our farm the real change has
taken place. The old piggery has been torn down and an attractive new
one built on the lower land, with a new fence allowing for the future of
an animal husbandry program to be carried on by the children. A new
fence enclosing the larger pasture has replaced the old. affording
necessary space for the care of animals. Children in training are thus
furnished an opportunity for expression in animal husbandry. All of
this work has taken place this summer and the entire project, under
the direction and supervision of our farmer, has been accomplished by
our senior boys. A great deal of hard work, extremely valuable training, as well as money earned toward the purchase of clothing, has been
the result of this farm endeavor. These benefits have more than justified
our efforts in this training program.

Referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes and to
