Transfer of Membership to New Lodge
At the present time an ambiguous situation regarding membership
occurs by reason of the operation of Section 162, paragraph 3rd of the
Ordinances of Grand Lodge which provides that: "One may acquire
membership in a Lodge by having been named in a dispensation for a
new Lodge as one of the petitioners therefor." Since frequently a
considerable length of time may elapse between the issuance of a dispensation and the creation of the new Lodge by Institution, the brethren
named in the dispensation are, apparently, members of a non-existent
Lodge, and lose their Masonic standing until the Institution of their
new Lodge, because of the effect of Section 175, which provides that
the membership of the signer of the petition for a dispensation shall
cease in his old Lodge upon the granting of the dispensation. The undersigned are of the opinion that the petitioning brothers should be members
of an existing Lodge at all times and therefore propose the following
resolution:
That paragraph 3rd of Sec. 162 be stricken and the following inserted in lieu thereof:
"3rd. By having been a petitioner named in a dispensation for a new Lodge as of date of institution."
That Section 175 be amended by inserting the words, "as of date
of institution" after the words "shall ipso factor cease".
Respectfully submitted,
GLENN C. HOLMES
WILLIAM R. HERVEY, JR.
WM. J. WILLIAMS
HAROLD MEYER
JAMES M. MACDONALD
WALTER A. PARKER
KENNETH R. FORD

Referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes and to
the Committee on Jurisprudence.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

131

Number of Members in New Lodge
As a result of our scrutiny of the Lodges under dispensation the
undersigned are of the opinion that under present day circumstances a
petitioning group having only twelve members would find the utmost
difficulty in establishing a Lodge on a sound and permanent basis. In
fact, there is good reason to believe that a larger number than the
present maximum would give additional strength and stability to any
group entering upon the arduous task of creating a Masonic Lodge.
Therefore, we propose the following resolution:
RESOLVED, That Section 101 of the Ordinances of Grand Lodge
be amended by striking out the present minimum of twelve, and maximum of twenty-five, and substituting therefor a minimum of twenty-five
and a maximum of fifty, as the number of Masons who may petition
for a dispensation for a new Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,
GLENN C. HOLMES

STANDING RESOLUTION

BE IT RESOLVED, That the following Standing Resolution be
adopted:
There shall be an Investment Committee of five members consisting
of the Grand Treasurer, who shall act as Chairman, the President of
the Masonic Homes Board, the Chairman of the Finance Committee,
and two additional members who shall be appointed by the foregoing
with the approval of the Grand Master; one to serve for 1 year, and
one to serve for 2 years. In the case of a vacancy or vacancies of an
appointed member or members, the remaining members of the Committee shall, with the consent of the Grand Master, fill such vacancy or
vacancies for the unexpired term. Upon expiration of the respective
terms, a successor shall be appointed in the same manner for a term of
3 years. The Investment Committee shall have the power to invest and
re-invest the funds belonging to or held in trust by the Grand Lodge,
and a majority of the Committee shall be empowered to act for and on
behalf of the Committee. The Investment Committee or a majority
thereof is authorized to acquire every kind of investments in the nature
of securities, specifically including, but not by way of limitation, corporate obligations of every kind, and stocks, preferred or common, which
men of prudence, discretion and intelligence acquire for their own
account. The Grand Treasurer and the Grand Secretary shall be em~
powered to sign such documents as may be necessary to carry out the
actions of the Committee.

Expenditures for Fraternal Intercourse
In the course of events in ~he activities of the small lodges, particularly those with membership less than 100, the permissible expenditures
of 20% for Masonic intercourse does not provide sufficient funds to
effectively meet the needs for those fraternal activities which are necessary to the benefit of the Craft. Most lodges of 100 or less members
are old lodges with a small overhead who own their own Temple, with
no rent to pay. The cost _of those activities today is relatively high
compared to income, at the time the 20% was established.
Therefore the following resolution is offered:
WHEREAS, The 20% of net income provided in Section 159 of
the Constitution does not provide sufficient funds to carry on Masonic

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

When completed, this new standard practice system was set up
within our Employment Offices. After one year of operation the Board
of Control felt that it had proved so successful that it was decided to
extend the system to include Boards of Relief.
This report reflects the result of the first complete year of operation
for all Boards of Relief under this uniform system and again the Board
of Control feels that the project is truly successful. Grand Lodge will
now have figures from records that are uniform, accurate, subject to easy
audit and are comparable. By the use of this system of records the
Boards of Relief can be operated more economically and efficiently.
An important feature of our present standard practice system is
that it is so set up that changes can easily be made within its instructions
should the occasion require.
·

The Board of Control submits herewith its 19th report to Grand
Lodge setting forth che results of the past year as shown by the annual
reports of Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus.
By ordinance, Grand Lodge has charged the Board of Control with
the responsibility of control and supervision of the activities of Bo~rds
of Relief and Employment Bureaus, making such rules and regulations
as it shall deem necessary for their effectual operation and to endeavor
to so standardize the work that their operation may be conducted economically and efficiently. This report will in itsel~ refle~t the v:ork ~f
the Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus in their relationship
with the Board of Control and will indicate that the Board of Control
has worked diligently and faithfully to accomplish these ends. It will
also show that they have been materially aided in their work by the
close cooperation of the Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus
and those Brothers who are active in the work of administering relief.

The book of instructions, which has been placed in the hands of all
Boards of Relief, is known as "Standard Practice Bulletin for Masonic
Boards of Relief and Employment Services." It is made up of fifteen
bulletins of some 47 pages and contains thirty-two illustrations of reports
and accounting and statistical forms.
During the year the Grand Secretary received letters of criticism
of the services of two of our offices. Both cases were referred to the
Board of Control for investigation. We are pleased to report that the
action of the Board on both cases absolved the office of any blame. The
first case was based upon the question of eligibility to register for employment. The Board ruled that the manager of the Employment Bureau
was correct in refusing to register one who was not eligible to use our
service. The second complaint was from a brother who claimed a need
for relief. Our investigation showed that his request had been received
but that he had failed to cooperate or answer questions necessary to
establish his need. He simply demanded $50 for immediate use. His
Lodge had been contacted by our Board of Relief and they wrote to
him offering their help. He would not answer their letters. Everything
was done to secure his cooperation without success. The Board feels
that the Secretary was patient, understanding and efficient in his handling of the case.

BoARD OP CONTROL

The Board of Control is made up of five members who have been so
selected geographically as to best serve the interests of those Boards of
Relief within their immediate or adjacent territory. At present the
Board members come from San Diego, Los Angeles, Fresno, San Francisco and Sacramento.
During the past year the Board of Control has ?eld meetings in S~n
Francisco, during last Grand Lodge, Glendale tn February and tn
Berkeley in June. All members of the Board were in attenda~ce at these
meetings. This represents more than one hundred ho~rs of time dev.oted
to the work of relief and employment by the Board in actual meetings.
In addition much time has been given by individual members of the
Board in working out specific problems assigned to them and in advising, counseling and corresponding with Boards of Relief and in the
analysis of audits and reports.
Two years ago the Board of Control, with the consent of the ~ra~d
Master, employed a nationally known firm of accountants to assist in
the preparation of a uniform method of handling records and in accounting procedure, so that when followed, the financial data and statistical
information accumulated at each office and the reports thereon would
be uniform and comparable. The data recorded and the substantiating
documents to be maintained in a manner which would make it feasible
to audit the transactions of each office with a minimum amount of work.
Forms for use in the various Employment Offices were to be made uniform.

135

It is the custom of some Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus
to hold an annual Breakfast to honor the Grand Master and to promote
the work of their office in the handling of relief and employment. This
year members of the Board of Control attended the breakfasts at Los
Angeles, Long Beach, Fresno and Sacramento. Other breakfasts were
attended under the auspices of Masters and Wardens associations.
San Jose Board of Relief breakfast was held in observance of constitution observance month and the Junior Grand Warden was the honored
guest.

from service bureaus requesting information concerning the operation

BOARDS OF RELIEF

With the addition of the two new Boards this year, we now report
that we have nineteen Boards of Relief operating within our jurisdiction. This represents 277 Lodges with a membership of 117,040.
Grand Lodge (under Section 264 of Ross' s Digest) permits Lodges
having concurrent jurisdiction to form Boards of Relief for the purpose
of properly relieving the distress of visiting Masons, their widows and
orphans and those dependent upon them who might be entitled to relief
from a Masonic Lodge. "Such Boards shall report annually to Grand
Lodge, showing their work, receipts and disbursements in d~tail, specifying separately what, if any, has been expended ~or re.he£ ~f nonaffiliated Masons, their widows and orphans therein SOJOU~i~~· of
this or other jurisdictions, and how much, if any, has been repaid.

The total of the surplus account of our Boards of Relief is $70,341.00.
EMPLOYMENT BUREAUS

Boards of Relief may establish and maintain Employment Bureaus
where careful survey indicates that such service is warranted in securing
employment for those who otherwise might be entitled to relief from a
Masonic Lodge.
Within this jurisdiction we are now operating seven such offices,
East Bay, Fresno, Long Beach, Los Angeles, Sacramento, San Diego
and San Francisco. The offices in the East Bay and Los Angeles employ
a full time manager whereas the other five offices combine the duties
of Manager of the Employment Bureau with that of Secretary of the
Board of Relief.
These Employment Bureaus are supported in part by the local per
capita tax and partly from an appropriation from Grand Lodge. Under
a ruling by the Board of Control and contained within the instructions
on Bulletin 12 Sheet No. 3 of the Standard Practice Bulletin, Grand
Lodge will not contribute an amount greater than the Lodges per capita
allocated to employment.
A summary of the reports submitted show the following as a result
of their years work:
Number of Lodges 222
Membership 97,537
Applications received 11,509
Placements 2,848 or 25%
Positions offered by employers 8,837
Fees saved those placed in employment are based upon an average
of the State of California's prescribed maximum which may be charged
by commercial agencies and are maintained for comparative purposes.
Our Brothers were saved these fees this year in the amount of $174,642.
This has been a trying year for Employment Managers. Layoffs,
strikes, union closed shops and the caring for their own members together with a general slackening of employment have created difficult
problems for our Employment Bureaus.

138

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

One of our constant problems is the large number of applications
from the older age group. These people are always hard to place in
jobs. They are a constant source of worry to our Employment Managers.
Many methods have been tried in an effort to relieve this situation.
Recently a plan was developed in the East Bay which has been successful enough to justify its mention here. They organized a "40 and Over
Club" made up of men 40 years of age and over. They hold regular
meetings, have inspirational speakers and endeavor to build up their
own morale. Each member tries not only to help himself but also to help
the other members. Their motto is "There is no substitute for experience." This is the thought that they try to sell employers and they
have sold it many times. Much credit is due the East Bay for the
originality of the idea.
In selecting this one example of the ability of those who work in
our Employment Bureaus, we do not intend to detract from the other
offices. A report of this kind does not permit further examples of their
work. Each has its merits and is entitled to your praise and support.

REIMBURSEMENTS

When a Board of Relief has been unable to secure repayment of
funds advanced through the customary sources, it has been the practice
of Grand Lodge to make them whole. The Board of Control agrees
with this custom believing that such action is in itself a method of
assuring the proper handling of relief cases, in that it removes any
possible tendency toward niggardliness on the part of those administering relief.

REPORT OF MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Masonic Homes Endowment Board desires to preface its
seventeenth annual report, covering the period from August 1, 1948
to July 31, 1949 inclusive, by a statement of our Most Worshipful
Grand Master:
"The Masonic Homes of California, in my opinion, is one of
the most valuable assets of Freemasonry in this Grand Jurisdiction. To participate in this great charity is a duty and a privi~e~e.
Now is the time to remember those placed in our care by D1vme
Providence", signed Edward H. Siems, Grand Master.
PURPOSE
The Masonic Home at Decoto for the aged. The Masonic Home
at Covina for children. These have become Magic Words to the
thoughtful Mason. The warmth of the hearts of ou.r brethren go ~ut
in real sympathy and love for the children, with the bght of the sunrise
in their eyes, and our older guests, both men and women, whose suns
are rapidly going down to the realm "where the rainbow never fade~,
where the stars will be spread out before us like islands that slumber m
the ocean, and where the beautiful beams that now pass before us
like shadows will stay in our presence forever".
For assisting in the adequate financial provision of these Homes
your Endowment Board was created by action of Grand Lodge (Constitution and Ordinances. Article V) and consists of fifteen members.
The purpose of such a Board was to enlighten the Brethren regarding
the work and needs of the Hom~s. and to afford an opportunity to make
contributions for their support. In short, the purpo~e of the Board is,
"to study. devise. and carry out plans for the securing of adequate
endowment for the Masonic Homes of California."
OBJECT
.
As a Board we have held constantly before us that the aims and
object of our creation were educational in nature. We have attempted
to continually present such an object through the officers, by correspondence. by literature and by visua! education.
PLAN
A well-formulated plan has been followed throughout the year.
having in mind the above purpose. This plan provided for the informing
the Constituent Lodges. and through them the brethren thereof. the
status of our Homes. the need of a sound Endowment program and the
opportunity that every Mason had in participating in this our greatest

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

141

over-all Charity work. Such a plan was carefully plotted and has covered the entire jurisdiction.
PERFORMANCE
We feel that the execution of such a program has been carried
through. Fortunately. your Board members are widely distributed and
represent all sections of the State. We are appreciative of the older
members who pioneered the work and have welcomed to the Board some
new and active members that have assisted materially in effective
performance this year.
In addition to the letters and thousands of pamphlets which have
been carefully distributed we have had a far greater number of requests
for assisting in Endowment programs at regular lodge, district and
special meetings. This augurs well for the increased interest and the
dissemination of the program. Perhaps the greatest contribution to
these programs has been the wide use of our 35 mm. Kodachrome slides,
which have given a more realistic and lasting picture of the true nature
of our Homes' activities. We trust they will be continued in use
throughout the year.
ACCOMPLISHMENTS

It is hard to evaluate the true results. Seeds are constantly being
sown which will in time bear fruit. This is manifest year after year in
the resultant number of bequests. The immediate yardstick by which
results are measured is shown in the subsequent financial statement.
We are pleased that the contributions through individual lodges is the
greatest in our history-$191,489.68. More promising for the future
is a steady numerical climb in individual participants.
We are proud that the Endowment Fund has passed the three and
a half million dollar mark. At the same time we are cognizant of the
fact that the income even from this sum is very inadequate to care for
the needs of the Homes. Consequently. the best we can say for accomplishments is that a good foundation has been laid upon which to build
the super structure, namely an adequate. permanent Endowment Fund.
APPRECIATION
Your Board has appreciated the privilege of working in this great
endeavor, but it humbly realizes that what has been accomplished has
been due mainly to the efforts of others. It is with sincere appreciation
that we extend our grateful thanks to the Most Worshipful Grand
Master, who has on every possible occasion given us the utmost assistance, has carried the Homes' message continually throughout the year
and to the entire Jurisdiction. He has been wonderfully well supported
by the fine Inspectors, who have been even more alert in directing sub-

142

stantial effort for the Endowment program. To the Masters, officers,
committee chairmen and hundreds of others we realize we owe a debt
of gratefulness as through them the final and individual contact is made
and the response received.
The Board's work has been materially aided and lightened by the
fine cooperation of the offices of the Grand Secretary. The operation
and handling of the constant reports through lodges would have been
a mammoth job except for the efficient cooperation through these offices.
The lodge Secretaries deserve special mention for the manner in
which they have turned in their lodge contributions. This is of extreme
importance since we operate in conformity with the Grand Lodge fiscal
year and recognition is made and the books closed as of July 31st. We
sincerely regret that in a few instances some lodges failed to get their
report in by this date and it necessarily will have to show in the next
annual report. We are particularly embarrassed that it is impossible
to show the splendid contribution of $1,034.00, which has been made
by Union Lodge No. 58 in Sacramento. Since the amount was received
after the close of the books for the fiscal year, it will show in the next
year's printed report. This embarrassment is gradually being removed
and we trust by another year all lodges can be given due credit in
proper form.
We solicit your careful indulgence in scrutinizing the attached de~
tailed statement which reveals the real progress and points the way to
the future.
Your Masonic Homes Endowment Board:

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC IDSTORY

three weeks we have written to approximately two hundred Lodges
and their Inspectors, urging their cooperation in this matter. We still
feel, even at this late day, that local Lodges could be of assistance by
sending to us material on themselves and their members worthy of
special mention. In doing so they will enable us to complete our task
with the assurance that we have not failed to honor any deserving
Lodge or brother in this Grand Jurisdiction.
We have completed the manuscripts of three volumes with a sum
total of 495,000 words. We feel that with the material on hand and
what we hope to receive in the very near future we will be able to
complete the final volume, which will make in all four volumes of at
least five hundred pages each.
Basing our estimate on the experience of the past twenty-two months
we believe it will take five more months to finish the manuscript, proofread the printed copy, properly index the same and fully correct all
errors, typographical and otherwise.
We have prepared and have attached hereto a proposed budget
which we feel should be sufficient to complete this work. The budget
for the further period of five months amounts to $3,645.40.
Therefore, your Committee offers the following resolution and moves
its adoption:

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & AM. of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History begs leave to submit the following report:
By October 1 of this year, we had consumed approximately one
year and ten months in an effort to complete the manuscript of a history
of Freemasonry in California in accordance with your directions. We
had sincerely hoped to submit the full manuscript at this Annual Com·
munication, but found the task much greater than anticipated. Our
work was unavoidably slowed by two major factors.
In the vast amount of historical material collected over a period of
twenty years, we have found countless errors, omissions and contra·
dictions which have necessitated additional research and the writing of
literally thousands of letters to Lodges and individuals in California
and elsewhere in quest of essential data.
This condition, fully covered in our report to the 1948 Communication of Grand Lodge, has shown but slight improvement with the
passing months. It is still necessary to double check everything for
accuracy.
A greater handicap, however, has been the failure of many Lodges
to respond to our requests for material.
One hundred and two of them are in Northern California-with
forty-two in the San Francisco Bay area alone. The response from
Southern California has not been much better, particularly from Lodges
organized since 1900. Many of them have acknowledged our letters
with the simple observation that they "have no history of interest."

In order not to slight any of these Lodges, we have been compelled
to search the Grand Lodge Proceedings for their vital statistics and
names of their first officers. We have even gone further. In an honest
endeavor to find something interesting on every one of them, we have
consulted items from county histories, Masonic periodicals, and local
press wherever the same are available. Included in this has been an
unrelenting effort to reconstruct the personal histories of Grand Masters
prior to the time their biographies were published in the Grand Lodge
Proceedings. This has necessitated consulting public records, libraries,
relatives, and business and professional associates all over the state.

RESOLVED:
1. That the present work of the Committee on Masonic History
be continued.
2. That the sum of $3,645.40 be appropriated and set aside for the
use of said Committee for the completion of the Manuscript of the
History of Masonry in California.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
GRAND LODGE RITUAL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
This report has to do with the appropriate words to be used in
speaking to the officers of this Grand Lodge and in referring to or
speaking about those officers in our opening, closing and installation
ceremonies.
The committee which is now reporting was appointed by our present
Grand Master pursuant to a motion adopted at the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge last year. That motion requested the Grand
Master to appoint a special committee to consider a portion of the report
of the Ritual Committee presented in 1948 containing recommendations
as to certain action taken at the 1947 Annual Communication with
reference to the ritual to be used in the opening, closing and installation
ceremonies. The following proceedings need to be recalled as a basis
for our report:
In the course of his report to the Grand Lodge at the 1947 communication, the Grand Lecturer stated (Proceedings 1947, pages 110 to 111 )
that his attention had been called to the language of section three of the
constitution of the Grand Lodge wherein it is provided that the address
of the several officers shall be: Most Worshipful, Right Worshipful and
so forth. He further stated, correctly, that the definition of address was:
"To direct words to anyone. To use a set form in accosting or greeting,"
but that in our Grand Lodge ritualistic work we used the addl'ess when
speaking of an officer and omitted it when speaking to him. This, he
said, was the reverse of the correct usage. He then proposed that the
constitution be amended to change the address to the title. The matter
was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence which reported later in
the session of 1947 ( page 260) that it disapproved the proposed amendments and recommended that they be not adopted. The report of the
committee was adopted.
Thereafter, at the same comµmnication in 1947, the then Junior
Grand Warden presented a resolution (Proceedings, page 261) that
"the opening, closing and installation ceremonies of the Grand Lodge
be amended to conform to section three of the constitution by deleting
the address of Grand Lodge officers whenever the speaker is not addressing the officer and, whenever the address. and title are combined
in speaking to an officer, by deleting the title, leaving the address only."
This resolution was referred by Grand Master Moore to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes. That committee reported that
in its opinion the opening, closing and installation ceremonies should
conform to our fundamental law and recommended the adoption of the

150

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

resolution. The committee report was adopted. The Grand Master
then put the resolution and it was adopted. When Grand Lodge was
called off that afternoon and again when it was called on the following
morning, the last day of the 1947 communication, the Grand Master
and other Grand Lodge officers used ritualistic work in conformity with
the requirements of the resolution.
At the 1948 communication the Ritual Committee made a report
to the Grand Lodge in which it recommended that the resolution adopted
at the 1947 communication be rescinded. On motion this report was
referred to a special committee for report at this, the 1949 communication.
In the report of the Ritual Committee in 1948 it is stated that "Before
the language of the ritual can be changed it is necessary for the Committee on Ritual to present such new language to the Grand Lodge for
adoption.'' We find no such requirement in the constitution. Nowhere
in our laws do we find that the Committee on Ritual is charged with
that duty.
The law relative to the duty of the Ritual Committee is contained
in section 52 of the Ordinances which provides:
"The Grand Lecturer and the four Assistant Grand Lecturers shall constitute the Ritual Committee, and the
committee as so composed from time to time shall be the
custodian of the esoteric work.''
In other words, the duty imposed upon that committee is custodial
in nature. It is a depository for ritualistic work. lts powers and duties
with reference to changes in the ritual would seem to be of a recommendatory nature only. Section 248 of the Ordinances provides that
the Grand Lodge alone has power to authorize changes in the ritual.
This phase of the matter is alluded to for the reason that at the
outset this committee was confronted with the question of the effect
of the resolution adopted by the Grand Lodge in 1947. Our conclusion
is that the language of the resolution was self-executing and that when
Grand Lodge adopted it the opening, closing and installation ceremonies
were modified in the particulars specified and no duty was cast upon
any committee or member of the Grand Lodge except to conform to
the action of the Grand Lodge. Grand Master Moore and the other
Grand Lodge officers were therefore correct in 19i7 in using the modified
form in calling off that same afternoon and in opening the following
morning.
As pointed out by the report of the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes in 1947, the opening and closing and installation
ceremonies of Grand Lodge should conform to our fundamental law.
The Constitution of the Grand Lodge of California is that fundamental law. Section 3 of Article II of the constitution provides:

"The Grand Lodge shall be composed of a Grand Master
(whose address shall be Most Worshipful), a Deputy
Grand Master, a Senior Grand Warden, and a Junior
Grand Warden (whose addresses shall severally be Right
Worshipful), a Grand Treasurer, a Grand Secretary and
a Grand Lec~urer (whose addresses shall severally be
Very Worshipful), a Grand Chaplain whose address
shall be Very Reverend ) , the Assistant Grand Lecturers,
a Grand Orator, an Assistant Grand Treasurer an
Assistant Grand Secretary, a Grand Marshal, a G~and
Standard Bearer, a Grand Sword Bearer, a Grand Bible
Bearer, a Senior Grand Deacon, a Junior Grand Deacon,
Two Grand Stewards, a Grand Pursuivant, a Grand
Organist, and a Grand Tiler (whose addresses shall severally be Worshipful): together with all the Past Grand
Officers and Past Masters of this jurisdiction, and the
Mast~rs and Wardens of the several chartered and duly
constituted Lodges, or the representatives thereof duly
elected."

. C~nformity ~th the language of the section just quoted would seem
to indicate th.at in ~?e opening ceremonies of Grand Lodge the response
to the question: Who compose the Grand Lodge of California?"
should be "The Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master the Senior
Grand Warden, etc." The effect of the resolution of 1947 ~as to omit
the address of "Most Worshipful." "Right Worshipful." and "Very
":'orshipful" i_n that response ~nd use. the address only when the particular officer is spoken to. This practice has been uniform in much of
our Grand Lodge proceedings. The purpose and effect of the resolution of 1947 was to make it entirely so. It should be emphasized at this
P_Oint. t~at the resolution of 1947 did not result in any change in the
r1tua~1sbc work of the subordinate lodges and is expressly limited to
operung, closing and installation ceremonies of the Grand Lodge.
There is no uniformity among the Grand Lodges in the United
States in this general field. The titles of officers differ from state to state.
some have officers unknown to us and we have officers possessed by
no other Grand Lodge, seating arrangements vary, the word is not
conveyed in some jurisdictions, the term Most Worshipful is not used
at all in Pennsylvania, in some jurisdictions Right Worshipful is used
in connection with a certain officer and only Worshipful in connection
with the same officer in another jurisdiction. Language comparable to
that in section three of our constitution is not to be found in the constitutions of 46 out of the 48 other Grand Lodges in the United States:
hence there is no guide to be found in the other grand jurisdictions
as to what the usage should be in California.

Your committee therefore reports that, in its opinion, when in 194 7
Grand Lodge adopted the resolution sought to be rescinded, it properly
eliminated from the opening. closing and installation ceremonies of
Grand Lodge the wording which was at variance with our fundamental
law and that no further action was necessary to effect those corrections.
It is obviously inappropriate to set forth those corrections in this
report. They may readily be noted in the "Code" furnished Grand
Officers for their convenience in preparing for the Grand Lodge ceremonies involved.
It is therefore recommended that the 1948 report of the Ritual Committee be filed and that the resolution of 194 7 be not rescinded.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
At the last annual communication of the Grand Lodge of California
the Grand Master made the following recommendation:
( g) I recommend the appointment of a special committee to study
Masonic trial procedures of the several Grand Jurisdictions and to
recommend revisions in our trial ordinances.
I believe that the quality of our trials and of our Masonic justice
can be improved and that the Brothers of the Lodges will welcome a
revision, which removes from them the burdens and responsibilities of
sitting in judgment upon one of their own members.
In many jurisdictions the trials are conducted by special panels of
experienced Masons appointed by the Grand Master for the particular
trial. and the case for the prosecution is presented by a representative
of the Grand Lodge.
Respecting this recommendation the following action was taken by
Grand Lodge:
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes to which was
referred that portion of the Grand Master's Message designated as
Recommendation ( g) by which the Grand Master recommends that a
special committee to study Masonic trial procedure of the several Grand
Jurisdictions and to recommend revisions in our trial ordinances has
given the same consideration.
Your Committee is not sufficiently advised at present to determine
whether there be a need for revision of our trial procedure but believe
that if this portion of our code can be improved it should be done, and
therefore approve the Grand Master's recommendation for the appointment of the proposed committee of investigation.
The undersigned members of the Special Committee on Trial Procedures beg leave to report as follows:
The California Met hod: Article 4 fo the Ordinances of the Grand
Lodge of California prescribes the method of trial of members of the
Order. A Mason may be tried for any violation of Masonic or moral
law, and reprimanded, suspended or expelled.
The first incident in a Masonic trial in California is the preferring
of charges. This may be done by any member in good standing. If
facts are brought to the attention of the Junior Warden warranting a
Masonic trial, it is his duty to prefer the charges unless brought by
some other Mason.
The charges are presented to the Master of the lodge. A special
meeting of the members of the lodge is then called. At that meeting
a trial commission is elected, consisting of not less than seven nor more
than nine members of the lodge.
The Master then names a time and place for the first meeting of the

154

155

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND •LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

trial commission, notifies the accuser thereof, and directs that summons
and copy of the charges be served upon the accused. The summons
advises the accused of the time and place of the meeting, and requires
him to appear and answer the charges.
At its first meeting the trial commission organizes. The accused
presents his answer to the charges and specifications.
If the accused pleads not guilty, testimony for the accuser and the
accused is heard before the trial commission, the trial continuing with
necessary adjournments until completed. The secretary with the aid
of a stenographic reporter, keeps a record of the proceedings. If the
accused does not appear or if he pleads guilty, the trial commission
nevertheless takes, and makes a record of the testimony substantiating
the charge.
After all the testimony is received, the commissioners deliberate
and determine upon their verdict as to the truth of the specifications,
and, if any of the specifications are found true, fix the sentence.
A complete record of the proceedings is then made up, certified by
the Master and Secretary, and forwarded to the Grand Secretary. This
is the trial record.
In California trial records are referred to the Committee on Griev~
ances. This Committee examines each of them, and reports thereon to
Grand Lodge at its annual communication. Grand Lodge may affirm.
modify, or reverse the judgment of the trial commission, or make any
other proper order relative thereto.
The method in other jurisdictions: We are indebted to our · Grand
Secretary, Lloyd E. Wilson, and to the Masonic Service Association
of Washington, D. C., for a comprehensive report on trial methods of
Grand Lodges of the United States, 'brought up to date June 9, 1949.
There is one characteristic common to every grand jurisdiction.
Masonic offenses are offenses against the dignity of Masonry, and the
Grand Lodge in the last analysis has complete jurisdiction over them.
This jurisdiction is exercised in California by Grand Lodge delegating
trials to commissions elected by subordinate lodges, reserving the right
in any case to affirm, modify, or reverse the findings and decisions of
trial commissions. And when Grand Lodge so acts its decision is final.
Trial by the Lodge: A number of grand jurisdictions stiU retain what
perhaps was the first method of trial. That is trial by the lodge. Testi~
mony is taken before the lodge itself, with its members present. After
the testimony is concluded arguments are had by the accuser and the
accused, and then any member present may express his opinion. Fina1ly
the lodge by vote of its members determines the guilt or innocence
of the accused; and again, by vote of its members, fixes the penalty.
Trial by lodge is, however, in every state subject to the paramount
jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge. Genera1ly this jurisdiction is exercised
by reference to a grand lodge committee similar to our own Committee

on Grievances. This committee reviews the record of the trial, and
makes its recommendation to Grand Lodge. The fo1lowing states still
use the trial by lodge method: Alabama, Delaware, Georgia, Indiana,
Ohio, New Mexico, and Vermont.
Trial in open lodge or by commission, or committee: Then we find a
combination of trial by the lodge or by commission, generally at the
option of the lodge. If the trial is by commission, the commission finds
the fact of guilt and recommends the penalty, as in California, with
Grand Lodge always having the final right of determination as to fact
and penalty. States using this method are: Arkansas, Colorado, Con~
necticut, Il1inois, Louisiana, Montana, Oklahoma, Rhode Island, Ten~
nessee, Wisconsin (commission): Iowa, South Carolina, Wasbington,
West Virginia and Wyoming (committee).
The trial commission method: Next we come to what may be termed
the trial commission method. A commission generally composed of
masters and past masters hears the evidence, determines the fact, and
fixes the penalty. This is the system in California as already described.
Other states using this method are: Arizona, Nevada, Oregon, and
Utah (commission elected by lodge).
In the following states the trial commission is appointed by the
master of the lodge: Michigan, Pennsylvania, and South Dakota.
In New Jersey and Virginia the commission is appointed by a
district grand master: in North Carolina by an officer of Grand Lodge
caHed a judge advocate, and in Texas by a lodge committee, and in
Kansas by a lodge committee appointed by the Grand Master.
Trial by commission appointed by the Grand Master: The fo11owing
states try their members by a commission appointed by the Grand
Master: Idaho, Maine, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska,
New Hampshire, New York, and North Dakota.
There are differences in details of appointment, qualifications of
commissioners, etc., but generally the pattern may be illustrated by
what may be termed the New York procedure:
Any Mason may make a complaint. The Grand Master passes
upon the sufficiency thereof. If found sufficient, he appoints a trial
commission of not less than three nor more than five masters or past
masters, members of at least three different lodges and not members
of the lodge whose member is to be tried. The commissioner first desig~
nated acts as chairman, and in practice is customarily a judge or out~
standing member of the legal profession.
Then the complaint is forwarded to a Grand Lodge officer called
a proctor. His duties correspond roughly with the duties of a district
attorney in a criminal case. The proctor prepares formal charges, has
them served upon the accused, and prosecutes the case to judgment.
The trial commission finds guilt or innocence and determines the penalty.

157

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Appeals go to an appeal commission, which functions much the
same as our Committee on Grievances.
Conclusions: California never had the lodge trial method. And for
many reasons we should never adopt it. It should readily be apparent
that such a procedure would degenerate into a contest of who can make
the most noise and rally the most votes.
The question with us is whether we should adopt a method similar
to New York's, or retain our own present procedure.
On this question your committee begs leave to present the following
observations: The New York method takes completely away from the
local lodge the right to try its members. It is our opinion that it would
be a mistake to deprive the subordinate lodges of the California juris~
diction of this right. The brother accused tried and convicted in his
own lodge feels better having been tried by a commission selected by
his own lodge from its own membership. And many times there are
questions of fact which turn on a hair, and which can be determined
we think more justly by a man's own brethren in his own lodge. .If
mistakes are made, they can be rectified by Grand Lodge.
True some trials become excessively burdensome in the expenditure
of time and work and money by the local lodges. That burden must
be borne somewhere and could not be more justly placed than on the
lodge whose member causes it, and where the burden now rests. And,
in any event, mistakes and miscarriages of Masonic justice can always
be corrected by Grand Lodge.
Should we have in California a proctor, as they.have in New York?
Masonic trials are technical because they deal with sacred Masonic
rights. Our Masonic brethren may not be deprived of these rights
without strict compliance with age~old rules scientifically worked out
by the legal profession. While ascertainment of the truth in a trial
tribunal is a science it should always approximate a jury trial under
some professional guidance such as is later outlined. Laymen not
familiar with legal rules and legal procedure should not attempt to
apply them in a Masonic trial.
Equally important is the paramount right of Masonry to rid itself
of individuals who bring discredit or disgrace upon it and who impair
its dignity and good name.
When men untrained in the law attempt to carry through a Masonic
trial trouble ensues. Time and again trials have to be done over, to
preserve the rights either of the accused or of Grand Lodge, which have
been overlooked or overridden.
·
It is quite possible that an officer like a district attorney, charged
with the duty of preparing charges and prosecuting them to judgment
would do a better job in Masonic trials in California.
This involves several perplexing problems. Would he be an officer
with state~wide duties? In that case Grand Lodge would have to name
a permanent officer.

Such an officer would quite likely have to give full time to the work.
We are of the opinion that no amount of salary which Grand Lodge
would feel proper to pay would command the legal services now readily
available in most of the lodges in our state. We are sure that there are
available now Masons in every inspectorial district in California, lawyers of ability, who would gladly perform these services without charge
if requested as a Masonic service. Ordinarily such services would be
required only occasionally. And we think that many of the difficulties
experienced in California in the conduct of trials by trial commissions,
have been because the services of members of the bar, at the same time
members of our craft, were not requested.
Therefore, we recommend that Masters who preside and brethren
who prosecute or defend at Masonic trials be urged to contact and
utilize this source of help. No changes in our present ordinances are
necessary for this purpose.
Finally, we feel that we should try the last suggestion for a time
at least before we change our present system of trial procedure.

HERBERT A. HUEBNER

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON DE MOLAY

To give you an idea how valuable the teachings of De Malay are
to the coming generation, just listen to a few comments from members
as presented in the Oriental Consistory News published by the Scottish
Rite Bodies of Y anktown, South Dakota.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The work of your Committee on De Malay activities is progressing
as well as can be expected but there is still much to be done before
our goal can be reached, that of causing Masons generally to be De
Malay conscious. This is our third report to the Grand Lodge and each
time we have endeavored to make it in such form as to stimulate those
present to take an active interest in our work by having De Malay
nights in your Lodges. Good Officers of Lodges are always on the
lookout for programs to present which will be of interest to the membership.
If it were possible for committee members to visit each Lodge in
the jurisdiction three or four times a year to keep the members thinking
about what De Malay is doing for the boy or young man who sooner
or later and it might be sooner than you think, is destined to replace
us in the affairs of life, we are sure that much better results could be
realized. As that is not possible we mt!st depend upon you representatives attending this session to carry our message back to your Lodges
and not let them forget it. We are sure that you will be both surprised
and pleased at the reaction of your members to both the De Malay
programs and to the keeping of its objectives before them.
The members of your Committee have enjoyed the carrying of the
message of De Malay to many Lodges and we are happy to report that
the results of past efforts are becoming more and more apparent, as
indicated by the change in the attitude of the Lodges which we have
visited, now they know what we are talking about, which was not the
case two or three years ago. We have also had the pleasure of appearing before the Bay District Master and Wardens _Associations.
Through the efforts of Brother K. V. Smith, the San Diego member
of the Committee; Knox Manning, the well-known radio commentator,
devoted a portion of his radio time on April twelfth, CBS coast-wide
broadcast, to a discussion of the origin, aims and accomplishments of
De Malay. This publicity is of course very valuable to De Molay and
while it is not a part of this Committee's duties to aid in adding to the
membership in De Malay Chapters we do feel that anything which aids
in its growth is worth while to the extent that it adds to the number of
fine citizens of tomorrow. Make no mistake about it, De Malay is a
power in this land of ours in making for good citizenship.
Also at the suggestion of Brother Smith, we are working on plans
for a get together of all the Lodges and Chapters in the San Diego
area for a dinner and entertainment. Chester Lauck and Norris Goff.
Lum and Abner to you and both former members of De Malay Chapters.
have agreed to take part in the program.

1. "No one thing has ever impressed me more than our first precept.
It has made me aware of the everlasting devotion due my parents.
If I should never obtain another thing from De Malay, I would
feel amply repaid for the time I have spent."
2. "I never had the ability to stand on my feet and express my
thoughts in a clear way without becoming confused and excited
until I joined De Malay."

3. "Young men who have taken the trouble to pledge themselves,
honestly to strive for De Malay ideals are just the kind of decent
companions a young man needs. In such comradeship, and
guided by men he respects, what boy can help but profit from
becoming a member of the order."
4. "The ritualistic work, the De Malay standards and ideals are
a beacon light to guide me through the plastic years before
manhood.''
5. "De Malay has strengthened my sense of civic duty. Since becoming a member of the Order I have made an clfort to be of
greater value to the community in which I live, a more vital
factor in the happiness and well being of my home and a greater
moving force in my church."

,

Here are five young men each getting a different lesson from the
teachings he received while taking the degrees, one--devotion to his
parents, one-self confidence. one--fine companionship, one--ideals for
future guidance and the last, increased sense of civic and church duty.
We have always discouraged the idea that the Masonic fraternity
considers De Malay as a recruiting ground for Masonry, however it is
a fact that young men who have attained their majority, after having
been members of De Malay Chapters, are naturally interested in an
order which provided Chapters Dads and Advisors whom they highly
respect. These young men, by virtue of the teachings and experience
with the ritual of De Malay, make outstanding members wherever they
have joined a Masonic Lodge and we think that you will agree that we
need young men of character more today than ever before in our history.
You will find no subversive elements coming from a Chapter of De
Malay. In many Lodges visited we found officers who had been active
in the work of De Malay.
Once more may we be permitted to suggest that you invite a Chapter
to exemplify a De Malay degree at one of your stated meetings. From
past experience we believe that you will find that more of your members

Your Committee on Masonic Information reports as follows:
The work of your Committee has unfortunately been retarded during
the past year an,d the continuity of its program somewhat interrupted,
with considerable loss of momentum. Obviously, a work of this kind
carried on among 600 lodges demands uniform and consistent effort,
so that it becomes routine and a matter of habit with lodge officers. A
break in its continuity necessarily results in inattention, loss of interest,
and, finally, a complete break down.
In 1947, your Committee recommended two small booklets entitled
"Address to the Candidate" and "Book of the Entered Apprentice."
These were approved by Grand Lodge, printed and distributed to the
lodges. These two booklets called forth numerous, unsolicited commendations from officers of lodges, leading your Committee to believe
that it was on the right course. Two reprints were soon necessary and,
at the present time, it is understood some lodges have exhausted their
supplies, which it is hoped can soon be replenished.
In 1948, your Committee presented manuscripts for two additional
booklets, the "Book of the Fellow Craft" and the "Book of the Master
Mason," the latter naturally being much more pretentious than the
others, since it included a general explanation designed to aid the newly
raised Master Mason in gaining a perspective of Freemasonry and
fixing his place in the Fraternity. It embraced a broad survey of Freemasonry, its teachings and purposes: a succinct statement of the privileges and duties of the Master Mason; some observations on the important matter of serving on Committees, particularly, Committees of
Investigation and means of guarding the portals of the lodge; the furtherance of peace and harmony; explanations of the positions and prerogatives of the Master, Inspector and Grand Master: an outline of the
organization and functions of the Grand Lodge; a brief treatise on the
laws and customs of Freemasonry; a word a.b out the Masonic Homes
and other charities, and, finally, an encouragement of the new Master
Mason to feel at home and to become an active participant in the affairs
of the lodge.
In short, this booklet is designed to give the newly raised Master
Mason, in concise form, not only for original instruction, but for future
reference, information that he would not acquire in the ordinary way
under several years.
Your Committee had anticipated having these two booklets, completing the series of four, in the hands of the lodges long ere this, but
due to the importance of the matter and the necessity for rendering
assurance of accuracy doubly certain, the text has been reveiwed by
the Grand Master and other Grand Officers and your Committee be-

REPORT OF TRUSTEES OF MASONIC CLUB HOUSE,
BERKELEY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
In view of the resignation of Past Grand Master C~arles Albert
Adams as President of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Club of
the University, Berkeley, I submit the following report summarizing the
work and activities of your board and the prospective expenses for the
coming fiscal year.
. For the benefit in general of all of you, but more particularly for the
information of the new Masters and. Wardens. who here represent for
the first time their respective lodges, may we at the outset remind you
just where the Berkeley Clubhouse is located. It is at the corner of
Bancroft Way and Bowditch Street in Berkeley, directly across the
street from the Women's Gymnasium on the Berkeley Campus. The
entrance is on Bancroft Way, just one block east of the busy intersection of Telegraph Avenue and Bancroft Way. We extend a cordial
invitation to all the brothers and their ladies to take this opportunity
while here at this annual communication, to visit the clubhouse and
see just how it functions and where your dollars have been expended.
It has been arranged for those of you who are going to the home at
Decoto in buses to return via the Berkeley Clubhouse. A map for your
direction and pictures of the building and improvements are on display
in the history section.
Located as we are, in close proximity to the fine newer structures
of the University of California in Berkeley, your directors have always
been of the opinion that you would want any home or clubhouse bearing
the name "Masonic" to be in keeping with the other structures in this
vicinty and to be a credit to our fraternity. Last year the Grand Lodge
very generously, and with the approval and upon the recommendation
of the Finance Committee, made available to our board for remodeling
the sum of $35,000.00, which is the largest sum Grand Lodge has ever
directly given or made available to the Berkeley Clubhouse. In other
words, this is the first major alteration program since the dedication
of the building by Past Grand Master Arthur S. Crites in 1924. You
appropriated directly from the General Fund $20,000.00 for this purpose
and directed the trustees to use at least $15,000.00 of our own reserve
funds to help pay the cost of such repairs and replacements, said com-

Here, we pause to pay tribute to three outstanding leaders of the
University Clubhouse movement whom we have lost as members and
officers of our Board this past year, namely, Brother Adams, by
resignation, and Brothers Farmer and Herms by death. We have
attached to this report as Exhibit 1 a copy of the resignation as member
and President of the Board, of Past Grand Master Charles Albert
Adams, effective October 1, 1949, which we have accepted with sincerest regret and with the same heart-wrench which he expresses
therein. It was my privilege to have been one of the original group of
students who organized in the year 1919 the first Masonic Club of the
University at Berkeley and I speak with first hand knowledge when
I say that he was one of the very first representatives of Grand Lodge
to envision a clubhouse to accommodate the many Masons returning
to the University following World War I. It was he who, during his
year as Grand Master, procUl'ed the initial appropriation from Grand
Lodge in the sum of $2,000.00 for the building. He was a member of,
and in constant attendance upon, all the preliminary meetings with the
many Past Grand Masters in the committees which prepared the plans
for the building and arranged for the raising by subscriptions of over
$150,000 from the Masons of this state. He was one of the original
incorporators of the Board and has been a member of it since its inception and is, as he states, the sole survivor of the original Board. It is
impossible in this report to adequately convey to him and to you the
deep debt of gratitude which we and the students of the University,
who have had the benefit of his initiative, his wisdom and his counsel.
all owe to Brother Adams. We treasure his friendship.
During the early part of this year we were shocked when we learned
of the sudden passing in Chicago of Judge Milton T. Farmer, who had
been our President for the past several years. He had just concluded
presenting a matter before the United States Supreme Court and died
of a heart attack. A man of strong character, firm but just, we will miss
him in the guidance of our affairs and in his representation of us here
in Grand Lodge.
Our Vice-President, Professor William B. Herms, thereupon assumed the post of President only to be likewise stricken on May 9,
1949 and within a few months of the death of the Judge. "Billy," as

he was affectionately known to our members, the students and the
faculty, like Brother Adams, was closely associated with the whole
clubhouse movement and the student organ~zation which antedated it.
He was also the principal organizer and Master Under Dispensation,
and first Master of Henry Morse Stephens Lodge No. 541. He was
an eminent scientist and gave the clubhouse and its Board and its
student members a close contact with the faculty of the University
where he was Professor of Entomology and head of the Department
of Entomology and Parasitology.
The services of these three men have been invaluable and their
wisdom and advice will be missed at all our forthcoming meetings.

Pursuant to the definite understanding at the time I consented to
accept the Presidency, after the deaths of President Farmer and Vice
President Herms, I am now resigning as President of the corporationand also as a Trustee.

Gentlemen:
The University Masonic Club at the University of California in
Berkeley enjoyed a most successful year in the academic year of 194849. The membership of the fall semester was 562, while that of the
spring semester was 468.

Because of my intimate association with the inception of the movement for the building of the Clubhouse, and also in view of the fact that
I was one of the incorporators, and a member of the first Board of
Trustees of which I am the sole survivor, it is naturally with keen regret
and a bit of heart wrench that I now sever my connection with the
institution which has meant so much to me for so many years.
It will be remembered, however, by some of the Trustees that I had
intended retiring from the Board at the end of the term for which I had
been elected in 1945; and that I was induced by Brother Farmer (without much persuasion on his part, I must admit) to continue for another
term.

It has been difficult for me, living here in San Francisco, to attend
as many meetings of the Board as I feel a Trustee should; and this has
led to my determination to resign as a Trustee as well as President of
the corporation.
You will therefore please consider this as my resignation as President and also as a Trustee, to take effect October l, 1949.
I trust that you who know me need no assurance of my willingness,
indeed eagerness, to serve the Club whenever, and wherever, I can.
With affectionate fraternal greetings to all of you, and with my best
wishes for the Club and for the young men and women who associate
themselves with it.
Sincerely and cordially,
CHARLES ALBERT ADAMS

The clubhouse, being centrally located and close to campus, was
used extensively throughout the year as a place for gathering with old
friends, for meeting and making friends with others having Masonic
affiliation, or as a place to rest and relax between classes, or to bone
up on that exam to be held later in the day. The club is all things to
all members; the noon hour may well illustrate the diversity of interests
as some prepare their repast in the kitchen so they may have a hot meal,
others bring a lunch from home while still others purchase theirs from
our own snack bar. There is ping-pong, pool, or bridge to relax the
over-taxed brain. It is difficult to estimate the number of members who
use the facilities daily, for so many are in and out many times daily.
An indication comes from the snack bar which served 50 to 60 persons
daily. An idea of attendance at the larger events of the two semesters
follows:

An attempt was made, during both semesters to present dances and
social evenings that would appeal to the majority of the mem'bership
while, at the same time, minority groups having interests in other fields
were not forgotten. Thus there were planned and executed in each
semester, a moonlight horseback ride and barbecue which were well
received by a small, but enthusiastic, group. In the spring, there was
a one--day snow trip by chartered bus to Echo Summit in the Sierras
which was sold out, one evening was devoted to the bowling and ice·
skating enthusiasts, and a very successful picnic was held at Mitchell
Canyon.
Some of the permanent special interest groups were quite active,
while others were not as active as they had been in the past. In the
former category was the club newspaper which was very helpful in
dissemination of club news and announcements. The snack bar was
quite active, keeping open daily from 11 :30 to 1 :30 and was a big
drawing card in bringing the members of the club to the clubhouse
during the noon hour. The photography club took pictures of all the
larger events and sold individual portraits to patrons of the dances to
help pay its loan to the Trustees. The idea of the photography club
being a "club within a club" was found to be unsatisfactory for several
reasons and arrangements have been made whereby the President will
appoint a qualified member as manager for the darkroom.
During the spring, considerable planning and thought, on the part
of Trustees and members, evolved a fine remodeling job for the clubhouse, and I am sure that the members appreciate the work that went
into this project. Unfortunately, during the spring, the club lost two of
its most loyal and unselfish trustees, Judge Milton T. Farmer and
Professor William B. Herms. Both of these fine men will be sorely
missed for their invaluable help and guidance.
The Fall President Jackie Clements, myself, and all members of the
club are especially grateful to Mrs. Morton, our club hostess and guiding
light, who has given unstintingly of her time to guide and counsel the
officers and members of the club throughout the year.
Sincerely and fraternally yours,
DoNALD A. MARSHALL, President, Spring 1949
University Masonic Club, Berkeley, California

REPORT OF BOARD OF DIRECTORS MASONIC CLUB
HOUSE AT LOS ANGELES

During the year special meetings of the Board of Directors were
called by the chairman every sixty Clays at the Club House. The
Directors in attendance broke up into groups of two and ate dinner
with groups of students. These special meetings were usually called
on Tuesday evenings, the meeting time of the student council. so that
the Directors might not only get the pulse of the students informally
about the table. but might observe them in their business sessions.
These meetings have not only been mutually beneficial, but have contributed to a sense of unity of purpose and further cemented the bond
between the Directors and the students.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California:

It was just twenty years ago that the Masonic Club House at the
University of California at Los Angeles was built and opened for the
use of students of Masonic affiliation. At that time one could see but
a few structures of any kind within a radius of several miles. The
University was about to move to its new campus and the Westwood
Hills were much as nature had made them. Today the enrollment at
the University has increased from less than 3,000 to the present official
figure of 15,016, 12,143 undergraduates and 2.873 graduate students
and there is scarcely a parcel of ground that is not improved for business or residential purposes.
During the past year student activities have been more numerous
and diversified than in any previous year. Six hundred and fifty students were dues paying members of the club. The program has included formal and informal social affairs, charitable endeavors and
recreational activities.
Seven major dances were held with an average attendance of 275.
Informal parties held each Friday have been devoted to dancing, ice
skating. theatres and other recreation. The average attendance at
these week-end affairs has been 100.
One of the highlights of the year was the formal banquet and
reception tendered to the Grand Master. Attendance was 400 and the
Grand Master brought a message which was inspiring and duly appreciated.
The increased charitable interest of the student group was evidenced during the year by: the donation of the proceeds from one of
the formal balls to the camp for underprivileged children, a Thanksgiving Day dinner for thirty boys and girls from the All Nations
Institute who otherwise would not have had a Thanksgiving, a bimonthly tour of the campus and dinner for different boys and girls
selected by the All Nations Institute and the supplying of five volunteer
workers each week to that organization.
With a social program which has been too extensive to set out in
detail herein, it should be remembered however that the Club House
has continued to be a haven for study on a crowded campus and many
students would find association with it advantageous for this purpose
alone. In addition it has been possible for them to obtain meals buffet
style at near cost prices. Termed a Snack Bar. the food dispensing
facilities have grown to the point where cooks and others are employed
on a fu11 time basis; a neat return to the student group has been realized.

At the August meeting of the Board and again in September the
Chairman of the Board tendered his resignation from the Board because
of his Grand Lodge office, but the Board refused to accept it.
The Board has prepared and adopted the following budget for
the ensuing year:

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CENTENNIAL
ARRANGEMENTS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Special Committee on Centennial Arrangements has continued
exploration of an appropriate and practical program for the Centennial.
In that respect there have been meetings of the committee and informal
conferences. Also some sub-committees have been designated. The
Committee has made advantageous use of the study and suggestion
of the preceding committee.
The objectives to be attained have not been definitely formulated,
and as the detail must conform to the plan there is nothing to report
in that respect. In fact, it is only practical to inform Grand Lodge
at this time that satisfactory prograss is being made and that a comprehensive report should be prepared and submitted to the respective
lodges at an early date. As related to the objectives, the Committee
recommends appropriate legislation to permit the attendance of Master
Masons during the opening of Grand Lodge.
It is hoped to lease the space (in the Balboa Building. 593 Market
Street) which has been occupied for the purposes of management and
committees related to the entertainment of those attending the recent
Triennial Grand Encampment of Knights Templar. It is conveniently
located and the space will be required for Centennial management
and committee operations. Also, Brother William llinmack has been
engaged to serve as General Manager.
While the Committee on Finances recommended at the 1948 Communication that the Centennials Committee be authorized to make con-

175

tracts an~ commitments, as indicated, and that the Grand Secretary
be authorized to honor warrants against the Centennial Fund, it is
believed that the procedure should be clarified. For purposes of convenience and efficiency the Committee on Centennial Arrangements
should be empowered to delegate authority to approve claims and
necessary expenditures, including salaries and wages, for payment,
and that such should he audited and paid by the Grand Treasurer in
accordance with the ex(sting Grand Lodge procedure.
Respectfully submitted,
FRANCIS v. KEESLING

REPORT OF MEMORIAL BUILDING COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
At the 1948 Communication of Grand Lodge the Committee, now
known as Memorial Building Committee, reported that the objective
was an edifice that would serve the purposes of Grand Lodge, be appropriate for a memorial and productive o{ income. The Committee also
referred to the complex problems involved, including satisfactory location for all purposes, and finance.
Proceeding in accordance with the objectives we report important
negotiations, but that nothing sufficient has been developed to warrant
firm preliminary commitment.
There are sites being considered which fit the pattern and diligent
efforts are being made to complete negotiations, so that having developed a satisfactory basic plan, it may be submitted with sufficient
information for intelligent action by Grand Lodge.
It is the recommendation of the Committee that a Memorial Building Committee be continued.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CONSTITUTION
MONTH OBSERVANCE

calculable rights which we denominate our Bill of Rights were to be
made the basis of our Government.
The .United States has emerged from the war as the most powerful
nation on earth. The system of government that has made all this possible, that has given us the highest standard of living ever known. that
has opened the way for our amazing progress. and has provided opportunity, happiness. and blessings not enjoyed anywhere else in the world
-such a system of government certainly is worth saving. And it must
be saved.
The Constitution of the United States has been a powerful force in
the lives of all of the people of the world and of all generations of people
ever since its adoption, although its authority does not extend beyond
the borders of our own country. Dictators and tyrants have succeeded
too well in keeping humanity in subjugation and ever in chains, but they
cannot extinguish the yearning for freedom from men and women who
know that for more than a century and a half a way of life has prevailed
in America which lends dignity to the people and enriches and ennobles
them according to their worthiness.
With such a system of government and law established in the world,
even though only one nation enjoyed it and prospered under it, no
aspiration for a similar way of life in any part of the world is futileand it is the worldwide understanding and appreciation of that fact
which has given universal importance to the Constitution of the United
States ever since its adoption.
As A~erica faces the future let us pause to recollect that the farseeing vision of our constitutional fathers resulted in an instrument of
government which no foe of human rights has penetrated and survival
of which has met every challenge to the natural rights of man. Our most
formidable fortress of defense in time of stress still remains the Constitution of the United States.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
I have the honor to submit a report of the Committee of the Grand
Lodge Free and Accepted Masons of California on Constitution Month
Observance.
The Committee is pleased to advise you that more interest has been
demonstrated throughout the Jurisdiction in the matter of this Observance during the year just concluded than has attended the efforts of the
Committee during any former year. The Brethren throughout the Jurisdiction have responded well to the various requests directed to them by
the Committee, and we wish to take this opportunity to thank them for
their support and interest. The Inspectors of the various districts were
also of considerable assistance, and we likewise express our thanks to
them. The Committee has worked in harmony, and the utmost assistance
and cooperation was present at all times. I wish to take this opportunity
to express my sincere thanks for the efforts which they have expended.
The Committee wishes to thank those members of the Craft too
numerous to set forth with particularity, but who responded so well to
our pleas for speakers.
The reports which the Lodges have forwarded to the Grand Secretary's office tabulate 330 meetings with a total attendance of 29,155
divided as follows:
214 Closed meetings: 14,317 attended.
116 Open meetings: 14,838 attended.
Constitution Month Observance in California has now become an
accepted tradition, and this is due in large part to the efforts of this
Grand Lodge. While it is true that for many years we were the only
fraternal organization in this State committed to an observance of the
birth of the Constitution, we now find that scores of other fraternal and
civic organizations have joined in a general observance of the n<:ltal day
of the Constitution. This is a healthy situation to note.
I wish also to express my sincere appreciation to our Most Worshipful Grand Master, Edward H. Siems, who during the entire Masonic
year impressed upon Mason and citizen alike the necessity for a strict
observance of this sacred document, and may I likewise express my
deep appreciation for the cooperation and assistance of our Grand Secretary. Lloyd E. Wilson. By reason of their endeavors Masonry
throughout the Jurisdiction has made substantial contributions to the
cause of good government, thus renewing our commitment to the American way of life and the worthy principles espoused by this immortal
document.

more. When our forefathers met at Independence Hall in Philadelphia
to frame the Constitution. they were familiar with the lessons of history,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON LODGE FINANCING
To the Most Worshipful Gr~nd Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Lodge Financing presents herewith a brief
review of its activities during the past year.
It is apparent from the number of applications received and inquiries
directed to the committee that, with few exceptions, the officers of lodges
and temple associations are anxious to comply with the provisions of
Section 78 and 152 dealing with lodge financing. Not only are they
willing to comply. but it is evident from the requests coming to the members of your committee for advice and counsel in financial problems that
they welcome the service we have endeavored to render.
While this report must necessarily be confined to a brief statement
concerning each application or request presented to your committee, a
complete file covering all the facts in each case is available in the office
of the Grand Secretary.

The most pleasing task before your committee during the year was
the consideration of requests for permission and consent given to commence the erection of Temples. In some of the cases enumerated all of
the labor incident to building was volunteered by craftsman lodge members, in others a goodly portion. It is particularly gratifying that the
financing of these buildings will include no fixed debt other than one
non-interest bearing loan by a Lodge to its Temple Association, with
possibly one exception, and in that case a small amount in proportion
to the total investment. Incorporated in the consent given to each
applicant was the stipulation that no liabilities be incurred beyond those
currently approved without further consultation with the committee.
Lodge room design had the attention of the District Inspector with
respect to suitability for proper tiling and where ground_Boor lodge
rooms were planned the attention of the Grand Master.

estimated cost of $100,000 were presented. To carry out the undertaking

found a variance could not be secured without considerable difficulty.
Therefore, it was the decision of the Lodge that the land be disposed of.
Application was made to your committee for permission to use an
estimated $12.500 of the corporation's funds to prepare the property
for sub-dividing and public sale.
Your committee was of the opinion, while it might be true through
a sub-division a handsome profit might be made for the corporation,
there was a definite business risk involved, and that it was never contemplated that Masonry should enter the business world with a venture
designed for financial gain; that Masonry was still a fraternal order

dependent upon its members, and not upon independent business ventures for support. The request for such project was, therefore, disapproved.
