REPORT OF SPECIAL TAXATION COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Taxation Committee composed of Robert R. York, James E.
Hammond and R. P. Wisecarver was appointed for the current Masonic
year.
The work of the Committee has been almost entirely devoted to
answering queries from the subordinate lodges or their temple associations. Each of these problems is governed by its special facts and no
good purpose would be served by a detailed discussion of each case.
All have been handled and disposed of by correspondence.
We insert the following letter as an example of the type of information given out by the Committee, because it has a wide application:
"We have your question relayed to us through Brother
Oliphant as to whether lodges have to carry workmen's compensation insurance. The answer is 'yes.'
"Section 3300, Labor Code, provides that every person is
an employer within the meaning of the Code, who has any
natural person in its service. A 'person' is defined as an individual. firm, voluntary association, or a public or quasi-public
or private corporation.
"Section 3351 provides that an employee means every person in the service of an employer under any appointment or
contract of hire or apprenticeship, express or implied, oral or
written, whether lawfully or unlawfully employed.
"Section 3352 of the Labor Code specifies certain exceptions, but none of them have any application to the Masonic
Lodge.
"Section 3700, Labor Code, provides that every private
employer must either procure insurance in an admitted compensation insurance carrier or procure a certificate of consent
to self-insure upon furnishing satisfactory evidence of financial
responsibility. The usual requirement is a minimum of
$30,000.00 bonds for such self-insurance.
"Section 3706, Labor Code, provides that if no insurance
is carried, the employee may bring a suit for damages against
the employer, may attach his property and it will be presumed
the employer's negligence caused the injury; and Section 3710
provides for a fine of $300.00 for failure to be insured, and the
employer's business may be abated as a nuisance.
"Hence, we repeat you had better be insured."
For the second consecutive year Congress has failed to act on
numerous bills pending that would greatly affect the Federal Tax situation. This stalemate will undoubtedly be resolved in the near future

expected.

Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren:
Your Committee on Application Forms and Investigating Committee Procedure reports as follows:
Our Most Worshipful Grand Master, in his travels throughout
the jurisdiction, found much concern in the subordinate lodges over
the form of some of the questions in our application forms, and the lack
of some questions which were thought to be essential to secure adequate information as to the past history of applicants for degrees and
affiliation.
Our Most Worshipful Grand Master also found great concern
over our present investigating procedures and the more or less superficial investigations of applicants which were being made, resulting in
many undersirable men becoming members of our fraternity.
In order to crystalize the thoughts which had beea expressed, and
solve these most important problems, our Most Worshipful Grand
Master wrote to many interested brethren, and to all of the Inspectors,
requesting that the recommendations of the officers and members of
the constituent lodges be ascertained and reported to him. A large file
of recommendations was thus accumulated which disclosed almost
universal concern as to the form of our applications and a unanimous
desire for more effective investigating procedures. This committee was,
therefore, appointed to review the fl.le and make its recommendations
to the Grand Lodge.
This committee compiled a digest of the recommendations of the
lodges, officers and districts, and is recommending to this Grand
Lodge the questions and procedures which were most universally
suggested.
We give you the background and procedure of this committee to
emphasize the fact that this report is not the ideas of a few men but is
the compilation of the wishes of the majority of those who reported.
It is a statement of what the majority of you brethren have asked for.
We will first cover the majority of recommendations for changes
in the application forms. They are as follows, and only apply to Applications for Degrees, unless otherwise stated:
1. That the question, "state explicity your business occupation for
the past ten years, and where conducted", be changed to, "state
you occupatiomt, name of employers, and location for past 10
years", followed by "From, To, Occupation, Employer, Employer's Address", with sufficient space to give the history of his
employment. The present question does not call for employer's
name or address and many reported that occupation was often
answered by giving only the employer's name. The detailed

194

195

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

information called for by the new form of question would be of
great assistance to the investigating committee. This recom~
mendation includes adding this question to application for affiliation forms also.
2. That the questions, "Have you resided in the State of California
the twelve months last past, and the place above named more
than six months?" and "Where have you resided the ten years
last past? If in more than one place, state the particular years
in each place", be changed to, "List the places where you have
resided during the past ten years and length of residence at each
place", followed by. "From, To, Residence (Street, Number,
City & State)". The present question can be answered by listing
cities. The new question would require detailed information as to
residence which would be very helpful to the investigating committee and answer the present long question. This recommendation applies to application for affiliations forms also.
3. That the .question, "Do you know of any physical. legal or moral
reason which would prevent you from becoming a Freemason?",
be changed to, "Do you know of any moral reason which would
prevent you from becoming a Freemason?", because the applicant
knows nothing of the physical and legal requirements of our
fraternity and is, accordingly. in no position to properly answer
questions on those requirements.
4. That the question, "State particularly any physical deformity
or defect". be changed to, "Describe thoroughly any physical
deformity or defect and any serious disease you have or have
had." The thought most universally expressed was the the
present question did not call for enough detailed information.
The questions the great majority thought should be added to the
application forms, and would not unduly lengthen the form, were as
follows:
1. That the question, "Of what country are you a citizen?", be
added in order to ascertain whether or not the applicant is a
citizen of the United States and if not, of what country is he a
citizen?
2. "Have you ever been arrested for a crime other than minor
traffic violations?-1£ so. where, when and what for?" It was
strongly felt we need that information so the investigating committee can check further and to put the applicant on record right
at the start. This recommendation applies to application for
affiliation forms, also.
. . . Those are the only additional questions ~e are recommending.
There were over 50 additional questions suggested. Some have been
included in a list of questions for investigating committees. There were

many general suggestions made as to investigating procedure. The
majority recommended as follows:
1. That the Inspectors be instructed to include a discussion of
investigating applicants in the program for one or more of the
district officers' association meetings.
2. That the officers, past masters and interested members, act as
a personnel committee or advisory board and meet with the applicant prior to the stated meeting at which the application is
received or will be balloted upon to thoroughly interview the
applicant. This would enable the officers to ge acquainted with
the applicant and supplement the investigating committee report.
The committee recommends:
1. That lodges have a regular committe for investigating applicants.
This committee would be appointed by the Master and its
membership would not be publicized. It would meet at the call
of the Master at least once a year, perferably in January. to
discuss and be instructed in the duties of an investigating committee and investigating procedures. Wherever possible. applica~
tions would be ref erred to members of this committee for invesfr
gation. It was felt that there are many members in our lodges
who would be glad to serve on this most important committee
and this procedure would gradually develop a competent and
fairly well trained group of· investigators to replace the more or
less hit or miss present system.
The recommendations as to the investigating committees themselves
were as follows:
1. That a printed sheet of instructions be furnished to each member of an investigating committee in place of the present form of
Reference of Application for Degrees. This form would read as
follows:
REFERENCE OF APPLICATION FOR DEGREES OR AFFILIATION

The adoption of this form would not increase the work of Masters
or Secretarys of lodges.
This has been a rather long and detailed report but your committee
felt that the importance of the problems to our fraternity and the great
interest shown by the lodges in their solution merited a full report and
discussion of the recommendations of the majority of the craft who
worked so diligently as was shown by their reports.
The recommendations of this report are your recommendations to
our Most Worshipful Grand Master and your committee recommends
the adoption of the recommendations reported herein. Full and complete investigation of applicants is the only way to maintain the standards of Freemasonry and keep our fraternity from being damaged or
destroyed by those who do not belong in Freemasonry and by those
who would join us to destroy us.

4. Has he any habits which tend to degrade his morals?
5. Does he pay his debts promptly?
6. Is he married or single? What family has he? Did you meet him
in his home and talk with his family?
7. Is his wife or family -in sympathy with his joining our Institution?
(This is quite important).
8. Does he live with and support his family as a husband should?
9. Has he provided for his family in case of death?
10. Is he likely to become a charge upon the Lodge or to apply for
admission to the Home of Decato?

13. Did you check his former employers or business connections?

15. Did you check his references?

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON BY-LAWS

Valle de France Lodge No. 329, to $100.00; Fruitvale Lodge No. 336,
to $125.00; Fort Bragg Lodge No. 361, to $75.00; Rockridge Lodge No.
468, to $125.00; Victory Lodge No. 474, to $100.00; Ionic Lodge No.

No. 650, to $100.00.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on By-laws has carefully considered the two hundred ninetrsix amendments to by-laws submitted by constituent Lodges.
At the October, 1948 Communication of Grand Lodge, the minimum
annual dues were fixed at $12.00. During the last year, two hundred
thirty-two Lodges amended their by-laws to conform thereto. The
Grand Secretary's office furnished to the Lodges a mimeographed form
to cover the necessary amendment. This procedure has been a great
help to the Lodges in amending their by-laws and has greatly aided
the work of our Committee in examining each of these amendments.
We found all to be in proper form and correctly completed. A duplicate
copy was returned to the Lodge as some Lodge records and files failed
to disclose previous by-law amendments, although such action had been
taken.

Decreasing fees: Kaweah Lodge No. 665, to $50.00.

•

Fifteen Lodges increased their fees, one Lodge decreased the fee
charged, and one Lodge adjusted its fees. Five Lodges took action affecting their affiliation fee. Thirteen Lodges amended their by-laws changing
date of stated meeting, one changing time of stated meeting, and two
took action providing for stated meetings falling on holidays. One
Lodge changed its annual election date to tl).e stated meeting in November now provided for under Article 4, Section 180 of the Ordinances.
Fifteen Lodges took action adopting the Uniform Code of By-laws.
Our Committee recommends that when such action is necessary, the
Lodge use the form available from the Grand Secretary's office. This
procedure will eliminate many omissions and difficulties. Secretaries
should be careful to fill in all blanks of the form when the Lodge takes
such action. Five sets of by-laws could not be approved and must be
continued, with your approval, for further amendments and additional
corrections by the secretary.
We feel that Masters during the past year have given special
attention to familiarizing themselves with the by-laws of the Lodge.
We urge that this be continued, in conformity with the admonition to
the Master in the installation ceremony.
All the following amendments have been approved by the Grand
Secretary and the Grand Master, as to form and Masonic law
requirements:

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PAY OF MEMBERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Pay of Members submits the following report
covering the 1OOth Annual Communication of Grand Lodge: ·
Those entitled to compensation are: the duly accredited Representatives of each Lodge, Inspectors, Past Grand Masters, Officers of
Grand Lodge, and the Chairman and Members of Committees enumerated in Section 68 of the Ordinances, who are actually in attendance at
Grand Lodge.
Compensation of members has been computed on the basis of twice
the one-way first class railway fare, plus Pullman sleeper, where necessary. As has been the custom for many years, no compensation is
allowed to members from San Francisco or the immediate vicinity, or
where the prescribed compensation does not exceed $1 .00.
We have computed the transportation rates from all points in California and Hawaii to San Francisco. We have checked the payroll
with the registration records as submitted to us by the Committee on
Credentials. The amount required to meet the transportation costs for
the 1949 Convocation is as follows : ·

Thanks is again due to Past Master Louis Sutter, and the AngloCalifomia National Bank, for making the necessary arrangements so
that members may cash their checks in this building at the close of the
Grand Lodge session. Checks will be ready for distribution following
the election of the Junior Grand Warden, Friday morning. Checks not
called for will be mailed by the Grand Secretary.

The Grand Master read a telegram of greeting as received from

October 8, 1949
WHEREAS, at the 99th annual communication of the Grand Lodge
a resolution was introduced proposing that the incoming Grand Master
appoint a special committee to investigate the purchase by the Grand
Lodge of the old historical Masonic Temple. at Benicia, which proposal
was recommended by the Committee on Policy and General Purposes,
and which resolution was adopted, and
WHEREAS, this committee was duly appointed by the Most Worshipful Grand Master. Edward H. Siems, and after due consideration,
careful investigation and deliberation, do find the following:
1. The wooden, two-story building situated at the rear of the present
Lodge Hall of Benicia Lodge No. 5, in the City of Benicia, is the first
Masonic Hall erected in California for purely Masonic purposes.
2. That this said building was commenced in the summer of the
year 1850, and was dedicated on December 27th of the same year by
the Deputy Grand Master, Brother John A . Tutt, who became the
second Grand Master of this jurisdiction.
3. That the erection of this first Masonic Hall was consumated
under the immediate supervision, direction, and through the energies
of the first Worshipful Master of Benicia Lodge No. 5. Brother Benjamin D. Hyman, who, in 1853 was the third Most Worshipful Grand
Master of this jurisdiction.
4. That the "Building Committee," named by and assisting Brother
Hyam consisted of Brother Ro·b ert Semple, Brother Alexander Riddell,
and Brother Lansing B. Mizner.
5. That Brother Alexander Riddell gave and donated to the Lodge
the ground upon which it stands and the milled siding for the outside
walls of the building: that Brother Ro·b ert Semple donated all the other
lumber, bricks and hardware which went into its building: that Brother
Lansing B. Mizner subscribed monies, along with others, and generally
assisted with the details of construction.
6. Brother Alexander Riddell was one of the pioneers of this State,
one of the first settlers of Benicia, an outstanding citizen and business·
man of his time, the third Worshipful Master of Benicia Lodge No. 5,
and well known for his M asonic works.
Brother Lansing B. Mizner was the second Worshipful Master of
Benicia Lodge No. 5: served his County. State and the nation in inter·
national affairs for over 40 years. He was a member of the Legislature ( 1865-1868): the 17th President pro tem of the Senate: the private
secretary to the Honorable Govern01; J3i9ler, himself a Mason, and

209

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

finally as United States Minister to Guatamala and other Central
American countries.
Brother Robert Semple came to California in 1845. He founded
the first newspaper published here, in Monterey, called "The Californian." He was a member of the well known "Bear Flag Party," at
Sonoma, which wrested California from Mexico and set it up as an
· independent republic. He founded the town of Benicia and a few years
later, the town of Colusa, in Colusa County. He was a member of the
Constitutional Convention which drafted the first constitution for Cali#
fornia, at Monterey, in 1849, and was elected and served as the President of that body during its deliberations. It is claimed by some that
he is the father of the free public schools of California because of his
zealous and. convincing arguments on their behalf before the Constitutional Convention. He was raised in Davy Crockett Lodge, in San
Francisco (now extinct), and dimitted to Benicia Lodge in March,
1850, where he remained a member until his death in 1855.

never again be available and may fall into the hands of parties who will
remodel or raze it, which circumstance in the opinion of your committee
would be a calamity to the Masonic fraternity as well as to the State
of California.

208

In view of all these facts, this committee points out that the first
Masonic Hall in California, at Benicia, not only was the very first
Masonic building to be erected and still standing, but that it has historical associations important to the people of the State of California
as well as to the Masons of this jurisdiction.
7. The committee finds that this building was continuously used
as a Masonic Hall by Benicia Lodge No. 5, until it became insufficient
for their purposes. In 1888 a new Masonic Hall was built on the adjoining property and the old historical Benicia Temple was sold to help
finance the new building. It has remained in foreign hands until this
present time, now being owned by Solano County. It is in an excellent
state of preservation, the Co~nty having but recently made repairs, and
remains in all its essential particulars as to architecture and design as it
was, when last used as a Masonic Hall by Benicia Lodge No. 5.
B. The committee finds that the last tenants of this first Masonic
Hall in California have recently vacated the property and that the
building is shortly to be offered for sale at public auction, by bid, by the
Board of Supervisors of Solano County, which is in accord with the
requirements of the law.
9. The committee also finds that a majority of said Board of Supervisors are members of this fraternity and as such would like to see this
first Masonic Hall restored to the craft; that they estimate its value
to be approximately five thousand three hundred dollars, ( $5300.00)
and that they legally will do all in their power to assist us and to cooperate with us.
Now therefore, it comes to pass that for the first time in two decades
the first Masonic Hall in California is available for purchase and may

To prevent these things from happening and to restore to the Masons
of California this historical shrine, the original first Masonic Hall in
this state, this committee finds the following to be feasible and rec#
ommends the adoption of the same by this Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge:
1. That this Grand Lodge appropriate the sum of five thousand
dollars ( $5000.00) for the acquisition of the first Masonic Hall in
California, still standing on its original site in the City of Benicia.
2. That Benicia Lodge No. 5, under resolution-a certified and
sealed copy of which is attached hereto, will underwrite the expense
of purchasing and reconditioning said Masonic Hall in excess of the
sum of five thousand dollars ( $5000.00) to the extent of two thousand,
five hundred dollars ( $2500.00).
3. That upon securing title to the said first Masonic Hall, Benecia
Lodge No. 5 will cause said title to be vested in the name of this Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge unless otherwise directed.
4. That, by resolution, certified and sealed copies of which are here
attached, Benicia Lodge No. 5 hereby offers to act as custodians, for
the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, of the building and property and
in the opinion of this committee are logically best situated so to act.
That they will turn the custodianship and management of the property
over to their Masonic Hall Board of Trustees who will establish a
separate bank account and books for the same, depositing all revenues
derived from rentals of the building and/or other sources, out of which
they agree to pay the cost of maintenance, insurance, taxes, repairs and
to underwrite the same should expected revenues prove deficient, all
without cost to, or for additional demands upon this Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge.
5. That to amplify revenue from use of the building, Benicia Lodge
No. 5 agrees to rent the lower floor from the Trustees for their own
recreational purposes for the sum of twenty dollars ( $20.00) for each
calendar month.
6. That the Trustees will cause the Lodge room in this first Masonic
Hall 'to be made available to all Lodges throughout this jurisdiction
for the purpose of conferring any of the three degrees and that for the
purpose of maintaining this Masonic shrine, and no other, that the
Trustees should have the right to establish fees for the use of the same
by said Lodges.

210

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

7. That upon securing title to said first Masonic Hall, Benicia Lodge
No. 5 agrees, in co-operation with the Masonic History Committee of
this Grand Lodge, to take steps to carefully, and as faithfully to detail
as possible, to restore and renovate said building so it will appear as it
did in said details when last owned by them: that in so doing they will
restore to said first Masonic Hall all the original furniture, such as
chairs, desks, altar, pedestals, altar candelabra, etc., still in their possession: that they will in fact be re-establishing this first Masonic Hall
as an historical Masonic monument and shrine and will, in the opinion
of this committee, creditably and ably discharge the duties which would
devolve upon them by virtue of the adoption of this report.

parallel similar action in eastern States where the craft has restored,
maintained and preserved their historical monuments for the good of
Masonry and the enjoyment of future generations.

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge
Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California
Whereas, at the 99th annual communication of Grand Lodge,
Lawrence X. Carroll, Master of Benicia Lodge No. 5, presented a
resolution proposing that the incoming Grand Master appoint a committee to investigate the purchase by Grand Lodge of the Old Masonic
Temple at Benicia, which proposal was recommended by the Committee on Policy and General Purposes and the resolution adopted, and
Whereas, this was the first building to be officially dedicated as a
Masonic Temple in the State of California, it having been completed
by Benicia Lodge No. 5 in October 1850 and dedicated by Grand
Lodge December 27, 1850, and
Whereas, the Temple is now owned by the County of Solano and
is now, for the first time in more than 2 decades, available for purchase,
and may never again be available and may fall into the hands of parties
who will remodel or raze it, and
Whereas, Benicia No. 5, whose present temple property joins the
old Masonic Temple, in consideration for the privilege of using the
ground floor of the old Temple as a clubroom will restore thereto all
the original furniture, etc., they still possess and will act as hosts to
Lodges desiring to visit this first Masonic Temple and will underwrite
Grand Lodge's expense of purchasing and reconditioning the old Temple up to the amount of $2500.00, and will assist the History Committee

212

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

in maintaining the old Temple by acting as custodians of the Old Temple
and by keeping it in repair.
Now, therefore, be it resolved that this Grand Lodge appropriate
the sum of Five Thousand Dollars ( $5,000.00) for the purpose of
purchasing and reconditioning the Old Masonic Temple at Benicia.
October 6, 1949
Walter L..Berger. Chairman
Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge Financing

Dear Walter:
Brother Carroll telephoned me this morning advising that he was
meeting with yourselves and Brother Whitsell relative to the purchase
by Benicia Lodge of the old, original Benicia Lodge temple, which adjoins their present temple site.
On September 5th, I met with the committee at Benicia to listen tci
their problem as well as to investigate their financial standing, in the
event of their presenting a request to our committee.
The old temple, which was the first building erected in California
to be used solely for Masonic purposes, was built in 1850. It is a twostory frame. of timber believed to have been brought around The Horn.
In 1890 Benicia Lodge erected its present two-story brick temple on
the Southwest corner of First and "J ." Due to financial difficulties
encountered, it was necessary that they sold the old temple, and at the
present time the old temple is owned by Solano County.
·
At the present time Benicia Lodge has 216 members. I am covering
on a separate sheet their financial standing.
It would be my recommendation that Benicia Lodge be granted
the consent to purchase the property in question for a sum not to exceed
$2.500.00, providing that they can present a future program indicating ·
the manner in which they plan to rehabilitate the old temple. If the
presented plan will provide for the use of the old temple as a clubroom,
it would release a store in the brick temple which should bring in an
annual income of approximately $1.000.00. This additional revenue
would then be available to pay taxes and insurance on the old temple.
F ratemally,
BERT

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Grand Master, during the past twelve months, has granted
dispensations and instituted the following Lodges:
Santa Ynez Valley Lodge at Los Olivos in Santa Barbara County
Rosemead Lodge at Rosemead in Los Angeles County
Westchester Lodge at Los Angeles in Los Angeles County
Orinda Lodge at Orinda in Contra Costa County
El Cerrito Lodge at El Cerrito in Contra Costa County
Bixby Knolls Lodge at Long Beach and Ponderosa Lodge at Fresno
were instituted prior to the last Grand Lodge communication.
The seven Lodges, under dispensation, have submitted their records
as required by law and they have been found in order.
BIXBY KNOLLS LODGE

Bixby Knolls Lodge was instituted July 31st, 1948 and at the last
Grand Lodge communication was continued under dispensation. The
ardor and enthusiasm so evident last year has continued to flourish.
Their ability to work together in peace and harmony has been
amply demonstrated by the work they have done. This Lodge has
conferred 121 degrees since their institution and now has a membership of 79, no indebtedness and a net cash balance of approximately
$1.900.00. We would like particularly to commend this Lodge for its
monthly bulletin. Those who read it cannot help but be better informed
Masons. Bixby Knolls Lodge has the wholehearted support of the
Lodges in the Long Beach area. This Committee, therefore, recommends
that a Charter be granted to Bixby Knolls Lodge No. 699 at Long
Beach in the County of Los Angeles.
PONDEROSA LODGE

Ponderosa Lodge at Fresno was instituted August 5th, 1948. This
Lodge, having been formed in a unique manner, comment in this report
is appropriate.
The Masters of the four Fresno Lodges, under the direction of the
Inspector of the District, appointed Committees to select four members
from their respective Lodges to become Charter members of the new
Lodge. This group of sixteen then selected nine Master Masons, resi~
dents of Fresno but holding membership elsewhere, 'being careful to
select those they thought most likely to see a new Lodge through the
first trying years.
The twenty-five thus selected have been working together for
over a year-ample time to demonstrate the success of this unusual
method of organization. To help keep their new Master Masons inter-

216

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

ested and active, they have formed what they call their "Side Liners
Degree Team" which is now ready to confer degrees when called upon
by the Master. Although _the Lodge has conferred a total of 85 degrees
and raised 19 Master Masons, the rejections evidence the fact that
their investigating Committees are functioning. The records show they
have no indebtedness and a cash balance of over $3,000.00.
Needless to say, the other Lodges in Fresno are proud of this
baby Lodge. This Committee, therefore, recommends that a Charter
be granted to Ponderosa Lodge No. 700 at Fresno in Fresno County.
SANTA YNEZ VALLEY LODGE

Santa Ynez Valley Lodge is located at Los Olivos, in Santa Ynez
Valley of Northern Santa Barbara County. The area served by Santa
Ynez Valley Lodge is rich in agriculture and is continuing to develop
on a sound and stable basis.
The need for a Masonic Lodge in the Valley has long been recognized by resident Masons. The area has a considerable Masonic
population and no Lodges within thirty miles of the three principal
towns of Solvang, Los Olivos and Santa Ynez.
A group of Masons believing much good would result, both to
Masonry and the community, in the establishment of a Masonic Lodge
in the Valley went to work. Their efforts were recognized and rewarded by the granting of a dispensation to form the Lodge and its
institution on January 22nd, 1949. Since that date they have accepted
twelve applicants for the degrees of Masonry and five applicants for
affiliation. Their .6.nances are in good condition, they have no indebtedness and $500.00 in the treasury.
The neighboring Lodges have been most helpful and co~operative
in assisting in the formation and operation of the new Lodge. Gifts
and loans of needed equipment have been of material aid and their
steady encouragement and support have been of great value to this
new Lodge.
While this Lodge may never be large in numbers, this Committee
believes that Masonry in California will be strengthened and enriched
by the granting of a Charter. We, therefore, recommend that a Charter
be granted to Santa Ynez Valley Lodge No. 701 at Los Olivos in, the
County of Santa Barbara.
ROSEMEAD LODGE

Rosemead Lodge was instituted on January 29th, 1949. This Lodge,
located in the thriving community of Rosemead in the County of Los
Angeles, is the outgrowth of the Rosemead Masonic Club. Rosemead
Lodge, at the present time, has a membership of i 1, having accepted

217

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

nine members by affiliation and raised twelve candidates. They have
over $1,000.00 in their treasury, no indebtedness and have a sound
financial program.
Surrounding Lodges have been most generous in their support
of this new Lodge, as evidenced by their donations of Masonic equipment and their interest. aid and assistance.
The ability and enthusiasm of the officers and members to continue
the progress of the Lodge and the apparent need for a Lodge in Rosemead has impressed this Committee. We, therefore, recommend that
a Charter be granted to Rosemead Lodge No. 702 at Rosemead in the
County of Los Angeles.
Westchester Lodge at Los Angeles in Los Angeles County, Orinda
Lodge at Orinda in Contra Costa County and El Cerrito Lodge at
El Cerrito in Contra Costa County, have had such a limited period of
operation, that it is the recommendation of the Charters Committee that
the above ·L odges be continued under dispensation.
Respectfully submitted,
GLENN

Custance

Death, as it must to all men, has within the past twelve months come
to 240 Masters and Past Masters, members of this Grand Lodge. The
heaviest losses were sustained by Friendship Lodge No. 212 and Golde_n
State Lodge No. 358, each lost four Past Masters. Tehama Lodge No.
3, Marin Lodge No. 191, Rising Light Lodge No. 397, and San Pasqual
Lodge No. 452, lost three each, 40 lodges lost 2 each, and 140 lodges
lost one each. Of our deceased brethren 16 have been members of the
Fraternity for fifty years or more.
One of these faithful servants was John Scalmanini, Past Master of
Speranza Italiana Lodge No. 219, who was raised in 1883, thus serving
the Fraternity faithfully for 66 years.
The Angel of Death made his presence deeply felt on the membership of the Board of Directors of our Club Houses, calling two from
Berkeley and one from Los Angeles. In the lnspectorial Group we lost
two active Inspectors and one who rendered valuable service to the
Grand Lodge in years past. The final call came also to one who served
recently as Senior Grand Deacon.
Each of these 240 brethren has earned and merited our admiration
and approbation. The limitations of time, however, prevent our paying
to all of them individually the tribute they so richly deserve. Their
paths having crossed ours has made our pathway through life much
brighter, and through association a love established which has successfully bridged the grave. As they have crossed the invisible chasm our
love for them has not diminished, nor can it ever be severed. The poet
Whittier expressed our thoughts in his lovely verse:

ROBERT KENNETH MC GUIRE

In the flush of life Robert Kenneth McGuire, Inspector of the 88th
Masonic District, died of a heart attack in San Bernardino, California,·
April 21, 1949. He was on a business trip. The attack occurred at 2:00
A.M. in his hotel room. He dressed, went to the garage for his car, and
drove across the city to the San Bernardino Community Hospital. where
he died the following evening at 8: 15 o'clock.
Bob, as he was familiarly known, was born November 16, 1907 at
Urbana, Ohio. When he was eleven years of age the family, believing
that the West offered better opportunities than the community in which
they were living, selected Southern California as the field for their
future operations. They came to Los Angeles and after a year's residence
in that city moved to Lawndale, where Bob received his education in
the Centinela Valley schools. In 1925 Brother McGuire returned to
the city of Los Angeles and entered the employ of the Globe Mills,
serving ten years in the milling department. In 1935 he was transferred
to the sales department, where he made an outstanding record. His
honesty, ability and efficiency placed him in an enviable position with
his employers, and his kindness, consideration and willingness to help
others endeared him to his fellow workers.
Bob McGuire's Masonic career began in 1929. On August 7 of
that year he petitioned Inglewood Lodge No. 421. He was elected
September 4, entered September 18, passed October 23, and raised to
the sublime degree December 18. The following year he was appointed
to the line and in December 1935 was elected and installed Master.
His administration was one of the most successful in the long history
of that outstanding lodge. Grand Master Frank M. Smith, recognizing
Bob's love for the Fraternity, his interest in its welfare and his devotion
to its teachings, appointed him Inspector of the 88th District in 1942.
This office he filled with honor and distinction. For six years he was
Master of Ceremonies for the Anual Beefsteak Feed in Inglewood. This
is one of the largest annual Masonic gatherings in California.

220

PROCEEDINGS OP Tl~E

Brother McGuire received the Scottish Rite degrees in the Spring
class of 1943 at Los Angeles, and until his death served as a me~ber
of the personnel committee of that organization. He joined Al Mala1kah
Temple of the Shrine in 1943.
Bob McGuire is survived by his mother, Mrs. F. J. Maher of Lawndale, California, and his widow, who was Frances Alecia Vernon of

MILTON THOMAS PARMER

A great jurist and a devoted Mason was lost to C~lifornia ~hen
Milton Thomas Farmer died suddenly of a heart attack m the City of
Chicago, Illinois, March 1, 1949. Judge Farmer had won a case. concerned with San Joaquin River irrigation, which he had argued before
the United States Supreme Court, and was on his way home to Berkeley
when stricken.
Judge Farmer was born December 7, 1883 at Woodland, California,
being the third child in a family of ten. His parents w.ere !3eo.rge
Thomas and Gertrude Ruggles Farmer. Shortly after Milton s birth
the family moved to Siskiyou County, but the rigorous winters of the
north section caused them to seek a more equitable climate, and they
established a ranch home in Kings County near Hanford.
Milton graduated from Hanford High School with high honors.
He attended San Jose Teachers' College for the full course and obtained a teacher's certificate. After teaching two years in Kings County
grade schools he matriculated at the University of California in January
1906 and graduated in 1909, having accomplished the requirements for
his B.A. degree in three and one-half years in spite of the fact that he
earned his way through school by working as an engraver in the old
"Co-op" and by teaching night school in San Francisco. He obtained
the degree of Doctor of Jurisprudence in 1911.
There was never an idle moment during his college days. He was a
football letter man, played on the Freshman and Varsity teams. He was
elected Graduate Manager during his graduate years, and served his
Alma Mater as Alumni Secretary during this period. His scholastic
attainments and his popularity gained him many honors, as he was a
member of the Abracadabra Fraternity, Winged Helmet, Golden Bear.
Big C Society, and the Phi Delta Phi legal fraternity. He was also
elected to the coveted Phi Beta Kappa.
In 1912 Brother Farmer was appointed Assistant Attorney for the
State Banking Department. and in 1913 was appointed by Governor

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

221

Hiram Johnson to the Superior Court bench of Kern County, becoming
the youngest judge of that rank in the State. Some years later he
resigned from the bench and entered the private practice of law. He was
nationally recognized as an authority on water rights, and his record,
a most remarkable one, was due not only to his technical skill but also
to the high ideals of justice which forbade him to accept cases which in
his judgment were undeserving of his effort.
Milton Farmer was an avid reader, an exceptional student of history.
and indulged his taste as a bibliophile with an extensive collection of
books. especially those on California history and those on the life and
times of Abraham Lincoln. Although a practising Christian of high
ideals he did not join any church until late in life, but upon affiliating
with the Episcopal Church he took much interest in the extension of
Christian influence. He was a vestryman of St. Clements' Church at
the time of his death.
Our Brother is survived by his widow, Helen Young Farmer, a
leader in the Berkeley Red Cross. Two daughters, Mrs. H. Stuart
Kimball of Orinda, California, and Miss Anne Farmer of Berkeley.
and three sons. William F. Farmer of Oakland, John Farmer of Berkeley. and the Reverand James P. Farmer of Alexandria, Virginia.
Brother Farmer's Masonic career began in his 23rd year, when he
petitioned Hanford Lodge No. 279. He was initiated December 29,
1906, passed February 16, 1907, and raised to the sublime degree
February 23 that same year. He remained a member of Hanford Lodge
for 6 years and then dimitted to Durant Lodge No. 268 at Berkeley
where he retained his membership for 2 years. :Upon his appointment
to the bench of the Kem County Superior Court he transferred his
membership from Durant Lodge to Bakersfield Lodge No. 224, where
he was appointed an officer and progressed to the position of Senior
Warden. Returning to the Bay area he affiliated with Rockridge Lodge
No. 468 of Oakland and served as Master of that Lodge in 1921. He
had other Masonic affiliations being a member of Kem Valley Chapter
No. 75 Royal Arch Masons, and of Berkeley Commandry No. 42,
Knights Templar. He was also a 14 degree member of the Oakland
Bodies of the Scottish Rite.
Judge Farmer's greatest contribution to Masonry was rendered as
a member of the Board of Directors of the Masonic Club House at
the University of California at Berkeley. This was an enterprise that
was dear to his heart, and from its inception in 1923 he gave un..
stintingly of his time, his talents and his substance. At various times
he occupied the responsible position of Secretary, Chairman of the
Executive Committee and President. Much of the success of the Club
House was due to his efforts.
We will miss his counsel and his advice, but the organization to
which he gave so much will remain his perpetual monument.

JOHN MATTHEW PLUMMER

Hundreds of people who knew him as a friend and as a Mason
were shocked and grieved at the untimely passing of John M. Plummer.
Stricken suddenly at 5 AM of May 7, 1949, at his home in Glendale
he died before any assistance could be rendered. He is survived by
his wife, Betty Plummer, and a son, Lt. Earle Plummer.
John Plummer was born in Bedford, Indiana, Jun~ 25, 1.899. ~e
came to Glendale, California in 1926 and soon established himself in
civic and fraternal affairs, and through the years carved for himself
a niche which earned for him the love and respect of the best people
of his community.
To his intimate friends and Masonic associates he was affectionately known as Johnny, but he was addressed as Captain Plummer ~y
the public. The title was derived from his position on the Glendale Fire
Department, which service he entered on July 26, 1927. He was advanced to the rating of engineer December 4, 1940, and to that of
Captain June 20, 1948. In addition to his official duties .in the, Dep~t­
ment Captain Plummer also active in the Glendale Fireman s Relief
Association, holding the office of President for one term, and was
also named as official Chaplain of the Department.
On April 18, 1930 John Plummer was raised a Master Mason
in Meridian Lodge No. 667, and for the balance of his life was a
devoted, sincere and diligent worker in the craft. His willingness to
serve and his desire to learn so impressed his brethren that he was
appointed an officer in 1938, and presided as Master in 1945. Grand
Master John R. Moore recognizing his capabilities appointed him
Senior Grand Deacon of the Grand Lodge of California and he filled
that important office with honor for the year 1947.
Johnny Plummer was active in other branches of Masonry. and
its associated orders, having served as a member of the Advisory
Board of the Order of DeMolay, and as Patron of Glen Eyrie Chapter
Order of Eastern Star. He was a member of Unity Chapter Royal
Arch Masons and Past Commander of Glendale Commandery No.
53. He was also a member of Al Malaikah Temple of the Mystic
Shrine.
Johnny's call to "that undiscovered country" brings his active
service to Masonry to an end, but the solid worth of his devotion
and character continue to flow on into time.

BENJAMIN GREEN WRIGHT

May 19, 1949 Benjamin Green Wright died after a brief illness at
the Hollywood Presbyterian Hospital. Hollywood, California.
The fourth child in a family of five, Ben, as he was affectionately

~

223

known to his intimate friends, was born on a farm near Moline, Rock
Island County, Illinois, January 9, 1879, the son of John Calhoun
Wright and Elizabeth May Scott Wright. About 1884 the family
moved to Moline, Illinois, and Ben received his grammer school
education in that city. 1893 found the family in Chicago, where Ben
attended Hyde Park High School. Coming to California in 1894 the
family settled on a farm near Ojai, where Ben worked until 1900,
when he entered upon a course of studies at the Santa Barbara Business
College, which he completed in the shortest. time and with the highest
grades in the history of that institution.
Few men have contributed more to public affairs than did Ben
Wright. Coming to Los Angeles in 1901 he immediately entered the
business, civil and religious life of the city. For the succeeding 48 years
he was most active in promoting the welfare and happiness of the
people in the community in which he lived. In the public interest he
served on many committees of the Los Angeles Chamber of Commerce,
Chairman Citizen's Committee Los Angeles Police Show from 1938
to the time of his death. He was instrumental in raising the funds for
the present building of the Goodwill Industries, and was Chairman of
the Board of Directors for many years. He served as Chairman Board
of Directors Los Angeles Downtown Y.M.C.A. for a long period.
President Board of Directors McKinley Home for Boys for the last
eleven years of his life. Honesty in business was an obsession with
him, and for 14 years he served the Better Business Bureau as
Director, Vice President, President and Chairman Executive Committee.
He was for many years a factor in the success of the Community
Chest activities.
Most of Brother Wright's adult life was spent in the employ of the
Southern California Telephone Company, where he held positions
of great trust and responsibility. As evidence of the esteem in which
he was held by his co-workers we quote from a tribute paid him by his
friends in the Company:
"In Memoriam-Benjamin Green Wright.
"In the early part of 1901, a big, tall, strapping young man went into
the local office of the Sunset Telephone and Telegraph Company in
Los Angeles and applied for the position of bookkeeper. The man to
whom he. applied for the job was the same sort of build and he remarked
that a big, strong man like him should be ashamed to come in and ask
for such a soft job, that he should be out doing a real man's work, and
that under those circumstances he had no job to offer him. So Ben
Wright then went to the Los Angeles Gas and Electric Corporation
and obtained a temporary job. In September of that same year his
tem~orary assignment was ended and he was on the loose again,
looking for a job.
·

224

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"As he had made up his mind that he was going to work for the
telephone company, he again came in and talked to the same man. When
asked what kind of a job he wanted he stated that he could do
anything--climb poles, work on books, or sell telephone service. His
application was immediately accepted and on September 13, 1901, he
was put on the payroll as an agent which, in today's parlance indicates
that he was a salesman.
"Four years later he was made manager of the West office, and
subsequently held many responsible jobs in the Commercial department. On March 1, 1924 he was appointed Los Angeles manager,
then on January 1, 1926 he headed up the Public Relations work of
the company as Public Relations Manager until he retired on January 31, 1944.
"All through his telephone service life Ben Wright was prominently
associated with the growth and development of not only his company
but the city of Los Angeles as well. He was one of the most admired
and respected business men in Los Angeles and was always connected
with activities which promoted the general welfare of the community.
and especially that of young people. For many years he served on the
Board of Directors of the McKinley Home for Boys. and during his
last few years he served as President of that body.
"He was a charter member of the Southern California Chapter of
the Pioneers of America, an employee body composed of members
who have served the telephone industry 21 years or more. He w~s
president for two terms, the years 1926 and 1930. He has the distinction of being the only person to serve two terms as president. This is
an indication of the popularity and the high respect in which Ben
Wright was held by his fellow workers.
"He was one of the organizers and a president of the Telephone
Masonic Club and was always active in its affairs. Needless to say,
he was held in the same repute in outside Masonic circles, and had
served his Lodge in many capacities."
His other business activities included the Los Angeles City Club,
the Los Angeles Electric Club. In both of these organizations he held
the office of President. He was also a Regent of Forest Lawn Memorial Park.
Ben Wright was a deeply religious man. He gave freely of his
time and his material possessions to the faith which he so dearly loved.
He was a prominent member of the Board of Directors of the Church
Federation of Los Angeles: rendered valuable service as Chairman of
the Board of Trustees Olivet Congregational Church until its merger
with Plymouth Congregational: Chairman Prudential Committee Messiah Congregational Church for _three years: President Congregational
Conference, and President Congregational Church Extension Society.

Brother Wright's efforts in behalf of Masonry have been exceeded
by few men in this Grand Jurisdiction. Appointed Senior Grand Deacon
by Grand Master George L. Jones in 1926, Ben gave to that exalted
position the dignity and efficiency which the office demanded. As a
member of the Pay of Members Committee and the Board of Control
his work was outstanding. At the time of his passing he was Treasurer
of the Los Angeles Board of Relief, having served that Board faithfully
for 25 consecutive years, and in addition to these duties he was Chairman of the Board in 1929. Ben was Chairman of the Committee to
raise funds for the building of the Masonic Club House at the University of California at Los Angeles. The campaign was so successful
that proportionate parts of the larger donations were returned to the
donors. He served as Vice Chairman of the Board of Directors of the
Club House and upon the death of Ira Thompson became Chairman,
and filled that important office through 1945. It was his unique combination of character and talent that enabled him to satisfactorily settle
the tangled affairs of the old Masonic Club of Los Angeles.
Ben Wright was raised in Golden State Lodge No. 358, July 31,
1913: occupied the Oriental Chair in 1925, and for the balance of his
life was a devoted supporter of all his lodge's activities. In other
branches of Masonry he was a member of South Gate Chapter No. 98,
Royal Arch Masons. and Los Angeles Council No. 11 Royal and Select
Master Masons. He was a member of the Scottish Rite Bodies of Los
Angeles, having received the 32nd degree December 9, 1933.
Ben Wright loved his fellowman, he loved his God. His life was
not in vain, and we were indeed fortunate that he cast his lot with
Masonry. His equal will not be found soon.

EDMUND BARDWELL SKINNER

At the last communication of this Grand Lodge the Committee on
Necrology in its report quoted a poem entitled "They are in the other
Room." That afternoon Edmund Skinner stated to a member of the
Committee that Dr. Robert Freeman of Whittier, California, had written this poem especially for the funeral services of Brother Skinner's
mother. We little thought at the moment that in less than two months
the same poem would be quoted at his funeral, for Ed died suddenly
on December 13, 1948 at his home in Whittier. The services were
conducted by Greenleaf Lodge No. 670 on December 16th at Lanier's
Colonial Chapel. More than 300 were in attendance.
Brother Skinner is survived by his widow, Ruth Skinner, one daughter, Mrs. John Cutler of Lafayette, California, two grandchildren,
Catherine and John Cutler, and one sister, Winifred E. Skinner of
Pasadena.
Born at Shellburn, Massachusetts, March 21, 1888, he was brought

226

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

to California hy his parents in 1901. The family settled in the City
of Pasadena, and Ed received his education in the public schools of
that city. In 1917 he entered the employ of the Southern California
Edison Company, and served that company until the time of his death.
San Pasqual Lodge No. 152 of Pasadena received the petition of
Brother Skinner in the spring of 1925. He was initiated May 20, passed
June 21, and raised September 30. Three years later he dimitted to
become a charter member of Greenleaf Lodge which was being organized in Whittier. In 1930 he was installed Master of Greenleaf Lodge
No. 670, and served with great distinction. In recognition of his unusual
qualiJkations and his devotion to the Fraternity, Leslie E. Wood, Grand
Master, appointed him Inspector of District No. 96 on January 1. 1913.
His duties and responsibilities were discharged with such proficiency
that each succeeding Grand Master re-appointed him, and his services
were ended only by his death.
Ed was also a member of Whittier Chapter No. 91 Royal Arch
Masons, Whittier Chapter No. 111 Order of the Eastern Star and
Fezzan Grotto, Mystic Order of the Veiled Prophets of the Enchanted
Realm.
Ed Skinner was a deeply religious man, a loving husband, a good
father, an exemplary citizen. His devotion to Masonry endeared him
to his brethren, and his contributions to the Craft made him a valuable
member of this Grand Lodge. We ask God's blessing upon him.
WILLIAM BRODBECK HERMS

William Brodbeck Herms, Past Master of Henry Morse Stephens
Lodge No. 511 of Berkeley, was suddenly called from an unusually
active life on May 9, 1919 by a heart attack.
Internationally renowned as an Entomologist and Parasitologist:
Councilor of Boy Scouts of the Western States and Hawaii: holder of
an award for Distinguished Citizenship: a Veteran of World Wars I
and II: President of the California State Automobile Association: active
in church, ·L odge and clubs, he was the recipient of many honors, distinguished titles and academic degrees. Yet, no title seemed more appropriate than "Billy," by which he was so lovingly known for his
cheery friendliness and constant efforts to be of service to his fellowmen.
Born at Portsmouth, Ohio, September 22, 1876, he attended the
public schools and business college of that city, after which he worked
for four years in lumber mills and a shoe factory, then entering Baldwin
Wallace College, from which he graduated in 1902. Later, he pursued
advance studies in Western Reserve, Ohio State, and Harvard Universities where he held Fellowships and teaching positions. He joined
the University of California at Berkeley as an Assistant Professor of
Parasitology in 1908, and had recently retired as head of the Depart-

'.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

227

ment of Entomology and Parasitology after forty years of service.
During that time he became the author of several books, and had just
completed the revised text for the fourth edition of one of them on the
day before his death.
During World War I he rendered valuable service in the study and
control of tropical diseases. Although over-age the Government called
him back into service of World War II with the Tank of Colonel, and
placed him in charge -of the control of malaria and other tropical diseases in the Pacific area. Doubtless many Americans owe their lives
to his untiring, efficient work. As a soldier he was a charter member
of Berkeley Post of the American Legion.
Lack of space prevents a full listing of his activities. Those that
follow will give an idea of the many facets of his diamond-like character. Head of the School of Commerce of Baldwin Wallace College;
Member of the International Congress of Zoology: Member of the PanPacific Food Conservation Congress at Honolulu: Member of International Hygiene Exhibit at Dresden, Germany: Investigator of Cocoanut Pests of Fanning Islands: President of Berkeley Board of Education, Berkeley Community Chest, Berkeley Lions Club, Berkeley and
Contra Costa Area Council Boy Scouts of America, Berkeley Breakfast Club. He held membership in Sigma Xi, Alpha Zeta ( agricultural), Delta Omega (Public Health), Phi Sigma (Biological), Scabbard and Blade, Alpha Kappa Lambda. He was a fellow in many
scientific societies and had been decorated by the Republic of France
with the Rank of Chevalier du Merite, Agricole. He had been president of the Entomological Society of America, with more than 110
scientific papers to his credit.
He became a Master Mason on March 27, 1913 in Berkeley Lodge
No. 363, and was Senior Warden of that Lodge in 1922, when he
dimitted to become the first Master of Henry Morse Stephens Lodge
No. 511. At about the same time meetings were held in his office which
resulted in plans for the Masonic Club House at the University of
California in Berkeley. He served as a Trustee of the Club House from
the start, and was President of the Board at the time of his death. He
was among the founders of the Berkeley High Twelve Club, and served
as its President. Although busy with many activities he was active in
his lodge work, and was an outstanding exemplar of Masonic principles and Christian practices.
He is survived by a wife, Lillie C., and three sons, William M.,
Herbert P., and George W . Herms, who have the memory of a kindly
husband and father.
"Billy" Herms has gone to the Supreme Lodge above, but his spirit
blesses the places he touched, and his fine influence over the men who
knew him, and of the many Boy Scouts who passed under his kindly
care, will continue for the good of the world.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

As we pause in our deliberations to pay this tribute to our brethren
who have taken the last sleep let us not forget that if they were with
us this day they would tell us not to mourn. They would tell us to
prepare for the inevitable, for each of us in our turn will go out into the
unknown, and we shall go alone, and from us to the living there will
come no word or sign. These words are filled with awe. To those of
little faith they are pregnant with fear. Man_is the only animal endowed
with a long ~emory and a vivid imagination. In his primitive state he
was least prepared of all the animals to defend himself. Enemies were
all about him. The birds, the beasts, and the elements. The birds could
seek safety in the air, some animals had protective coloring, others were
fleet of foot, many possessed great strength.
Man's only protection was the darkness of a cold and damp cavern,
and the use of an undeveloped brain. Fear was his constant companion.
In the passage of millenniums man developed his brain and became the
master of his environment; became supreme over the birds and the animals. While he cannot control the elements he understands the cau.ses
of natural phenomena, and can take the necessary precautions to decrease their destructive power. Notwithstanding man's progress and
development, the enormity of the problems that confront the world
today frequently causes him to forget his marvelous accomplishments
and his great spiritual advancement, and he burdens himself with the
accumulated fears of the past, and adds an unreasoned horror of the
future.
In reality. man now has only two enemies-his fellowman and death.
We of this Fraternity are of many creeds, but we are one in our
belief in the Supreme Architect of the Universe, by whatever name He
may be called. The Supreme Being, knowing man's fears of his fellowman and death, has given his children an answer to the problem. The
answer in "Charity." Not charity in the narrow sense of alms, or acts
of benevolence to the poor, as worthy as these may be, but in its broader
and deeper significance, the vesture or act of loving God with a love
that transcends that for creatures, and of loving others for the sake
·
of God.
In every great religion we have assurances of God's charity toward
us. but nowhere in religious literature has His love for man and his
assurance of life beyond the grave been more beautifully expressed
than in the 16th verse of the 3rd chapter of the Gospel according to
St. John: 'For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten
Son, that whosoever believed in him should not perish. but have everlasting life." Our belief in God is our only salvation, and His love for
us our only weapon against fear. It is this love that fills the universe.
and will in time bri~g all men to the realization of their obligations to

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

229

their fellowmen; His love so great that death will have lost its terror;
His love so boundless that it passes comprehension.
"Could we with ink the ocean fill.
And were the skies a parchment made;
With every stick on earth a quill,
And every man a scribe by trade,
To write the love of God above,
Would drain the ocean dry;
Nor could the scroll contain the whole
Though sketched from sky to sky."
We leave our departed brethren in our Father's love, and thank
Him that they were with us for a little while.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRIEVANCES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
To your Committee on Grievances there has been referred a total
of 43 records. By this report, your Committee proposes to recommend
affirmance of the Findings of the Trial Commission in 29 cases. The
remaining 14 cases, a number of which involve Petitions for Restoration,
will be separately reported to you.
Section 332 of our Ordinances has again demonstrated its usefulness. Many extensive and time-consuming trials have been avoided
by resort to automatic expulsion, as authorized by this Section, when
the accused has been convicted of a crime classified as a felony, imprisoned in pursuance thereof. and does not demand a trial after having
been given due notice and an opportunity so to do. It seems necessary,
however, to caution the officers of Lodges to follow carefully the provisions of this Section and to exercise the greatest of care to see that the
notice to the accused required thereby is properly given to the accused
at his last known place of address. which frequently is the place of his
incarceration.
One of the trial records hereinafter listed involves the trial of the
Master of a Lodge. This is the first time in many years that such a case
has come before Grand Lodge. In this case the accused was found guilty
of repeated acts of drunkenness, which served to reflect discredit upon
the Lodge of which he was Master. Perhaps it is a little 'impertinent
upon the part of the members of your Committee to call this to your
attention during Grand Lodge week.
In some instances, we find that trials are conducted on an entirely
too informal basis. Dignity should surround all Masonic trials. Witnesses should be properly called, examined and cross-examined and the
entire matter conducted in accordance with the ordinances of Grand
Lodge. We find that the best results usually obtain when both the
accuser and the accused are represented by counsel.
In one case ( 1182), the accused was acquitted by the Trial Com-

of the following cases. We find that in each instance the trials have
been conducted in accordance with Masonic Law: that no errors substantiaJly a.ff ecting the result occurred in said trials and that in each
instance, substantial justice has been accomplished.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee to which was referred the petition of J.C.P. for
restoration to and the rights and privileges of masonry, reports as
follows:
~etiti?ner was expelled in 193.1 after trial in his lodge on three
specifications, namely ( 1 ) that he had induced the accuser to invest
$1500 in a corporation organized by petitioner to manufacture and
market a dental product devised by him ( 2) that petitioner had sold
stock in this corporation without a permit, and ( 3) that petitioner in
bankri.tptcy proceedings following failure of his corporation had concealed some of his assets.
The trial commission found petitioner guilty on the 1st specification,
and not guilty on the 2nd and 3rd specifications.
Petitioner has heretofore presented three applications for restoration; the first in 1933, the next in 1935 and again in 1937, each of which
w~s d~nied by Grand Lodge, without prejudice, because of the petitioners failure to support his application with sufficient proof of his rehabilitation since his expulsion.
Again petitioner comes to Grand Lodge, acknowledges his error,
and a~ks for restoration. Notice was given to his Lodge and a special
committee "'.'as appointed to investigate and report to the Lodge. The
lod~e committee made a report recommending disapproval of the application, and the Lodge voted 30 to 10 against favorable action.
Y~ur committee has interviewed the chairman of the investigating
committee and as a result of that interview believe that the committee
did not base its report upon the petitioner's conduct since his expulsion,
but largely upon the facts which resulted in petitioner's expulsion.
The question before Grand Lodge is this:
Has the petitioner now so rehabilitated himself that he will reflect
honor upon our institution?
Because of the present circumstances, your committee has been
careful in its scrutiny of the many letters of recommendation on behalf
of the petitioner. We have talked to the brother who as counsel for the
accuser, prosecuted petitioner before the Lodge. He recommends restoration of the petitioner. We have interviewed Masons who·are members
of the lodge and others who are members of other lodges in petitioner's
community. Our interest was in discovering what petitioner's conduct
has been since his expulsion. Our first inclination was to defer action
until next year on this petition, by reason of the fact that the record
there was unsatisfactory as to the conduct of the petitioner in the last
few years. We have now in the course of our own investigation, received satisfactory informatiun in that respect. The petitioner, we find
was practicing his profession of dentistry from 1941 to 1947, in San

244

245

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Francisco-that he was diligent in that practice and highly esteemed
by his associates; that in 1947, by reason of the failure of his health, he
found it necessary to retire; he is now an invalid, having suffered a
paralytic stroke and is in grave condition. He comes of a highly esteemed masonic family and he himself devoted many years to Masonry,
before his expulsion. To defer action upon his application until next
year would probably mean that Grand Lodge during his life could not
restore him and that neither he nor his fine family could have the benefit
of this act of clemency by Grand Lodge.
Your committee is aware of the fact that by restoring him, he will
not become a member of his former Lodge, or of any Lodge. If restored
by Grand Lodge he will become a Mason at large until elected to membership by some lodge.
Under all of the circumstances, your committee believes that the
showing made on behalf of this petitioner is sufficient to show rehabilitation and therefore offers the following resolution:
RESOLVED: That the petition of J.C. P. for restoration to all the
rights and privileges of masonry be and the same hereby is granted.

stated meeting voted unanimously to recommend that petitioner's application for restoration be denied.
Petitioner presents in support of his application three letters from
reputable business men of Oakland, and two from attorneys of that
city. which letters urge his restoration.
Your committee believes that the first step to be taken by a man in
the process of rehabilitation is the frank recognition of his error, and
to repent of that error. This petitioner has not taken that first step, but
excuses his conviction by charging dishonesty and misconduct against
the then District Attorney, in whose integrity the Grand Lodge of California, has we believe the utmost confidence.
If and when the petitioner can come to masonry with sincere repentance in his heart, and a satisfactory showing of that repentance,
and that his conduct since his offense has been praiseworthy, we feel
sure that Masonry will not continue to condemn him.
Your Committee believes that this petitioner does not so come at this
time and therefore offers the following resolution:
BE IT RESOLVED: That the petition of B.F.B. for restoration to
the rights and privileges of Masonry be and the same hereby is denied.

Adopted.

Your Committee to which was ref erred the petition for restoration
of the accused in trial record No. 840, respectfully reports as follows:
The petitioner, E. M. R. was expelled on September 6, 1934, for
unmasonic conduct based upon two specifkations, ( 1) that he had deserted, neglected and wilfully failed, for a period of two years, to provide
for his four minor daughters, then of the ages of 16, 14, 13 and 5, all
of whom were dependent upon him for suppport, and ( 2) that he was a
fugitive from justice, a warrant for his arrest having been issued under
Section 270 of the Penal Code of the State of California, charging
failure to provide for his minor children.
It appeared at the trial that a reasonable effort to locate the accused
had been made, and the trial proceeded even though there was no evidence that the accused had really received a copy of the summons and
charges. The evidence at the trial showed that the wife of the accused
had obtained a divorce from the accused and had custody of the minor
children. She testified that he had failed to support them and that she
was living upon relief provided by the county.
The accused, now a Master Sergeant in the U. S. Army, files his
petition for restoration, advising that he has been connected with the
U. S. Army practically all of the time since December, 1940. At the
present time, he is located at the Military Science Department of the
University of Cincinnati, but for the greater portion of the time he was
with the Army, he was stationed near Tucson, Arizona. The petitioner
does not indicate his occupation between the date of his expulsion in
1934 and 1940 when he entered upon his Army duty. The petition for
restoration is supported by three letters of recommendation, one from
a Congressman and former attorney for the family. one from an investigator in the Sheriff's office in Phoenix, Arizona, and one from a Past
Master residing in Seattle, Washington, and who served with the accused in the U. S. Army during World War II. The letters are general
letters of recommendation and do not indicate that the recommenders
knew of anything that the accused had done to provide support for his .
minor children.
It is the well-established principle of this Grand Lodge that a petitioner, in an application for restoration, has the burden of showing that
he has made a complete atonement for his errors and, therefore, deserves
favorable consideration. A mere expression of sorrow is not sufficient.
In this particular case there is no evidence that the petitioner in the
fifteen years since he was expelled from his Lodge, has made any contributions for the support of his children. The youngest of his children
was only five years old in 1934 when he was expelled, and would just
be reaching the age of majority at the present time. If the petitioner
had within the limits of his available income, made some effort to support

Trial Record No. 1087

I

To the M. W. Grand Lodge of California:
Trial Record No. 1087 is now before Grand Lodge for the third
successive year.
Briefly, the history of this case is as follows:
The accused, a mem·b er of Golden Rule Lodge No. 479, was formerly Sheriff of Santa Clara County. During his term of office, he was
indicted by the Grand Jury on a charge of Conspiracy to Operate Slot
Machines and other accompanying devices in that County. When the
criminal case was tried, acting upon the advice of his counsel, he did
not take the stand and ~estify as a witness in his defense. The jury,
after a very long period of deliberation, returned a verdict of "Guilty."
While the crime of which the accused was charged is classified as a
felony. it was automatically reduced to a misdemeanor by virtue of the
fact that the trial judge did not send the accused to the penitentiary
but only caused him to be imprisoned in the Santa Clara County Indus·
trail Farm for a period of four months and assess~ng a fine in the sum
of $2000. Golden Rule Lodge No. 479 took no action on the case until
directed so to do by the then Grand Master Brouillet. On the lodge
trial, occurring in 1946. the record of conviction was introduced in
evidence. This created a prima facie case of guilt. The accused, how·
ever, testified at some length, asserting his innocence and charging that
his prosecution in the state courts was motivated by politics. The Trial

250

251

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Commission unanimously acquitted the accused. As. the trial was
regular in all respects. your Grievance Committeee recommended to
Grand Lodge that the acquittal be affirmed. Past Grand Master Arthur
Brouillet vigorously opposed this recommendation of the Grievance
Committee, with the result that the Grand Lodge. by a sharply divided
vote, reversed the case and remanded it for a new trial. The case was
again retried by Gold Rule Lodge and again the accused, by a vote of
the Commissioners of seven to one, was found "Not Guilty." At the
meeting of Grand Lodge in 1948, your Grievance Committee again
unanimously recommended to Grand Lodge that the finding of the
Trial Commission be affirmed. The recommendation of the Grievance
Committee was predicated on Section 341 of our Ordinances, which, in
substance, provides that no judgment of a Trial Commission shall be
set aside unless Grand Lodge shall be of the opinion that errors committed at the trial resulted in a miscarriage of justice and also because
Grand Lodge has previously declared a judgment of acquittal by the
subordinate Lodge of .which the accused is a member should not be
reversed or disturbed by the Committee on Grievances or by the Grand
Lodge except in a case of gross violation of Masonic Law by the Trial
Commission or by the Lodge acquitting him. Again, Past Grand Master
Brouillet vigorously opposed the recommendation of this Committee.
Grand Lodge. by a sharply divided vote, adopted a resolution reversing
the recommendation of the Committee and the finding of "Not Guilty"
of the Trial Commission and remanding the case for retrial in a Lodge
to be designated by the Grand Master. Pursuant to this resolution,
the Grand Master designated California Lodge No. 1 to conduct the
retrial. The accused, on this trial. by a vote of six to one of the Trial
Commission, was found guilty. By a vote of five to two, the penalty
was fixed at expulsion. Evidence in all essential respects was substantially the same as it had been on the two previous trials of the
accused by his own Lodge. This last trial record is now before Grand
Lodge.
·
During the trial, the attorney for the accused objected to the jurisdiction of California Lodge No. 1 to try the case, claiming that the
accused was entitled to be tried in the Masonic District or in the County
in which his alleged unmasonic conduct took place. It was also asserted
that the accused could not compel the attendance of necessary witnesses
at a trial held in San Francisco. An objection was also raised that the
accused, by a retrial. was being placed twice in ,jeopardy for the same
offense and that a fair trial could not be had in San Francisco: that the
dictates of common justice required the accused to be tried in the then
County of his residence where he was known. The Master presiding
over the trial overruled all such objections and directed that the trial
proceed. Counsel for the accused gave oral notice of appeal to Grand
Lodge.

Your Committee advises Grand Lodge that in its opinion California
Lodge No. 1 having been designated by the Grand Master to conduct
the trial pursuant to a resolution of Grand Lodge, did have jurisdiction
of the cause. California Lodge No. 1 flied a new charge against the
accused. It was, however, identical with the charge as originally preferred. Grand Lodge had twice reversed the finding of "Not Guilty"
of the charges as originally preferred. There was, therefore, no final
judgment on such charges. This was in effect a retrial upon the same
charge and by reason of this fact, the plea of being placed twice in
jeopardy was not well taken. The rulings of the Master were. therefore,
correct.
In the opinion of your Committee, there is no substantial error
reflected in the record which would warrant Grand Lodge on the face
of this record alone in reversing the present finding of "Guilty" and
the sentence of expulsion. The evidence presented a question of fact
for determination by the Trial Commissioners. The evidence was such
that it would have supported either a finding of "Guilty" or an acquittal.
just as it was also sufficient, in the opinion of your Committee, to support
the two previous acquittals. Findings of guilt or of acquittal by Trial
Commissions should not be lightly overruled by Grand Lodge. A reversal of the determination of a Trial Commission should only occur
where there has been errors in the trial of the case or such a complete
disregard of the evidence as to result in a miscarriage of justice. Such
has long been the guiding rule of Grand Lodge.
Your Committee is still of the opinion, which was shared by a substantial number, including several past Grand Masters, that the two
prior verdicts of acquittal should have been sustained and that the
present finding of guilt and sentence of expulsion, while warranted on
the face of the present record. can only be upheld because of the action
on the part of Grand Lodge when this case was before it in 1947 and
again in 1948. Of the total of twenty-three Trial Commissioners before
whom the accused has appeared, sixteen have voted him "Not Guilty"
and seven have voted him "Guilty."
While not agreeing with the end result in this case, your Committee
must accept the action of Grand Lodge taken in 1947 and 1948, and
finding the present record sufficient to sustain the finding of the Trial
Commission, must recommend affirmance of its findings.
We therefore reluctantly offer the following Resolution and move
its adoption:
RESOLVED. that the Finding of "GUILTY" by the Trial Commission and the fixing of the penalty at expulsion, be and the same
hereby is ratified, affirmed and approved.
Brothers Hoyt and Paul join in the Resolution. but not in the report.
Adopted.
