Trial Record No. 1129
. To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
This is a petition for restoration by H. G. an entered apprentice
Mason of Bay City Lodge No. 526. He was suspended by action of the
Grand Lodge 1948.
In May 1946 when H. G. was made an Entered Apprentice Mason,
he was employed as a real estate salesman by J. B. a real estate broker,
and a member of a lodge in this jurisdiction. As a result of a real estate
transaction, J. B. preferred charges of unmasonic conduct against H. G.
and he was tried by Bay City Lodge therefore and given a reprimand.
When the record of the case came before Grand Lodge, it was returned
for further trial because no finding had been made on the specification.
It further appeared that if H. G. were guilty of wrongdoing, so was
J. B., the employer who preferred the -charge, and, therefore, Grand
Lodge ordered that both parties be tried by a neutral lodge, the two
being members of different lodges. After separate trials, both were
found guilty of unmasonic conduct. H. G.'s penalty was fixed at ex;.
pulsion but thereafter reduced to suspension by Grand Lodge. The
petition for restoration was filed August 17, 1949.
In his petition for restoration, H. G. invites attention to the fact
that at the time of his transgression, he was a novice in the real estate
business and was badly guided by his employer, J.B., who was an elder
and more experienced real estate operator. He also invites our attention
to his candor and straightforwardness at both trials, where in he attempted to fully and correctly set forth all of the facts of the transaction.
He recognizes that his acts were wrongful but he believes himself to be
rehabilitated and points to his conduct since 1946.
The petition is supported by a letter from the Master of Bay City
Lodge who states that he has known the petitioner for many years and
has always held him in high esteem. He believes that the petitioner
has had ample time to consider his actions and has repented. ·
The Secertary of Bay City Lodge, by a communication dated Sep;.
tember 30, 1949, advises that the petition for restoration has been discussed with the master and wardens of the lodge. and while no official
action was taken by the lodge, it was the belief of both the master and
the secretary that H. G. had been sufficiently punished for his misdeeds
and that his application should be granted.
The record shows that notice of the petition has been duly given to
both Bay City Lodge in which H. G. was made an Entered Apprentice
Mason, and Fidelity Lodge No. 120, in which he was tried and found

Your committee on Grievances to which was referred Trial Record

Accused, H. R. D., a member of Downey Lodge No. 220, was convicted in the state courts of ten counts of lewd conduct with two girls
under fourteen years of age, his stepdaughters, aged 8 and 10 years
respectively, and was sentenced to imprisonment in San Quentin prison,
to which he was committed. On appeal to the state District Court of
Appeal, the convictions on all but one count were affirmed. It was held
that one count was a duplication of one of the other counts, and the
conviction as to that count was reversed. The judgment as to tqe other
nine counts thus become final.
Accused was brought to trial in the lodge on charges filed against
him specifying the nine separate counts of lewd conduct for which he
had been convicted in the state courts. Whether any proceedings were
first taken for automatic expulsion does not show in the record, and, if
not, no explanation is offered or is apparent why that procedure was
not followed where the accused was convicted of a felony and was
sentenced to imprisonment therefor.
The summons was served on accused by mail at a prison forestry
camp where he then was. He did not appear at the trial either in person
or by attorney.
The evidence at the trial before the commissioners consisted of
certified copies of the charges and judgment against accused in the
state superior court and certified copies of the judgment of the appellate
court affirming the judgment on nine counts. These documents made
out a prima facie case of guilt against the accused at the Masonic trial.
He was found guilty of all nine specifications and of the charge of
unmasonic conduct, and was ordered suspended.
The finding of guilt was proper. However, Grand Lodge has consistently held that where a Mason is convicted of a crime against the
state involving moral turpitude, and unless there are circumstances in
mitigation of the punishment, the penalty should be expulsion. Certainly
nine violations of Section 288 of the California Penal Code, lewd and

Your Committee to which was referred Trial Record No. 1161
reports as follows:
The accused, W.C.H., was tried in Laguna Beach Lodge No. 672,
but had been a member of a lodge in Illinois from which he had been
suspended for non-payment of dues some years ago. The charges were:
( 1) "That on or about the 28th day of October, 1947, he did ask to
visit Laguna Beach Lodge, a right reserved only to Master Masons in
good standing while he was knowingly not in good standing in any
reular lodge of Masons, having been suspended" by the lodge in Illinois.
( 2) That on said occasion "he did gain admission to a meeting of
Laguna Beach Lodge by the practice of fraud and deceit, thereby cheating, wronging and defrauding a Lodge of Master Masons out of that
which was not his just due, all of which was done with willful intent
to violate the Laws, Rules and Regulations of Masonry."
The trial before the commissioners of the lodge consisted mainly
of a lengthy cross-examination of the accused by the accuser, counsel
for accuser, and commissioners. There was no competent evidence introduced against him except a visiting card which he had signed on the
occasion in question.
The statement of the accused was that he had been suspended in his
Illinois lodge some years ago for non-payment of dues and was now
living in California; that he knew that his son was to receive his third
degree in Laguna Beach Lodge on the night in question; and almost
two months earlier he mailed a check for $70.00 to the Illinois lodge
with a request for reinstatement. He said that sum was more than
enough to cover his delinquency, but that he received no answer.
His son-in-law 'phoned him the day of the degree that he had discussed the matter with some member of Laguna Beach lodge and that
it would be all right for him to come to the meeting that night, which
he then did. He entered the lodge hall with his son-in-law, who said
to someone in the anteroom, "This is Brother H, the father of the candidate. I can vouch for him," and that he was then given a visiting card
to sign but that nobody asked to see a receipt or anything. He had

..

256

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

brought along his check book so he could show the stub for the $70.00
check sent to Illinois, which was in apparent sequence in the book and
in proper place to correspond with the date he claimed to have mailed
it. This check stub was displayed by him at his trial.
Not only was the accused allowed to visit, but he was even called
on to act on a visiting committee for another visitor and signed that
visiting card as a member of the examining committee.
A letter was introduced from the secretary of the Illinois lodge
stating that he could find no record of any $70.00 check 'being received
nor of any reinstatement of the brother there. This was hearsay evidence, and does not disprove the testimony of the accused that he was
acting in good faith in making this visit to Laguna Beach lodge.
The trial commissioners found the accused Guilty of the first specification and of unmasonic conduct, but they divided 3 to 3 on the second
specification, which was not therefore a finding of Guilty on that. He
was sentenced to suspension.
The son-in-law, who had vouched for accused, had been tried separately for his offense and ordered reprimanded, which finding and penalty
was approved by Grand Lodge a year ago.
As above stated, the vote of three for Guilty and three for Not
Guilty on the second specification is tantamount to an acquittal on that
count. The first specification, on which conviction was had, does not,
in our opinion, state a Masonic offense. It charges merely that the
accused asked to visit a Masonic lodge. Asking such is certainly no
offense.
.
It seems that there is no evidence to contradict the fact that the
accused acted entirely in good faith in making this visit, desiring to
witness his own son receive the third degree, and that if the officers
of the lodge had required the showing of a receipt for dues under the
seal of his lodge as required by Section 170 of the Ordinances of this
Grand Lodge, he would not have been permitted to complete his blunder.
Accused testified that he felt that he had been reinstated in Illinois and
that he would hear from the lodge there in due time, and when his sonin-law reported to him that a lodge member had said a visit by him
under those circumstances would be all right, it was natural for him to
believe that such was the case. It does not appear that his action was
wilful or unlawful in any way. Not only does the specification fail to
state a Masonic offense, but the finding of Guilt in this case was not
justified or supported by the evidence at the trial. The letter from the
lodge secretary in Illinois was rank hearsay and contained statements
that the former secretary had told him he knew nothing of the $70.00
being received from the Accused, etc. It does not contradict the testimony of the accused and his showing of good faith.
Because of the lack of proof of any fraudulent intent on the part of
the accused we feel that this proceeding should be entirely terminated,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Accused J. P. F. was charged in two specifications-owning and
operating a bar and being a bartender. Upon the trial he pleaded guilty
to both charges and presented facts by way of extenuation, indicating
that he had gone into the liquor business in order to recoop moneys

appeal.

commit either of these offenses, "shall be deemed guilty of unmasonic
conduct, and shall, upon due trial and conviction of said offense, forfeit
all Masonic rights and privileges, including membership in any Lodge.''
Reference is made to the reports of the Committee on Grievances
on Trial Records No. 1134 and 1149, wherein at its last annual Communication the Grand Lodge adopted resolutions modifying the penalty
of suspension and fixing it an expulsion for violation of Section 210
of the Ordinances, for the reason, as stated by the Committee, that the
language of Section 210 " .•• does not permit of the penalty of suspension and commands the penalty of expulsion."
We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
RESOLVED: That the finding of guilt by the Trial Commission in
Trial Record No. 1173 be and the same is hereby affirmed and approved,
but that the penalty of reprimand be and the same is hereby modified
and the penalty fixed at expulsion.

Most Worshipful Grand Master and the Grand Lodge of California:
The Most Worshipful Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Masons
of the Philippine Islands, through the Grand Secretary, has written a
letter to me stating that it would be a great privilege for him to be pres ..
ent in this Grand Lodge Annual Communication; but that, it not being
possible for him to be here, he has appointed me as his personal repre..
sentative to extend fraternal greetings from him and the Grand Lodge
of the Philippine Islands to you and the Grand Lodge of California.
I appreciate this honor and privilege and your courtesy in receiving me
as such representative. Our Grand Lodge takes pride in the fact that the
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of California is its Mother
Grand Lodge, and I take this opportunity to express to you and your
Grand Lodge our appreciation of the cordial fraternal relations which
have at all times existed between these two Grand Lodges, and we are
happy to anticipate the continuance of such fraternal relations.
I cannot give you from my personal knowledge a complete report on
present conditions of Freemasonry in the Philippine Islands, as I have
been absent from that Grand Jurisdiction since November 20, 1941,
when I left Manila on vacation in the United States. I anticipate that
your Grand Lodge must be particularly interested in the present condi..
tions of the Masonic Lodges in the Philippines since the organization
of the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands and the results of the
invasion of the Islands by the Japanese Imperial Army during the late
war and its efforts to suppress the Masonic Fraternity in the Philip..
pines, and I can better give you this information through the reports
of certain officers of the Grand Lodge who have personal knowledge
of those conditions.
It is very generally known among the members of the Fraternity in
California that prior to American occupation of the Phillippines the
majority of the Lodges then existing in that country were chartered
by the "Grande Oriente Espanol," of Madrid, Spain; but that within
a few years after the American occupation of the Islands, between
1901 and 1907, charters were granted by the Grand Lodge of Free·
and Accepted Masons of California to three Lodges in the Philip ..
pines, namely. Manila Lodge No. 342, of Manila; Cavite Lodge No.
350, of Cavite, and Corregidor Lodge No. 386, of Manila.
Between 1906 and 1909 the Grand Lodge of California had a committee investigating the origin and status of the Spanish Lodges in the
Philippines. That investigation showed that the "Grande Oriente

260

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Espanol" had invaded the Grand Jurisdiction of Pennsylvania by the
issuance of charters for lodges in that Grand Jurisdiction. For that
reason the Most Worshipful Grand Master of California considered
the "Grande Oriente Espanol" as irregular and not worthy of recognition, and he prohibited the three Lodges in the Philippines chartered
by that Grand Lodge from having Masonic intercourse of any kind
with the lodges chartered by the "Grande Oriente Espanol."
The three Lodges in the Philippines chartered by the Grand Lodge
of California were sufficient in number for the organization of the Grand
Lodge of the Philippine Islands, but the officers and members of the
three Lodges wanted to have all the regular Lodges in the Philippines
to unite in organizing the new Grand Lodge. There were two other
regular Lodges in the Philippines which were chartered by the Grand
Lodge of Scotland, namely, Perla del Oriente Lodge No. 1034, in
Manila, and Cebu Lodge No. 1106 in Cebu.
Finally, in 1912, the three Lodges chartered by the Grand Lodge
of California severally adopted a resolution in favor of the organization
of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the Philippine
Islands, and fixed November 17, 1912, at 8:00 o'clock, P. M., Masonic
Temple, Manila, as the time and place for the preliminary meeting for
that purpose. However, the two Scotch Lodges did not send any dele~
gates to that preliminary meeting, and it was unanimously agreed by
the delegates from the three lodges under the Grand Lodge of California
to postpone the preliminary meeting to December 11, 1912, at 8:00
o'clock, P. M .• in the Masonic Temple, Manila, in order to give the
Scotch Lodges an opporturnity to take action on this matter in their
next stated meetings. But the Scotch Lodges did not send any delegates
to the meeting on December 11, 1912, and it was rumored that they
could not take any action in the organization of a Grand Lodge without
obtaining a dispensation from the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge
of Scotland.
Inasmuch as the three Lodges chartered by the Grand Lodge of
California had the legal right to organize a Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the Philippine Islands, it was decided to proceed
with the organization of the new Grand Lodge. The organization was
completed in the early morning of December 19, 1912, and all the
elected and appointed officers present at that time were installed in their
respective offices.
The new Grand Lodge was quite promptly recognized by practi~
cally all the regular Grand Lodges of the world during 1913, 1914, and
1915; and during that time efforts were being made to bring about the
so-called "Unification" of all the Masonic Lodges in the Philippines
under the new Grand Lodge.
In November, 1916, the officers of the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands and the officers of the various other Lodges in the Islands

•

261

came to an agreement upon the method of bringing all the Lodges under
the authority of the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands, and on and
after November 11, 1916, Most Worshipful Grand Master William H.
Taylor issued dispensations to the several Spanish Lodges to which
dispensations had been previously issued. This completed the unification of all the Masonic Lodges under the Grand Lodge of the Philippine
Islands, except Perla del Oriente Lodge No. 1034, of the Grand Lodge
of Scotland, and with that one exception all the Masonic Lodges in the
Philippines, for more than thirty years, have been granted charters by
the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the Philippine
Islands.
The Japanese Imperial Army sought to suppress Freemasonry in the
Philippines and deliberately killed the Junior Past Grand Master, M.
W. Bro. Jose Abad Santos, and the Grand Master, M. W. Bro. John
R. Mc~'ie, and the Deputy Grand Master, R. W. Bro. Jose P. Guido,
and maltreated and abused other prominent Masons while they were
held as prisoners or internees in Fort Santiaga: and they damaged and
destroyed the properties and records of the Masonic organizations in
the Philippines. But, in spite of such merciless and criminal activities,
the Lodges and other Masonic bodies have been to a great extent rehabilitated, and the latest information is to the effect that Freemasonry
is still thriving in the Philippines. The Filipino people and most of the
foreign residents in general appreciate the Masonic Fraternity and its
good teachings and practices. The appreciation of Masonry by the
Filipino Brethren was very well expressed by the M. W. Grand Master
Esteban Munnarriz in his inaugural address at the last Annual Communication, when he said:
"In our beloved Philippines, not everything looks rosy at present.
There are some discordant elements which are trying to disrupt the
peace and harmony in our homes, in our institutions, and in our established government. Our sons of old have given their lives to fight
tyranny and oppression for the liberation of our country; and Masons
are those who continued the peaceful struggle for the independence
which we are now enjoying. As Filipinos we certainly owe a debt of
gratitude to Masonry. As Masons of today, ours is the duty to find
ways and means to eliminate the presence of those discordant elements
who, like termites, are trying to weaken the foundations of our structures. If strong measures have not been successful in eliminating them,
let us try to use benevolent means. Let us. all be instruments of peace.
Where there is hatred, let us sow love. where there is doubt, faith:
where there is despair. hope; and where there is sadness, joy. In this
way we may be able to succeed and enjoy once more the blessings of
peace in our homes and in our institutions, ancl we shall find the way
to our ultimate goal of universal peace and brotherhood."

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Brother Mauro Baradi, Grand Orator of the Grand Lodge, in his
oration under the heading "Masonry in Progress," in part, said:
"In spite of the persecution. prosecution, and punishment of its
adherents on questionable and flimsy grounds and under adverse cir~
cumstances. Freemasonry has taken root in the world, and its member~
ship considerably increased. Such is our Craft. It is progress.
"We need not go far to illustrate our point. Postwar Masonry in the
Philippines furnishes an illustration. We who have suffered and are
still suffering from the disastrous effects of the last global conflict are
familiar with the facts. To mention a few will suffice.
"When after a period of over three terrible and seemingly endless
years of enemy occupation, our country was liberated early in 1945 by
the armed forces of Democracy. the Brethern who survived the holocaust
found themselves in a destitute condition. Some lost their loved ones
and all their property and some knew not what to do; and the others,
deprived of home and shelter. knew not where to go. The immediate
problem had to be solved, which was relief to the distressed worthy
Brethem, their widows and orphans. Officers of the Grand Lodge at
the time, with characteristic foresight, made the corresponding appeal
to friends across the seas. We had a feeling of anxiety for those close
to us and genuine solicitude for those in want. But, true to Masonic
tradition, the encouraging reply was not long in coming. The honor
roll of those who responded is impressive as it is inspiriting. It consists
of more than 38 Grand Lodges in the United States and Canada,
besides other organizations and individuals. · The substantial sums
contributed were received through the Grand Lodge of California and
the Masonic Service Association of the United States. To each and
every one of these benefactors, we reiterate our gratitude and express
our thanks. Their liberality and benevolence we will not soon forget,
but shall long remember. Theirs is a treasured memory, a golden tie
that binds us together in the name of Masonry."
On the subject of rehabilitation of the subordinate Lodges and the
ban on Freemasonry, Brother Baradi said:
"Another problem was the reestablishment of subordinate Lodges.
It was but natural that the members wanted to resume their labors as
soon as possible. The ban on Masonry issued during the war only made
them more eager to start anew. The task was not easy. Traveling was
still dangerous and distance a hindrance. Doubt and hesitation would
have caused further delay in the work, if not another setback to the
undertaking. To advance was more preferable than to retreat. The
obstacles were overcome, and within a comparatively short period most
of our Lodges, including those in China, were reorganized and others
constituted.
"Still another item in the agenda had yet to be disposed of. namely,

I

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

263

the repair or reconstruction of Lodge buildings or the erection of new
ones. Practically all Masonic documents. jewels, and paraphernalia
were looted, libraries burned, and temples ruined. This involved a
question of financing. In all the Lodges the situation was the same.
Everybody was broke. Many were down, but not out. And the remedy:
borrow and build, or dispair and quit. Masons are not quitters. Their
honor was at stake and they gave until it hurt. What appeared impos~
sible to do would be done again. And so it was done with the result
that bigger and better buildings have risen where small ones stood
before: and new and inspiring structures have been erected which
ordinarily could not have been built at all.
"Our progress of rehabilitation, reconstruction, and reorganization
is far from being finished. And more men, money, and materials are
still required to complete the enterprise. But we have had the will, and
we worked hard, and we accomplished something."
According to the report of the Grand Secretary in the last Annual
Communication, there were then 101 Lodges in active operation, four
of them being under dispensation, and the Lodges have 7,099 Master ·
Masons, 198 Fellowcrafts, and 390 Entered Apprentices. The gain
over the preceding year was 81 7 Master Masons.
Brethren of the Grand Lodge, the foregoing extracts and other
information from the official records of the Proceedings of the Grand
Lodge of the Philippine Islands in the Annual Communication of 1949
show to some extent the progress that Freemasonry is making in the
Philippines in spite of the efforts of hostile forces to ban and destroy
the Masonic Fraternity in that country.
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren, I thank you one
and all for your courtesy, kind attention, and interest in permitting
me to bring to your attention some of the difficulties and trying con~
ditions that we have had to contend with in the establishment and
maintenance of Freemasonry in the distant outpost of the Philippine
Islands. I trust that this limited information may be sufficient to
demonstrate to you the good Masonic character of our Brethren in the
Philippines, and that you are convinced that our Filipino Brethren and
other Brethren associated with them in the Grand Jurisdiction of the
Philippine Islands are worthy of the assistance that we have given
them and may hereafter give to them in their further progress in their
aims and purposes in Freemasonry.
GEORGE R. HARVEY

Number of Members in New Lodge
Minimum and Maximum Membership
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under
consideration the Resolution submitted by the Committee on Charters,
relative to the minimum and maximum number of Masons who may
petition for a dispensation for a new lodge.
Section 101 of the Ordinances of Grand Lodge now provides that
the minimum number of Masons who may petition for a dispensation to
form a new lodge is twelve, and the maximum twenty-five. The members of the Committee · on Charters ask that the Section be amended
to provide for a minimum number of twenty-five and a maximum number
of fifty.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes agrees with the
view of the Committee on Charters that under present day conditions,
a petitioning group of twelve members would experience much difficulty
in establishing a lodge on a sound and permanent basis, and that an
increase of the maximum to fifty would give additional strength to any
group entering on the task of creating a new lodge.

Masonic Club Within A Lodge
Your committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered
that portion of your Grand Masters' message wherein he recommended
against the creation of a Masonic Club by a constituent Lodge, membership to which would be limited to the members of that Lodge.
Your committee is in complete accord with the belief of the Grand
Master that the creation of such a club within a Lodge would sooner
or later result in the development of cliques and possible disharmony.
Your committee approves the Grand Master's recommendation
against the formation of the club.
Adopted.

Grand Lodge Ritual
There has been referred to your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes the resolution offered by Most Worshipful Chester Warlow,
P.G.M., proposing that Section 3 of the Constitution of the Grand
Lodge of California be amended to read as it did in the year 1854 with
the addition of the names and titles of such Grand Lodge Officers as we
now have, who were not provided for in our earlier constitution in those
simpler days.
·
Your Committee has given the same careful consideration and believe that such legislation should be adopted as to effect the change. ·
We are in that situation explained by our Right Worshipful Deputy
Grand Master when he was Junior Grand Warden which requires if
we are to be consistent a change in either the Constitution or in our
rituals for the opening and closing of Grand Lodge, the Grand Lodge
Installation Service, the Laying of Corner Stones, the Dedication of
Cemeteries, the Constitution of Lodges, and possibly other ceremonies.
For one hundred years a member of our Grand Lodge has used the
phrase "Most Worshipful Grand Master" in addressing that officer
instead of simply "Most Worshipful" as I have opened this report. We
feel that long custom in the manner of addressing our officers in the
various ceremonies and the conduct of Grand Lodge proceedings outweighs the merit of maintaining the modern wording of our constitution.
It may be added that we arrive at consistency with one change by this
method whereas many alterations in our ceremonies become necessary
to effect consistency if the constitution remains as it now is.

Adopted.

Method of Receiving a Plea of Guilty
Most Worshipful 'and Brethren of Grand Lodge:
There was referred to your committee on Policy and General Purposes the resolution offered by R. W. Arthur Paulsen, Senior Grand
Warden, and W. Warren Libby, P. M. of Blackmer Lodge No. 442,
providing for the enactment of a new section of the Ordinances of this
Grand Lodge to be numbered Section 309.1 which provides for a method
of receiving a plea of "guilty" by the accused after the receipt of charges
of unmasonic conduct by the Master, and before the trial by the Commissioners.
Your committee has given the resolution careful consideration and
has heard the statements of those in favor and opposed thereto.
The primary purpose of the proposal seems to be to save expense,
avoid publicity and possibly to secure speed in infliction of the penalty.
On the other hand it would appear that an opportunity is afforded for
the accftsed to say with some basis of truth, "I resigned from that outfit-that's how much I think of them": there is but one penalty provided,
viz., expulsion and it would seem that the punishment is severe for a
minor offense or an accidental or unintended breach of our code; the
record would be insufficient to permit the Grievance Committee to
adjust the penalty to the offense or in fact to intelligently consider the
facts on the automatic appeal or in fact to pass upon any questions save
whether or not the charges have been admitted by the accused: that if
at some future time application should be made to Grand Lodge for
reinstatement, the facts of the case would be a matter of the word of
the Master against that of the accused who might charge that he was
induced to sign the admission under coercion of the Master: at such
late date the witnesses who could have testified to the truth of the
charges might be dead or addresses unknown and be beyond reach of
the Master; that charges by the accused of coercion, falsification and
vilification could be of great embarassment to an honest conscientious Master who would be helpless in the face of such charges by an
unscrupulous person; that the plea of guilty should be received and
made of record before more than one person and the existing ordinances
provide a proper, plain and ample method for such procedure and for
the making of a record upon which future consideration of the case can

272

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

be had upon a record containing all the facts with such certainty and
verity as to be 'beyond impeachment by the accused.
That section is 314 of the Ordinances and reads as follows:
"The accused should now present his answer to the charge
and specification which answers may be either oral or written and
should be made a part of the record. In this answer he may make
a general or particular denial of all the specifications of the
charge, or he may deny some and admit others, and make statements in justification or extenuation of those committed; or he
may admit all, with expressions of sorrow for his misconduct; or
in fact, he may make any answer which to him, or his counsel,
shall seem meet."
This section follows that other section which provides for the assembly of the commissioners and its organization, and the above section
provides that the statements of the accused shall be made a matter of
record.
Your committee is of the opinion that these proceedures are essential
not only to the safe9uarding of the rights of the accused but for the
protection of our Masters against calumny, false charges and vilification
and for the other reasons here expressed and we therefore recommend
that the legislation be not adopted.
I move the adoption of the report.
Adopted.
( See note at end of the report of this Committee for consideration
of alternative legislation.)

Expenditures for Public Schools Week Observance
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The resolution presented by six lodges concerning the expense of
conducting the observance of Public Schools Week and recommending
that such expenditures be paid out of the general funds of the lodge
and not charged to the refreshment fund, has been referred to the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes and it has had our consideration.
Your Committee is of the opinion that no change should be made
in existing law upon this subject.
The general funds of the lodge are. charged with the payment of
the expenses of operation, Grand Lodge dues and assessments, and
relief. We think no added burden should be placed upon this fund. The
cost of operating our. lodges is increasing, the Grand Lodge per capita
assessment is increasing, and while it may not be felt as yet, we may
reasonably expect in the not too distant future increasing requests for
relief.

I

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

273

It is the understanding of your Committee that lodges are not
expected or required to incur any large expense in this connection.
The Grand Lodge of California initiated many years ago the movement in America for the fixing of a special time during which the attention of our countrymen should be directed to our public school system.
The movement has gained impetus down through the years and has
received the endorsement of schools, societies of various character, the
National Educational Association, States and Grand Lodges. We think
the time has come when all that is necessary on the part of our lodges
is to encourage, cooperate in and foster this work. This ought not require
any large expenditure on their part.
We therefore recommend that the resolution be not adopted.
Adopted.

.
Your committee feels that the dissemination of the proposed notice

into the hands of the profane and thus make public matters which
should be known only to members o1 the Craft. This might result
many times in embarrassment and trouble to both the lodge and candi~
date. Rather than risk this danger, it would appear that the present
provisions for notice to the mem·bers of applicants for Degrees or for
affiliation should suffice.
Your Committee therefore recommends that the resolution be not
adopted.

Discretionary Expenditures
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
There has been referred to your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes a proposal of Crockett Lodge No. 139 that Section 158,
Ordinances of Grand Lodge, be amended to permit expenditure of not
to exceed $20.00 by donation to the Endowment Fund of Grand Lodge
in memory of a deceased brother if his family should request a donation
to charity instead of Bowers. The present provisions of Section 158
authorize a Lodge to remember a deceased brother by a floral gift.
Your Committee feels that Lodge funds should not be diverted from
purposes now permitted, and, especially so in this case, since the families
of deceased brethren would object to Bowers only in rare instances. The
purpose of our floral remembrance would not be served by a donation
to charity and, in any event, the amount of the gift would not justify
this departure from our traditional practice.
Your Committee therefore recommends that the resolution be not
adopted.
Adopted.

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under

Sec. 159-A lodge may expend, in its discretion, not to exceed

The present law limits such expenditures to twenty per cent of the

In view of the changing economic conditions and the certainty that
greater demands will have to be made upon the general funds of the

Postponement of Lectures
.To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Worshipful Brother Irwin G. Beadle, Master of Corona Lodge No.
324, makes formal suggestion that the Master's lectures of the First
and Third Degrees be eliminated from the regular Degree Work and
that at the end of the Master's year, all candidates raised during his
term be assembled and a revised lecture to cover the Three Degrees 'be
delivered to them at that time.
Lectures of the Masonic Degrees, as well as the First and Second
sections of that work are, when properly rendered, both beautiful and
instructive, not only to the candidate, but also to the brethren assembled.
Within the framework of these lectures are to be found many wise and
serious truths and their oft reptition more firmly imprints these lessons
upon the minds of our members.
If the lectures of these Degrees were to be consolidated and to be
delivered but once a year, there certainly would .be a material loss of
beauty and impressiveness of our ceremonies.
The Committee therefore recommends that the suggestion of Brother
Beadle be not adopted.

Centennial Arrangements
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The report of the Committee on Centennial Arrangements was
referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
This report contains one specific recommendation for Grand Lodge,
in these words, "The Committee recommends appropriate legislation
to permit the attendance of Master Masons during the opening of
Grand Lodge."
In view of the fact that the recommendation is offered by the Committee on Centennial Arrangements, it is presumed that they have in
mind the opening and closing ceremonies of the Grand Lodge on the
specific occasion of its Centennial Communication in 1950.
The Centennial celebration of this Grand Lodge is certain to attract
the attendance of Masons from all parts of the world. In anticipation
of that attendance, a large auditorium in San Francisco has been reserved for the formal Communication in that year. In that structure,
there will be available a seating capacity for several thousand members
of the Craft.
While there might be some objection that persons not members of
the Grand Lodge of California, or otherwise not entitled to be present
at the opening ceremonies thereof would thus hear and see the formal
opening of our Grand Lodge in ample form, yet it is the opinion of this

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Committee that the importance of the occasion and the desire to bring
the impressiveness of our ceremonies to all visiting brethren, overrules
such objection.
It is therefore the recommendation of the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes that all Master Masons in good standing be admitted
to the opening and closing ceremonies of the Annual Communication
of this Grand Lodge in 1950. and that legislation for that purpose,
limited to that specific year, be prepared and adopted at this present
Communication of Grand Lodge.

Inspectors Residence
The Grand Master's message contains a recommendation that the
words "a resident of the District for which he is appointed" be stricken
from Section 53 of the Ordinances.
This recommendation was made by the Grand Master in connection
with the appointment of inspectors, and particularly in relation to the
difficulty in some cases of finding a man residing in an inspectoral
district, who is qualified and willing to take over the responsibility.
It is the intention to allow, in such cases, the appointment of an inspector
residing outside the inspectoral district.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes approves the
Grand Master's recommendation and refers the same to the Committee
on Jurisprudence.
Adopted.

Masonic Funerals
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has ·h ad llnder
consideration that portion of the Grand Master's message dealing with
the subject of Masonic funerals, and particularly with situations more
or less embarrassing arising out of the ruling, in 1916, of Grand Master
Burnett, that the Masonic Lodge shall "have charge of and conclude
the service.''
It appears that argument is occasionally created as to the part that
clergymen participating in the funeral service shall have, particularly
with reference to concluding the service and pronouncing the final
benediction, etcetera.
The Grand Master recommends that Sections 647 and 648, Edicts
and Resolutions, be rescinded, and that our Lodges conduct Masonic
funerals in accordance with Section 266 of Ordinances. This Section
makes no mention of clergymen and the Grand Master observes that
should it be the desire of the family that the minister of the deceased
brother conclude the service, give a eulogy, or word of comfort, or
pai:ticipate at the beginning of the service, the Master, the family of the
deceased, and the minister of his church should mutually decide the
order of the service, bearing in mind, of course, that our entire service
must be given.
Your Committee approves the recommendation of the Grand Master
as to policy.
Adopted.

In accordance with the action of the Grand Lodge at the last Annual
Communication, the auditing procedure has been changed during the

has proved very satisfactory and has facilitated the preparation of the
annual audit report.

the Endowment Fund. and also the financial portion of the report of
the Trustees of the Masonic Homes all of which have been certified
by the auditors. In our opinion they reflect the true condition of the
affairs of the Grand Lodge and its constituent organizations. We be~

coming year, and are recommending in the proposed budget an amount
which we believe will be sufficient to cover the additional cost.
PRUDENT MAN RULE

by the Committee on Policy and General Purposes. We have no inten~
tion of prolonging discussion of the matter except to express, for the
record. our approval of the legislation which is proposed. and to suggest
that all members of the Grand Lodge endeavor to familiarize themselves
with the principles under which the Prudent Man Rule operates so
that they may be prepared to express themselves at the next Annual

BENICIA LoDGE No.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

5

The request for $5,000.00 for purchase of the old Benicia Lodge has
been referred to this Committee. While the Committee on Finance is
in sympathy with the laudable desire to acquire historical sites and
buildings, it views with alarm the increase in requests for Grand Lodge
funds for such purposes and is frankly afraid to set a precedent in this
respect.
It is the opinion of the Committee that such funds, if approved by
Grand Lodge should come from special assessments to be levied on the
constituent lodges. It also feels that the financial burden on many of
the constituent lodges is already heavy and with indications of a slackening of candidates, applications, the burden may be come heavier in
the future,
The Committee on Finance recommends no appropriation for this
purchase and suggests that this matter be referred to the Committee
on Lodge Financing for further discussion with Benicia Lodge, and that
Benicia Lodge itself give serious consideration to finding ways and
means of acquiring the old temple through its own resources: provided
however, that if after thorough investigation, Benicia Lodge is found
unable to finance the acquisition of the Temple, the Grand Master is
authorized to extend assistance to Benicia Lodge No. 5 for this purpose
in an amount not to exceed $5,000.00, and with the approval of the
Chairman of the Finance Committee, and the Chairman of the Committee on Lodge Financing.
GRAVEL RANGE LODGE No. 59
GEORGETOWN loDGE No. 25

Two years ago an appropriation of $13,000.00 was made to enable
this lodge to rebuild its temple. Of this amount $12,578.00 was utilized.
Your Committee on Finance reported last year that this amount was
being carried on the books of Grand Lodge as an account receivable
under the heading of "owing from Gravel Range Lodge." Also at that
time we reported that it was too early to determine what amount of the
above advance should· be eventually returned by Gravel Range Lodge.
Our investigation of the affairs of this Lodge, with its membership of
66, indicates to us that the Lodge is not at the present time, nor can it
reasonably be expected at any time in the foreseeable future, ever be
in a position to repay any portion of the amount advanced to it by
Grand Lodge. The account in our judgment is uncollectable, and we
recommend that the amount be written off.
Last year the Grand Master reported upon the need of this Lodge
for financial assistance to aid them in the rebuilding of their temple.
The matter was referred jointly to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, and the Committee on Finance. Following a conference

285

between the two committees, your Committee on Finance reported that
it was its considered opinion that some method of relief should be
determined upon, it being understood that the final disposition, that is,
whether it is to be an advance or an outright gift, shall be determined
at this session of Grand Lodge. During the past year Georgetown
Lodge has had plans prepared for a building to meet their requirements,
on which they have an estimated cost of approximately $15,000.00 to
build. To their everlasting credit this small group, 62 members, have
raised a sum slightly in excess of $5,000.00 toward the _project. We
recommend that Grand Lodge advance to Georgetown Lodge as needed
and as a gift for the purpose of rebuilding their temple, a sum of not
to exceed $10,000.00.
While we are sympathetic toward both Gravel Range and Georgetown Lodges in the plight in which they find themselves, and are willing
to come to their assistance, still we can not feel that their officers in the
past have followed good business practice. In fact, we feel that they
have been extremely careless in the handling of the business affairs of
their respective Lodges. The fact that fire insurance rates in these
somewhat isolated areas may be high, is no excuse for not carrying
ample fire insurance. The high rate is just another proof of the fact
that the risk is great. In both of these cases the buildings were destroyed by fire. In neither case was there anywhere near ample insurance coverage. Grand Lodge cannot be expected to carry on ·a policy
of assuming the financial burden of rehabilitating Lodges which throqgh
their own carelessness have failed to take the ordinary precautions that
prudent business men should exercise. In view of these developments,
we recommend to all lodges in the Jurisdiction that they make a careful
survey of their insurance coverages, both fire and liability, to determine
whether or not they are amply protected, and if not, that they take steps
to place such additional insurance as may be necessary so that in case
of the loss of their property by fire, they will not be found in the same
unfortunate circumstances as the two lodges heretofore mentioned.

GEORGE WASHINGTON NATIONAL MASONIC MEMORIAL

In accordance with the actions taken at the 1947 and 1948 Annual
Communications of this Grand Lodge, a fifteen cent per capita tax has
been levied in the past two years for the purpose of bringing our participation in this most worthy project to the level set by the Memorial
~ssociation as being required to complete the edifice in a suitable manner. In its report to the Grand Lodge at the 1947 Annual Communication, the special committee estimated that our quota could be met by a
levy of 15 cents per member per annum in less than ten years.
Your committee recommends that this levy be continued, and therefore offers the following resolution:
RESOLVED: That a per capita of 15 cents be levied and the proceeds therefrom added to the fund known as the George Washington
National Masonic Memorial Fund, and that said fund or any portion
thereof 'be remitted to said Memorial Association upon the authority
of a Committee composed of the Grand Master, the Grand Treasurer,
and the Chairman of the Finance Committee or as authorized at some
future Communication of the Grand Lodge.
MASONIC HOMES

Your Committee on Finance has carefully reviewed the report of
the Trustees and the audit on the Masonic Homes, and the request of
the Trustees for a $1.00 per capita to be levied for the operation of the
Homes.
The principal source of income for the Homes for the past six years
has been the $25.00 contribution of each initiate. Since 1947 the revenue
from this source has been rapidly dropping, and the estimate of the
Grand Secretary's office is that it will continue to drop. There was a

290

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

small operating deficit in the year ending July 1, 1948, and a deficit of
$81,000.00 in the last fiscal year. In the coming year the revenue from
the per capita of 50 cents voted last year for the Homes will be availa~le,
and if the operating expenses do not increase, the Homes should Just
about break even. However, the Trustees estimate that the expenses
will be increased between five and ten per cent due to the additional
hospital and dwelling facilities provided in the current building pr.ogram.
In the following year, with the revenue from the $1.00 per capita, the
Homes should be able to cover their expenses and probably return some
of the funds borrowed from the Grand Lodge and other sources.
Your Committee, therefore, concurs in the recommendation of the
Trustees that a per capita of $1.00 be levied for the operation of Masonic
Homes, and offers the following resolution and moves its adoption:
RESOLVED: That a per capita of $1.00 be levied for the operation of the Masonic Homes.

Therefore the only change in the per capita tax is occasioned by the
Increase from fifty cents to one dollar for the benefit of the Masonic
Hames.
In concluding its report, your committee on Finance offers the following resolution; and recommends its adoption:
Resolved that expenditure of $276,865.38 as represented by the
budgeted items and appropriations shown in the foregoing report be
approved.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence respectfully proposes legislation
on subjects submitted to it for consideration and recommendation as
follows:
Centennial Arrangements
RESOLVED. that Section 33 of Ross Digest be repealed and that
the following 'be inserted in place thereof, to wit:
"None but members of the Grand Lodge, the Grand officers. Past Grand officers and Representatives of other
Grand Lodges, and the members of the Grand Organist's
choir, shall be present at the opening of the Annual Communication, or during an election therein, provided, however, that Master Masons may be present at the opening
of the 101st Annual Communication in October, 1950.
Master Masons may be present also at the opening of
all special communications.
Adopted by 5/6 vote.
Expenditures for Fraternal Intercourse
RESOLVED, that Section 159 of the Ordinances be repealed and
the following substituted:
SECTION 159 "A Lodge may expend, in its discretion,
not to exceed 30 per cent of its total revenue for purposes
of refreshments and the promotion of fraternal intercourse. In the discretion of the Lodge, this fund may be
cumulative in an amount not to exceed 20 per cent between
January 1. 1920 and January 1, 1950. and in an amount
not to exceed 30 per cent thereafter."
Adopted by 5/ 6 vote.

Decisions of the Grand Master
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has had under consideration the
decisions of the Grand Master as set forth in his message, and reports
as follows:
Decisions 1 and 2 and the ruling of the Grand Master as to Lodges
that failed to obey Section 251 of Ordinances are manifestly in accordance with our law for the reasons therein stated.
We therefore recommend that these decisions of the Grand Master
be approved.

Dispensations Issued
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has had under consideration the
special dispensations issued by the Grand Master during the year and
also his approval of Resolutions relative to Life Memberships, and
·change of meeting place.
We .find that all the acts of the Grand Master in regard to these
matters have been in compliance with the requirements of the Jaw. We,
therefore, recommend that the acts of the Grand Master therein be
approved.

Adopted.
Answering inquiry of Crocker Lodge No. 454, the Grand Master's
decision No. 3 defines "total revenue" as used in Sections 159 and 630,
Ross' Digest, to be gross receipts "less operating_ expenses, such as
taxes, insurance, custodian, depreciation, etc." The Grand Master
states that in so doing the decision of the late Grand Master Burnett
( Ross Digest Section 630) is not concurred in.
In light of the divergent facts involved in the two decisions we
believe there is no inconsistency and that both are correct: Grand Master Burnett, dealing with ordinary receipts of a lodge having no revenue
from investments, held that total revenue means "gross revenue";
Crocker Lodge, however, owns income bonds and real estate with a
building, including lodge and banquet rooms, and store rooms rented
for commercial purposes; the real property is incumbered and its maintenance necessarily requires payment of taxes and other expenses including depreciation. Such expenses must, as held by the Grand Master,
be 'deducted from the gross receipts from such investments in determining the total revenue of the lodge, 20% of which may be used for refreshment purposes.
Adopted.
Decision Number Four rendered by the Deputy Grand Master, held
as follows:
1. A Lodge cannot grant a waiver of jurisdiction on an Entered
Apprentice who has been denied advancement therein unless and until
the 'ban against him has been removed by a majority vote of the Lodge
in pursuance of the provisions of Section 220 of Ross Digest.
2. If the ban is removed and the waiver is granted, it is incumbent
upon the Lodge to which the waiver has been granted to make a searching investigation of the applicant in the usual course as prescribed by
Sections 225 and 226 of R.o ss Digest.
The foregoing decision is in accordance with Masonic Law.
Adopted.

297

Adopted.

Membersbii> Information
There has been submitted to your Committee on Jurisprudence for
enactment in our Ordinances as sub-division 12th of Section 202 the
following:
"12th. To certify the Masonic standing of a member of his Lodge
when requested so to do by the Secretary of any body or organization
the prerequisite to membership in which is that the applicant be a Mason
or related to a Mason."
Under the unwritten, and written law of this Grand Lodge, only the
three degrees in Masonry are recognized. The information sought to
be obtained as contemplated by the proposed amendment is available
for the benefit and convenience of the constituent Lodges only and to be
compelJed to divulge it to outsiders would be contrary to traditional
Masonic law. Your committee therefore recommends that the proposed
sub-section to Section 202 of Ordinance be not adopted.
Adopted.
Masonic Funerals
WHEREAS the Most Worshipful Grand Master in his message
recommended a change in our Edicts and Resolutions as set forth in
Sections 64 7 and 648 of the Edicts and Resolutions pertaining to the
conduct of funerals, now, therefore, be it resolved that Sections 647 and
648 of the Edicts and Resolutions be and the same are hereby repealed.
Adopted.

Dimits for Entered Apprentices and Felfow Crafts
Past Grand Master Warlow moved that the proposed amendment
be amended by deleting therefrom the first sentence.
The Amendment to the Amendment was adopted.
The proposed legislation thus specified that Section 173 of the
Ordinances be amended to read as follows :
"Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts have only the right to sit
in the Lodge in which they received the degree or degrees when open
in a degree taken by them, and the right to advancment therein after
passing satisfactorily a strict examination in open Lodge. They are not
required to pay any dues and are not entitled to vote or spea~ in the
Lodge, nor are they entitled to burial with Masonic honors, nor are
they or their widows or orphans entitled to relief from the funds of the
Lodge. They cannot, acting in a lodge, open in the degree taken, exercise any control over the funds of the Lodge for charity, or for any
other purpose. They cannot withdraw from their Lodge or apply for
membership or advancement in another Lodge without a waiver of
jurisdiction. If an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft has permanently
removed from the jurisdiction of California, his Lodge may issue to him
a dimit in order that he may apply for advancement in a Lodge in the
jurisdiction to which he has permanently removed. Charges may be
preferred against them for offenses committed, which shall be made in
the same manner and tried by a commission of Master Masons elected
as prescribed for trial of individual Masons. If found guilty the same
punishment may be inflicted as is prescribed for trial of individual
Masons, and they may appeal in like manner."
Adopted by unanimous vote.

Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California
September 30, 1949
San Francisco, California
Gentlemen:
.
We have audited the books of account and records of the· Grand Lodge
F. & A. M. of California for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1949 and present
herewith the following statements:
Consolidated Statements
Exhibit AA: Consolidated Statement of Assets and Liabilities, Owned or
Under Control of Grand Lodge, July 31, 1949.
Exhibit BB: Consolidated Statement of Cash Receipts and Disbursements,
from Fund of or Controlled by Grand Lodge, August 1, 1948 to July 31, 1949.
Grand Lodge
Exhibit A: Statement of Assets and Liabilities, July 31 ,1949.
Exhibit B: Statement of Cash Receipts and Disbursements, August 1,
1948 to July 31, 1949.
Exhibit C. Grand Treasurer's Statement of Cash Receipts and Disbursements, August 1, 1948 to July 31, 1949.
Exhibit D: Grand Secretaqr's Resume of Cash Received.
Schedule 1: List of Securities, July 31 ,1949.
Schedule 2: Statement of Grand Lodge Per-Capita Dues Collected from
1948 Annual Returns.
Schedule 3: Statement of Masonic Homes $25.00 Contributions Received
During the Year 1948-49.
Schedule 4: Comparison of Budget and Expenditures, 1948-49.
Comments
The revenue from per capita dues and other sources exceeded the expenses and appropriations by $2,105.92 as shown by Exhibit D.
All per capita dues, as reported on the 1948 annual returns from constituent Lodges, have been paid in full. Our Schedules 2 and 3 show proof
of the revenue due from the Lodges in accordance with their 1948 returns
and the $25.00 Homes contribution reports for the first three quarters of the
fiscal year 1948-49. The total revenue due, as shown, agrees with the total
cash received from the Lodges by the Grand Secretary.
Cash receipts were accounted for and deposited in the proper banks.
disbursements were made by check and supported by properly approved
vouchers. The disbursements made by the Grand Secretary were from his
Operating Funk bank account. Reimbursements to the Operating Fund by
the Grand Treasurer were not made until we had audited and approved
the bills, which was done semi-monthly. No bill was approved unless an
appropriation had been made in the budget and the appropriation had not
been used up. Items not covered by the budget and expenditures in excess
of budget were not reimbursed until approved by the Grand Master.
Bank balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries.
A certified list of the securities was received from the Anglo California
National Bank which holds the securities for safekeeping. All interest and
dividends due were received.
The former War Relief Fund, in amount 158,507.44, has been transferred
to a Special Purpose Fund to be held for the use of the Memorial Temple
Committee, in accordance with the recommendation adopted at the 1948
communication of Grand Lodge.
Sotoyome Lodge No. 123 has fulfilled its agreement during the year;
$150.00 monthly was paid by Grand Lodge and $100.00 monthly was received
by Grand Lodge from the Lodge. No payments were received on the money
advanced to Gravel Range Lodge No. 59.
We certify that, in our opinion, the attached statements present fairly
the financial condition of the Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California as at
July 31, 1949 and the result of its activities for the fiscal year 1948-49.
·
Respectfully submitted,
BURROWS, PARKER, CARSON & HARMS
Certified Public Accountants
·
Walter A. Parker.

Masonic Homes Endowment Fund Audit
Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California
September 28, 1949
San Francisco, California
Gentlemen:
We have audited the accounts and records of the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1949 and present herewith the
following statements:
Exhibit A: Statement of Assets, July 31, 1949.
Exhibit B: Statement of Cash Receipts and Disbursements, August 1, 1948
to July 31, 1949.
Exhibit C: Statement of John and Lena Luckenbach Fund, July 31, 1949.
Exhibit D: Statement of Income and Capital Accounts for the fiscal year
ended July 31, 1949.
Schedule 1: Securities on hand, acquired prior to July 31, 1948.
Schedule 2: Securities received and purchased during the fiscal year ended
July 31, 1949.
Schedule 3: Statement of securities redeemed and sold during the fiscal
year ended July 31, 1949.
Cash:
COMMENTS
The bank balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries.
All interest and dividends due from investments and savings bank accounts
were received by the Grand Treasurer and deposited in the bank accounts
of the Masonic Homes. The total income received by the Homes from the
Endowment Funds amounted to $85,995.31.
Securities:
Securities on hand that were acquired in prior years are listed on Schedule .
1. Securities received through contributions and bequests, and bonds purchased during the current year are listed on Schedule 2. Securities redeemed
and sold during the current year are listed on Schedule 3.
Bonds purchased are listed at actual cost. Donated securities are listed at
market value when received, or at a nominal value of $1.00 if the actual value
is unknown.
Certified lists of securities held for the account of the Endowment Fund
were received from the Anglo California National Bank. The records were
checked to these lists and the securities not listed were found in the office
of the Grand Secretary and were inspected by us.
Increase in Fund:
The combined assets of the Endowment Fund and the Luckenbach Fund
show the following increase for the current year:
Amount of funds, July 31, 1949..·-····-···········································$3,619,154.02
Amount of funds, July 31, 1948..·-··························-······-············· 3,390,643.35
Increase ·················································································-··-··-$ 228,510.67
The increase is accounted for as follows:
Cash donations and bequests....·-···-······--········-······-·-····-··--···$ 225,287.03
Securities by donation and bequest..........................·--···-··-··-···
4,152.00
Loss on sale of securities.....................-··········-········-··-····-··--·····
(928.36)
Increase ..........................................................................................$ 228,510.67
The donations received through Lodges were confirmed by correspondence
with the individual Lodges as at June 15, 1949.
Other Endowment Assets:
The books of the Masonic Homes carry the records of the Harriet C.
Wadleigh Endowment Annuity Fund. After the death of the beneficiaries
of this fund, the remainder will be transferred to the Endowment Fund.
Schedule 7 of the Masonic Homes report shows that this fund had a balance
of $22,608.76 as at July 31, 1949.
The Masonic Homes also hold several pieces of real estate for the account
of the Endowment Fund. Whenever a sale is made, the proceeds will be
deposited to the account of the Endowment Fund.
Certificate:
We certify that, in our opinion, the attached statements present fairly
the financial condition of the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund as at July
31, 1949.
Respectfully submitted,
BURROWS, PARK.ER, CARSON & HARMS
Certified Public Accountants
Walter A. Parker

Investments:
The securities owned by the Masonic Homes are all government bonds
and are shown on Schedule 1 and are listed at actual cost. The bonds w~re
verified by a certified list fr~m the Anglo California National Bank which

to the general fund of the Homes.

Properties:
The value of the properties as shown on the Balance Sheet, Exhibit A,
is the cost of the two homes at Decoto and Covina, owned by the Masonic
Homes of California. During the current year, $350,041.48 was disbursed
for the construction of new buildings and for improvements to the old buildings and for new equipment.
Other Funds:
The Masonic Homes has numerous separate funds which have been
created for definite or special purposes. Some were created by donation and
by bequest to the Homes for a particular purpose, and others by action of
the Board of Trustees to set aside money that is to be used only for the
purpose indicated by the title of the fund. Full details of these funds are
shown on the attached statements, Schedule 2 to 12, inclusive.
All interest and dividends due on the investments of these funds were
received and deposited in the proper bank accounts. The investments not
pB:Ying interest or dividends are so noted. Payments of principal and
interest have been received on the notes and contracts owned by the Monthly
Grant Fund. Insurance premiums and taxes due on real estate have been
paid. Proper payments were made from the annuity funds in accordance
with the contracts and agreements.
·
All bank balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries.
The securities were accounteod for as held by the Anglo California National
Bank, or in the office of the Grand Secretary. Those held by the bank were
verified by a certified list from the bank, and those in the office of the Grand
Secretary were inspected.

RHenue and Expense:
A detailed audit was made of the revenue and expense accounts and we
aatisfied ourselves as to the general correctness of the accounting records.
The Endowment Fund interest received is in agreement with the Endowment Fund report. Interest due on the investments was received. All records
of the contributions received through Lodges were examined and the
amounts received appear to be all that can be collected. All disbursements
were made by check and supported by proper vouchers.
'!'.he 1948 annual returns from the Lodges were audited and the $25.00
contributions due thereon, plus the contributions received during the first
~quarters of 1949, agreed with the amount turned over to the Treasurer
w. the Home by the Grand Secretary. There was no per capita levy this year.

loss of revenue came through a decrease of $44,000.00 m $25.00 contributions.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
FOREWORD
We of your Correspondence Committee again present the report of
our explorations through the proceedings of the several grand lodges,
wheresoever dispersed around the globe. We here can give you only
the essence of our discoveries, wishing that every member might have
the opportunity to read with us the complete record.
Pride, and even exaltation, is inevitable when we view the proportions and the virility of our beloved order. Masonry abhors and shuns
group action and has always been dedicated to the task of working on
the individual so that each man may exert his own beneficent influence
on the world. In carrying out this fundamental purpose, many jurisdictions show evidence of activities such as the publishing of periodicals,
the maintaining of libraries, and the propagation of the doctrine of the
public school and constitutional government.
The strength of Freemasonry lies in the infinite variety of its forms
and practices, together with its complete unity as regards principles and
purposes. No central authority dictates its course, but each jurisdiction
fits Masonry to the needs and traditions of its own section. Some may
be orthodox and some liberal, some conservative and some progressive,
but all adhere to the Ancient Landmarks with a singleness of purpose
which permits no deviation from our basic tenets.
We were glad to be able to strike from our report the material concerning clandestine Masonry when on May 11, 1949, at its Quarterly
Communication, the Massachusetts Grand Lodge voted, "That the
vote of this Grand Lodge on March 12, 1947, relative to the Prince Hall
Masonry be rescinded.'' Thus a technical dispute which threatened a
serious schism was resolved in accordance with correct Masonic Law.
It is not our intention to again present the comprehensive and bulky
. review of postwar Masonry which we presented last year. That report
was separately printed and was received with commendation and approval throughout the Masonic world. It has become a standard reference book in many libraries. The February issue of The New Age,
published in Washington, D. C., stated, "The importance of this
domestic and global survey of Freemasonry will be apparent when we
realize how hopeless it would be for the individual lodge member or,
for that matter, the officers of the average lodge, to know what was

476

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

477

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

going on in Masonry even in his own country, let alone around the
globe."
In the present compilation of Masonic thought, as it is revealed in
the published proceedings of the several jurisdictions, we have selected
the inspirational rather than the factual. Under each category we have
endeavored to develop as a continuity an expression of the ideals and
aspirations of the Fraternity. We present it to you with confidence,
knowing that you will receive as much inspiration from it as we have.

APOSTROPHE TO THE FLAG
The opening ceremony of every Communication of a Grand Lodge
is an impressive and well remembered service, including as it does, the
introduction and reception of The Flag of our Country, with its resulting heart surge of love and devotion.
In our world-wide reviews we are pleased to note that generally
full ceremony occurs as well as PROPER RECORDING in the Minutes
·
as illustrated by the following selected excerpts.
It is our contention and urge that due mention should be made in
the official Minutes of every Grand Lodge as well as its subaltern unitsthe Lodge itself.

Maine, 1949
Reception of United States Colors
The Grand Lodge was opened in ample form, prayer being offered
by the Rev. DAVID L. WILSON, L. H. D., Grand Chaplain.
The Gra.n d Marshal retired, and subsequently the Colors were advanced by a Color Guard, in uniform, composed of the following members of the Harbor Defenses at Fort Williams, Portland, Maine:
Master Sergeant ROBERT B. HOLMES, Atlantic Lodge, No. 81.
Sergeant ROBERT E. BORDEN, Hiram Lodge, No. 180.
Corporal RussELL S. BICKFORD, Sebasticook Lodge, No. 146.
The Communication then sang one verse of "America" and one verse
of "God Save the King."

Wisconsin, 1948

Reception of United States Colors
The United . States Flag was presented by the Grand Marshal,
assisted by a guard of honor, and was received and placed in its station
on the dais at the right of the Grand Master.
The pledge of allegiance to the Flag was then given and the members of the Grand Lodge joined in singing "the Star-Spangled Banner."

Knox Lodge No. 919, Fort Knox, Kentucky, led by M/Sgt. Guy E.

William M. Hamm, Junior Warden.
After the pledge of allegiance to the Flag, the delegates joined in

North Dakota, 1948

Colors Introduced

Grand Lodge Procession at Opening

The Stars and Stripes and the Union Jack were presented by the
Senior and Junior Deacons, supported by the Senior and Junior Stewards. The Grand Lodge was called up as the colors were announced,
and joined heartily in singing one verse of America and God Save the
King. The enthusiasm with which these hymns was sung clearly indicated how close were the ties which unite the English speaking peoples in
these critical days in our World's history.

Minnesota, 1948

The Brethren assembled were called up by the Right Worshipful
Grand Marshal, whereupon the procession of Grand Lodge Officers,
headed by the United States flag and the banner of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Texas, with an honor guard, followed by the Most
Worshipful Grand Master and his staff, the Grand Officers and Past
Grand Officers, entered the Grand Lodge room through the main entrance, the Past Grand Masters forming in two lines, ·b etween which the
active Grand Officers, led by the Most Worshipful Grand Master,
passed in reaching their respective stations, except the color guard who
posted the colors in front of the altar facing the Grand East.

The Grand Master opened the Grand Lodge in Ample Form, prayer being offered by the Acting Grand Chaplain.
The National Colors and the Union Jack were presented by a Color
Guard, after which the "National Anthem" and "God Save the King"
were rendered on the organ.

Led by the Most Worshipful Grand Master, the Brethren assembled
joined in repeating the pledge of allegiance to our flag, after which the
colors were posted in their respective places in the Grand East.

TRIBUTE TO THE FLAG
Our Flag stands before us today, a symbol of hope. As we view with
alarm the uncertainties of the future, Old Glory alone appears unchanged. It stands for all that we hope for. What, then, makes our Flag
what it appears today? Is it something handed down to us by our forebears, or do we have a part in its making? If our future hopes are bound
up in the Flag, and what it represents and stands for, it must be of the
present as well as the past. Our Flag is what we make it.

COMMENTS RE GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
New Hampshire, 1948 (Correspondence Report) :
Any attempt to give a clear picture of the doings of this great Grand
Lodge of ramified interests and accomplishments, its numerous Boards
and Committees, within the limits of our alloted space would be utterly
futile.
Through the efforts of their Masonic Homes Endowment Board
contributions in the amount of $186,399.55 were received. An all time
high, attesting the truly Masonic spirit of our brethren of California.

Idaho, 1948 (Correspondence Report) :
California maintains the distinction of holding the longest Grand
Communication anywher~five days. And, of course, the amount of
business transacted, the length of the committee reports. and the number of persons in attendance were quite in keeping with the magnitude
of this Grand Jurisdiction. The current Grand Officers (no DDGM's)
number 25; the Past Grand Masters present, 21; and the officers and
representatives of 552 Lodges, 1625-considerably like a meeting of the
United Grand Lodge of England.
Grand Master Chester H. Warlow, and Grand Secretary Lloyd E.
Wilson, of the Grand Lodge of California, were visitors to the Grand
Lodge of Guatemala in March, 1948, as reported in "Acacia", the official
organ of the Grand Lodge of Guatemala.

iowa 1948 (Correspondence Report):
What California does is always of interest, and what is said in their
meetings is of superior quality.
Curbed by a limitation of space, a Reviewer can only inadequately
comment rather than to amply quote.

Maine, 1949 (Correspondence Report) :
M. W. Bro. Warlow was obliged to condemn carelessness in the
investigation of applicants for the degrees, and to deprive a degree team
of the privilege of doing further work. In regard to this case, the Grand
Master said: "Masonry is not a playground. It seeks to teach wise and
serious truths, and a candidate is not brought to a realization of this
purpose if his degree is conferred in an undigni•fied manner."

Connecticut, 1948 (Correspondence Report):
The policy in California with regard to degree teams is stated by the
Grand Lecturer as follows:
"Any Master permitting willful violation of our ritual by a
degree team will be cited to the Grand Master for judgment. The
team involved will be barred from further Masonic activity for
such time as may be determined by the Grand Master."

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

487

Indiana, 1948 (Correspondence Report) :
Appendant Bodies-What to do with organizations which require
Masonic affiliation as a prerequisite for membership but which persists
in violating Masonic rules of order and decorum has been a thorn in the
flesh of many a Grand Jurisdiction. During the year Connecticut and
California had to resort to disciplinary action. Ohio and California had
trouble with Masonic clubs, and each Jurisdiction sought unsuccessfully
to curb their activities.

South Carolina, 1948 (Correspondence Report):
A resolution proposed would make it possible for a Lodge to use
30% instead of the present 20% of its total revenue for refreshments
and promotion of fraternal intercourse. We have no restriction on these
matters. We permit a Lodge to spend its money as it chooses. So far we
have found no justifiable reason to interfere in such matters. We believe
in permitting as much freedom as possible to the Lodges with regard to
the use they make of their own money. The resolution was not adopted.

Idaho, 1948, Grand Lodge
The Grand Lodge was favored at this time by a very inspiring address by Most Worshipful Brother Chester H. Warlow, Grand Master
of California. This is the first time a Grand Master of California has
visited the Grand Lodge of Idaho and we sincerely hope it will not ·be
the last.
Honorary Past Grand Masters
At this time Past Grand Master Frank Knox moved that the following Brothers be elected Honorary Past Grand Masters of Idaho:
M. W. Brother Chester H. Warlow. Grand Master of California.
M. W. Brother Lloyd E. Wilson, Past Grand Master of California.
The motion was seconded by Past Grand Master Clyde I. Rush and
unanimously carried. It is a great pleasure and honor to have these good
Brothers added to our Idaho Masonic family. Similar honors were conferred upon the Grand Masters of Oregon and Utah.

Arizona, 1948, Grand Lodge
Distinguished Guest Presented and Addresses Grand Lodge
The R.".W.'.Junior Grand Warden Brother Arthur Paulsen, personal representative of the M.'.W.'.Grand Master of California, was
presented at the Altar, welcomed by Grand Master Cox, escorted to the
East and given the Grand Honors, and before being seated in the East
Brother Paulsen addressed the Grand Lodge in a very able manner,
bringing greetings from the M.'.W.'.Grand Master and the Masons
from that great Jurisdiction of the "Golden West."
