Washington, D. C., 1948
Scottish Rite News Bulletin
U. S. A. and Foreign Masonic Activities Shown in Report
How much does the average Mason know about Masonry in his
own country. let alone what it accomplishes around ,t he world? Or, for
that matter. how much do the officers of the average Lodge know about
activities of Masonry beyond the confines of their own town or country?
Considering that there are slightly under 28.000 Masonic Lodges in the
world, of which more than 15,000 Lodges are located in the United
States of America, and that the total membership of Masonry throughout the world is a trifle under 5,000,000, of whom nearly 3,250,000 are in
our own country, this lack of information is not to be wondered at.
However, the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of ·California set about, in 1948, to supply ·t his and sundry information for its

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

..

Grand Lodge of California Reports on World Masonry
The Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of California set
out, in 1918, to find out what Freemasonry around the Globe is doing.
To accomplish this end is appointed a Correspondence Committee that
consisted of James K. Fisk, Chairman, Frederick 0. Eaton, Newcomb
Condee. Herbert G. Polhill, Lynn H. Hostetter, Elwood D. Bona, and
Oscar C. Olsen.
By correspondence and numerous visitations they have assembled
a mass of information that covers 306 pages. Copies of the report have
been distributed to Grand Masonic Bodies.
There are so many apt comments on lodge matters that it is indeed
difficult to compress them into a brief review such as this, without at
the same time doing an injustice to those comments which must be omitted ·because of lack of space.
The California Correspondence Committee has every reason to feel
a wholesome satisfaction in a difficult and massive work well done,
which sheds a further bright light on Masonry for the benefit of Masonry
and the world.
S.W.

COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
The functions of the Committee on Correspondence can be traced
back to Revolutionary days. In order to maintain contacts between the
various Colonies committee3 were appointed for this purpose. and afterward this procedure among Grand Lodges was adopted in order that the
members might be informed of what was transpiring in the different
jurisdictions.
The Chairman, or Correspondence Committee of any jurisdiction,
after reviewing the Proceedings of the various Grand Lodges, perhaps is
in a better position to give to the Craft what has occurred during the
preceding year. Extracts from the forewords of the chairmen of a number of jurisdictions, some of which follow, are perhaps the best index as
to what is taking place in Masonry at the present time.
-Jesse M. Whited, California Chairman, 1940.

Utah, 1948
My "Five-Foot Shelf'
At the beginning of the year-if one really has a beginning-since
the reading and noting and writing continues right along regardless of
the month. But we might say the beginning is when the Grand Lodge
accepts the MSS at its regular communication and a new set begins to
form. They make a far more interesting flve-foot shelf than one where
the same book rests in the same spot year after year and there is no
growth. Here throughout the year new voluumes come to hand and in
them-new writers are met, old activities are treated in a new manner.
new problems are discussed and so they take their places in the line.
One marvels at the closely knit kinship of the men whom we call
Brethren, whatever their nationality, or color, or faith, or the language
they speak. And yet it really is no marvel, no accident, no miracle, it is
that Spirit of Masonry which we are taught leads to the more perfect
life for all -mankind.
To have and to hold that which uplifts. to reach higher ourselves: to
increase the desire in those around us to spread that vital appeal for a
Universal Peace among mankind. To handle anew in forgotten and forbidden places the faith that Truth, that Forbearance, that Desire for
Universal Friendship, that is our Duty, our Privilege, and our Reward.

Idaho, 1948
The Chairman of this Committee reviews a large number of the
Proceedings of Grand Lodges around the world. This is a fascinating
task, and one that lasts all through the year. The mass of printed

492

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

volumes, pamphlets, and letters that rolls in from the Grand Secretary's
office to the Foreign Correspondent is appalling, and his work, like that
of the traditional housewife, is truly "never done". His duty is to use
selective eye and present reviews that are interesting, and long enough
to cover the subject. lt is a great privilege and a great responsibility.
Only occasionally, however, does one encounter a blessed soul, who expresses appreciation for one's efforts and says that he reads the Reviews
not only a miraculous once, but actually three times! May his tribe grea~
ly increase.

New York, 1948
The labor of your committee is over for another year. Though it is a
heavy task to study so many volumes of reports, the rewards are great.
However divided the Craft may be in respect of the borders of sovereign Grand Jurisdictions, the truth remains that in all spiritual senses it
is one. The problems of one Grand Lodge are pretty much the problems
of all. It is our belief, after pursuing this assignment for several years,
that we American Masons are essentially one Brotherhood, united in
loyalty to the great underlying and fundamental teachings of the Fraternity.
Iowa, 1948
I call this report to your attention not because it is the production of
my mind and pen, but because it will carry to you a broader knowledge
of what your great Fraternity means, because it will carry a reflection
of the thought that is manifest in so many widely separated parts of the
world, ·because it will give you the expression of that thought, sometimes in words that will touch your heart and bring to you not only personal but spiritual solace and comfort, because it will inform you on the
trend of the thought of Masonry of the present day and permit you to
make comparison of the days long past.
With the report in your hands, though, a book you can take home
and read in the quiet of the evening when your labors of the day are
done, and your mind is at rest, and ·b oth mind and soul are receptive
to the principles of Masonry, you may get it better than I could give it
to you here. However, while I have appreciated the privilege of doing it,
let me remind you that it meant much work. If you will read the book that
is before you, and multiply that by the 64 jurisdictions whose Proceedings I have read, you can figure how much Masonic service goes into the
preparation of this book.
New Jersey, 1948
There is inspiration in reading the record Masons have written in so
many Grand Jurisdictions. To him who wishes more light, is commended

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

493

these reviews of some seventy Grand Lodges. This year there appears
a topical review in addition to one for each Jurisdiction. If you would
improve yourself in Masonry you will read and thereby be compensated.
We realize we only can put this "food" before you and remind you that
it is not entirely indigestible. Take it for enlightment, for information,
for use, for the glory that is in the Craft.

Tennessee, 1948
The report of M. W. Bro. J. Rice Williams, Grand Lecturer is a gem.
He feared the tendency he found in Brethren 40 to 50 years of age to
tum the work over to what they call "young men" would result in disaster. His advice is so sound we quote a portion-

" Permit me to sound a note of warning, even fear, over this trend.
You have NOT done, and you are NOT now doing, your part, unless
you are willing to serve until such time as qualified men, regardless of
age, can be found to fill the stations and places.
"Neither youth nor age qualifies anyone for office in a Masonic
Lodge. Extreme youth, either biologically or masonically, certainly disqualifies one for the office of Wors~ipful Master. It takes years of observation and study to imbue one with the ground work, usages, customs, and Landmarks of the Institution. Until thus imbued, the tendency
of youth is to regard the Institution as just another club. What it has
taken centuries to build may easily be wrecked by placing the Fraternity
in the hands of masonically immature Masters.
"Freemasonry is distinctly and definitely NOT a club. Freemasonry
is an Institution in that it has from time immemorial stood for the highest principles of mortality and virtue. It is founded on enduring principles
which must go down through the ages, if Masonry is to survive. Its landmarks are unchangeable. If Freemasonry should ever be modernized,
streamlined, it would cease to be Masonry and would soon go the way
of so many organizations that follow the current trend. In the beginning,
its business, when in Lodge assembled, was transacted with dignity and
decorum.
"The tendency of youth, until seasoned, is to be iconoclastic, to look
for something new. Let us set ourselves solidly against the idea of elevating to the East the bright young man who 'learns the work' before he is
grounded in the true Principles of Freemasonry. It is as important, if not
more important, that we 'Shall transmit unimpaired the true Principles
of Freemasonry to posterity as that we shall keep the Ritual pure."
... " 'Tis true, 'tis pity;
And pity 'tis, 'tis true."-Hamlet.

proper meaning. Our Fraternity is a Craft and its ceremonies are Work.
We must remember that work is ennobling. An Order is an asso~iation.
A Craft is something more than an Order, because it inculcates and
teaches a mystery. The word craft means skill and power, or the unexplained ability by long ·practice, to produce a desired,result. Therefore,
a Craftsman is one skilled in the mysteries. The petitioner is the rough
ashlar in its rule and unfinished state. The Lodge, by its Craftsmanship,
should work upon him until he becomes, through the practice of our
virtues, a perfect ashlar.

I watched them tearing a building down,
A gang of men in a busy town.
With a ho-heave-ho and a lusty yell,

I asked the foreman, "Are these men skilled,

He gave a laugh and said, "No, indeed.
Just common labor is all I need,
I can easily wreck in a day or two

Mississippi, 1948 (Grand Orator):
"Before the questions, What is Masonry? and What is ·t he secret of
its power? I stand amazed and silent. My soul echoes the query: What
is this experience that kindles aspiration for moral and spiritual excellence in the midst of our dull, drab lives, and gives us a devine sense of
eternity in time, Perhaps the true spirit of Masonry is indefinable, illimitable. Can you put a rim around the perfume of roses, Or fence in
a spring breeze blowing through an apple orchard? Or imprison the
glory of a sunset? Or sculpture the harmony of a mockingbird's song?
Or record in mere words the sweet, ecstatic fancies of a lover's dream?
Or measure the pulses of suffering love and vicarious sacrifice of a
mother's prayer? No. These are imponderables. They are realities that
have little or no relation to the precise instruments of scientific enquiry.
They are psychic, personal-they are vital, creative soul-values.
"This is true of Masonry. Its light is never seen on land or sea, but
in the mind. Its greatest secrets are not in the ear but in the heart. Its
spiritual realities of truth and righteousness are inarticulate, indefinable.
After all our nicely turned phrases are uttered there remains a margin of
mysticism that ·baffles speech.

lodge room and find companionship and courage. There is something indefinable in Masonry I can find nowhere else in the world. Familiar as

and we are all at peace.

life is thrown aside. Only that which is important counts.
Masonry has taught me the follies of petty distinctions and the shame
of pride and place. I am grateful to it for this.-Edgar A. Guest.

others to do to you, do not do to others." Isocrates said in 375 B.C .•~

been deemed worthy of preservation, has expressed the same sentiment
in different words. The Book of Common Prayer of 1662 put it this
way: "My duty towards my neighbor is to love him as myself, and do
to all men as I would they should do unto me." But Edward Markham
brings us up short with his pithy remark: "We have committed ·the
Golden Rule to memory; let us now commit it to life."

Scottish Rite News Bulletin, 1949
What Masonry Means to Me
I take great pride in my Masonry. I was received into the Craft almost a quarter of a century ago and am sure today I have not exhausted
even the smallest vein of its richly laden ore.
It is a source of help and comfort and pleasure I can absolutely rely
upon. When I have wearied of other labors I can tum confidently to my

. 497

l

The Masonic Fraternity seeks no control over processes of government and the enforcement of the law, and as an organization, it takes
no part in the solution of industrial and social problems except through
the influence of its teachings upon the character and conduct of its
members.
The primary ·p urposes of Masonry are to enlighten the mind, arouse
the conscience, stimulate the noble and generous impulses of the human
heart. It seeks to promote the ·b est type of manhood based upon the
practice of Brotherly Love and the Golden Rule.
When these results have been accomplished the mission of Masonry
has been achieved.
Throughout the ages Masonry has taught and advocated the principles of free government, free speech, and freedom of religion. Masonry
has undertaken the education of free men and devoted itself to the ideals
of Toleration, Liberty, and Justice.
In those lands and under those governments that thrive upon tyranny, oppression, and dictation, Masonry has been condemned: Masons

have been persecuted and imprisoned: Masonic lodges have been closed,
and their properties and archives confiscated and destroyed.
Masonry's history is replete with struggles against tyran~y, ignorance, and superstition. Its principles and ideals are deflected m the free
way of life enjoyed by every Canadian and any effort to destroy the free
institutions of this country is an attack upon Freemasonry.
The "free" in our historic name stands for and means something
very difficult to express in simple terms-it does refer to a way of life.

GOOD AND WELFARE

Minnesota, 1948 (Grand Master} :
Fraternal Assistance at Rochester
Important among our Masonic service is the special work of this
Grand Lodge at Rochester on behalf of those who come here from every
corner of the globe to take advantage of the healing arts of the great
Mayo Clinic. From year to year, without any true comprehension, I have
listened to reports on the continuing work of Bro. Frank G. Warner, our
representative there. In reviewing his monthly reports throughout the
year I was amazed at the extent and variety of his activities.
During 1947 alone he contacted more than seven thousand new
arrivals. On an average day he makes about thirty personal calls on
patients and receives others at his office. For these patients and their
families and friends he writes and receives numerous letters and telegrams, arranges for ambulances and wheel chairs, finds rooms and
hotel accommodations and renders a variety of services too numerous
to review.
All of these services are rendered in the name of our Grand Lodge.
It is a most unselfish Masonic activity, freely given on behalf of our
Brethren from other Jurisdictions, the truest expression of the fundamental precepts of our Fraternity. Their worth is attested by the hundreds of messages of appreciation received by Brother W amer on his
own and our behalf.

Arkansas, 1948 {Grand Master) :
Mack Valentine
For more ·t han 30 years the cook at the Masonic Home at Batesville
had been a negro man, Mack Valentine. He was one of the most dependable and best loved employees the Home ever had, which is manifested by the boys and girls who were reared in our Home wanting to
know about him the very first thing when they return, either to the
Home or to the office of the Grand Lodge. At no time was he ever paid
more than $80.00 per month, which made it impossible for him to accumulate any savings. Now that we have closed the home and because
of his age and some physical handicaps, he has had a hard time making a
living.
Grand Master Stockburger, upon learning of his plight, directed the
Grand Secretary to give assistance to Mack when it was necessary, as
he did not want an old and faithful employee of the Grand Lodge to
suffer after he had given the better part of his life in our service. This
has been done and when these conditions were made known to me I
directed the Grand Secretary to continue the policy of giving Mack
Valentine such financial assistance as is required to keep him from suffering.

Arizona, 1948 (Grand Lodge) : ......
.Resolution .Re Separation of Church and State
1. It is the unequivocal policy of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge
of Free and Accepted Masons of Arizona to oppose with every
means at its command the use of money collected as taxes by any
political sub-division of any city, county, or state or by the Federal Government as payments(a) to any person or organization for the purpose of teaching
religion in any public school of the United States
( b) for transporting to or teaching in any private or parochial
school in the United States
( c) for assistance of any other kind to private or parochial
schools in the United States
It is the unequivocal policy of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of
Free and Accepted Masons of Arizona to seek, at all times, by every
means at its command to make effective the complete separation of
Church and State in the United States in the firm belief that only by
such complete separation can that liberty, equality, and fraternity, for
which Masonry stands, be attained.-( Unanimously Adopted.)

Colorado, 1948 (Grand Lecturer) :
The Hat/
It is becoming increasingly difficult to obtain the type of hat generally worn by the Masters, that is the silk variety, and I am coming to be
more and more a believer that this type of headgear should not be worn
unless the officer is properly clothed for same: and such proper clothing
is formal attire.
I find that some Masons appear to believe that it is a Grand Lodge
regulation that this formal hat should be worn by the Master. They are
wrong. no such regulation exists. There is a regulation that the Master
should be covered while presiding. but it is inferred that it will be in
accordance with common sense and good taste.

Indiana, 1948 (Grand Lecturer) :
We have had several serious disasters in the nature of fire and windstorms this year and several of our Lodges have suffered great losses.
It would be prudent for each and every lodge, immediately, to study
their insurance situation and take steps at once to correct any and all
present insurance policies so as to be adequately insured in case of loss.
All Lodges can afford to pay the necessary premium year by year to
maintain adequate insurance coverage, but no Lodge can afford to pay,
on its own, the cost of replacement when a full loss is sustained.

Washington, D. C., 1949 (The New Age):
Investigating Committees
Here, perhaps, is the weakest link in the entire Masonic chain. After
a petition for the ( Masonic) Degrees is received, the first test the candidate must pass is the inquiry of the Investigating Committee. Approved
by this committee, only a dark ballot will prevent his initiation into the
Lodge. Once in, about all that will get him out is nonpayment of dues.
Expulsion is very rare. Having taken him, the Lodge is stuck with him.
Obviously, therefore, the responsibility of the Investigating Committee is grave indeed, and in the proper discharge of this duty the skill
of a biographer, the integrity ol a saint and the wisdom of a judge are
required. Because of this, members selected to serve on these committees should be chosen with care. Preferably, they should be brethren
little if at all acquainted with the petitioner to avoid any possibility of
bias, consciously or unconsciously exerted.
Frequently, visits to the petitioner in his home are omitted entirely,
and this is one of the gravest mistakes made by an Investigating Committee. Other inquiries will develop what his reputation is and has been.
Skillful interviews with the man himself in his home will go far to reveal
what' he actually is and thinks. Much can be learned by observation
alone. Attempted discussion of Masonry would be pointless since he
knows nothing of it. But adroitly managed discussion of subjects with
which Masonry is concerned, such as religion, government, neighborliness, duty, faithfulness to obligations, charity, education and selfcontrol, will bring out the required facts. When all that has been learned
is assembled, the investigator who has served honestly will know
whether or not the petitioner is worthy and well qualified. And to
discover that is the high and vital duty of each and every brother
appointed on such a committee.-The Masonic Chronicler.

Utah, 1948 (Grand Orator):
No doubt it is true that some men seek membership in our Order
because of the fellowship and conviviality that we enjoy at our Lodge
meetings. Good fellowship and conviviality are excellent things. There
is nothing intrinsically wrong for men to join an organization solely for
the purpose of having a good time, but if a Mason's interest is only in
this he performs no good by reason of being a member of the craft,
although from a personal standpoint he perhaps gets immense benefit.

Missouri, 1947 (Grand Master):
Blackballing
During the year my attention was called to a distressing situation
which existed in one of our Lodges. For a considerable period some
misguided member seems to have felt that it was his duty to blackball
every candidate who petitioned the Lodge, with the possible exception
of a single one at long intervals. I set my District Deputy to work on
the case and through his tact and good counsel. accompanied by a
solemn warning if the evil continued, he was able, at least for the time
being, to effect a cessation of the practice and, I hope, permanently.
If certain refractory members of a Lodge persist in a policy of wholesale blackballing and persistently ignore well-meant and timely warnings
from the Grand Master or his District Deputy, there seems to be but
one logica-1 course to pursue and that is to arrest the charter. That drastic
remedy has been applied a number of times in the history of our Grand
Lodge and can be resorted to again if necessary.

Louisiana, 1949 (Grand Lodge) :
The Lambskin Apron
WHEREAS, many candidates coming into Masonry go no further
than the Entered Apprentice or the Fellow Craft Degree:
AND WHEREAS, such candidates sometimes have no need for
a Lambskin or White Leather Apron in the future and are not entitled
to all its rights:
AND WHEREAS, many Master Masons do not have their aprons
properly inscribed as to date of initiation, passing and raising:
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that hereafter the apron
shall be presented to an Entered Apprentice Mason at the time of his
initiation as formerly, but same shall remain in the custody of the Lodge
until such time as the candidate shall have received the Master Mason's
Degree, at which time the dates of his initiation, passing and raising
shall be properly inscribed and attested to and the apron presented to
the candidate.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the Committee on Work be
authorized and directed to make any necessary adjustments in the
monitor or ritual to conform with the action directed by this resolution.
(ADOPTED)

North Carolina, 1947 (Grand Master):
Newly Made Masons
When a man receives the Sublime Degree of Master Mason, we
congratulate him, slap him on the back and tell ' him how glad we are
to have him. He comes to the lodge a few times after that and nobody
pay~ him an~ attention. He then finds somewhere else to go, and I
don t blame him. Just after a man has been raised to the Sublime Degree
of Master Mason, he is imbued with the spirit and purpose of Masonry,
and wants to help do something about it. That is the time that we
should see that this interest is directed toward Masonic activities, and
not all~w the newly made Mason to drift away. He should be given
something to do. He should be given instruction in Masonic law and
procedure. He should be directed toward te proper kind of Masonic
reading, he should be made to feel that he is a Mason among Masons.
If he is inclined toward ritual. he should be given something to do in
degree work. If not, he should be given something else to do, and
there are plenty of things to do. By so doing we make of a newly made
Mason a working Mason instead of a mere dues paying Mason.

(A worthwhile job for Past Masters.)

Wisconsin, 1948 (Grand Lodge):
Report of Committee on Methods of Election Used in Other

Grand Lodge Jurisdictions
It is our firm conviction that our system of the secret ballot is sound
because it follows the democratic principal of voting as we have come to
know it. While some objection might be made to the time spent in
balloting, it has been our ex·perience politically that when we give up a
right, we have lost it forever. Accordingly and as a part of our Masonic
citizenship we should not adopt our politically apathetic attitude and
deny this matter of voting the time it deserves. Further, and by the
secret ballot the Grand Lodge will be in position to elect the best officers
without prejudice or pressure and that in and of itself justifies its retention. If additional time is needed for the business of the Grand Lodge,
then the Communication should be extended rather than doing away
with this priceless prerogative by some unhappy and unfortunate reform.

Illinois, 1948 (Grand Master):
Discipline
This word, when it is spoken, creates an unpleasant reaction in one's
mind: it implies that a violation of an established standard has occurred
which was of sufficient gravity to merit a punishment commensurate
with the offense.
In our organization the responsibility for the exercise of discipline,
when required, rests upon the officers and lodge members, and the Grand
Lodge Officers, especially the Grand Master. It often is an unpleasant ·
responsibility, yet it is one that must not :be evaded upon any pretext.
Freemasonry teaches a respect for and obedience of the law, both civil
and moral: our field of discipline has to do especially with the moral,
and our own codes.

Preservation of Records

Unfortunately men are received into our lodges who have little or
no regard for either; they have not assimiliated into their souls the
lessons of morality and virtue as exemplified in our degrees: the¥ ~re
Masons in name only. Therefore, there arise conditi~ns when d:Isc1plt~e
must be exercised, otherwise our leaders would be gmlty of closing their
eyes to violations of the teachings of our Fraternity and of the c!vil law.
It is the responsibility of every master to rule and govern his lodge
under all conditions. Far too often some brother usurps the conduct
of the lodge affairs because of a lack of courage, strength and leadership
on the part of the master, and the lodge becomes a one man organization.
This condition need never be tolerated in any lodge: it should never 'be
allowed to exist.

Missouri, 1948 (Grand Lodge) :
The Report of Missouri Lodge of Research
I also must urge, as I have so many times in the past, that every
Masonic body in Missouri see to it that its records are stored in vaults,
where they will ,be safe from fire and vandalism. These records contain
much important Missouri history. All need to be preserved. Without
them good history-important history-will be lost forever.
And now let me say again that the objects of the Missouri Lodge of
Research will not be accomplished until the history of every Masonic
body in the State has been carefully written and made available to any
and all Freemasons who may be interested.

Ohio, 1948 {Grand Master) :

West Virginia, 1947 (Grand Master):

Supremacy of the Grand Lodge
The Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of Ohio is the only
sovereign and independent body of Master Masons existing within this
Grand Jurisdiction. Its regulations, its rules, its constitution, laws, and
edicts are binding upon all Master Masons of this Jurisdiction, and the
obligation strictly to obey the same can never be lost sight of no matter
in what other Masonic or semi-Masonic activities said Master Mason
may become interested or active.
These are fundamental and long~established principles of Freemasonry. It is sincerely hoped that this Grand Lodge will never find it
necessary to exercise the plenary powers which it possesses, but it is
quite essential that every Master Mason in this Jurisdiction knows and
realizes that there is one great fundamental mother Organization to
which all Masons owe primary allegiance. Otherwise we would be
confronted with a great ship, with many rudders, in many hands.

At the beginning of this Masonic year I stated it would be to these
fine Masons I would look for counsel and advice. Many times it was
necessary to seek their aid, and each time they have given me the help
needed.

Connecticut, 1948 {Grand Master) :
Past Grand Masters
It is with a most humble sense of gratitude that I as Grand Master
pay tribute to that distinguished group of brethren, the Past Grand
Masters. Down through the years every Grand Master has realized
the value of the wisdom, advice, and co-operation of these faithful
brethren. I have been no exception and throughout my term of office
I have called on them time and time again for advice and counsel. On
every occasion they have been most willing to help, aid, and assist, never
with the slightest intention of trying to rule, govern, or dictate but
always with that fine spirit of friendliness and co-operation as though
responding to a call for service and a duty to this Great Fraternity.

We feel that we have adequately taken care of a situation in which

which he was raised, by the provisions which we have for dual membership. A brother by thus affiliating with the Lodge in the place in which
he resides, is thereby·making himself a part of the community and encouraging his brothers residing there in their Masonic activities.

Wisconsin, 1948 {Grand Master):
Question-Is the participation of a member of "H" Lodge in illegal
activities during a strike to the extent that he was arrested and found
guilty of disorderly conduct a Masonic offense?
Decision-Sec. 1, Art. 1, of the Trial Code, appearing on page 225
states, "The Grand Lodge cannot by a general rule circumscribe within
equitable bounds the conduct and practice of all members. It must be
left primarily with the subordinate lodge to determine in the light of the
surrounding circumstances whether any member by his conduct is, or
is not, bringing repr.oach to the institution of Masonry." That case
was referred back to the constituent lodge.

in the Temple, the profit arising from this dinner to be donated by the
Eastern Star to the Masons for redecorating the lodge rooms?

Missouri, 1948 (Grand Master) :
Centennial Lodges
There are eight Lodges operating today that were chartered by the
Grand Lodge of Missouri in 1847 and 1848. They are as follows:
Multnomah No. 84, Oregon City, Oregon Territory: Western
Star No. 98, Benton City, California. Multnomah is now No. 1 at
Oregon City, Oregon, and Western Star is No. 2 at Shasta, California,
I attended a meeting and banquet of Western Star Lodge No. 2 at
Shasta, about six miles out of Redding, California. . They have the
original charter issued by the Grand Lodge of Missouri 100 years ago.
Their hall was erected 95 years ago and is in fine state of preservation,
The heavy steel plate shutters are still on every door and window. The
finishing lumber was all sawed and planed by hand. They had to turn
away many who were not able to get in the hall. Here I present~
them with a plaque similar to the one at Oregon City. It was also well
received. They also presented me with an engraved gavel.
On the 21st I visited a Lodge at Selma, California, where an old
cousin of mine is the senior member and past master. He was made a
Master Mason in my little Lodge 62 years ago. He has since celebrated
his 82nd birthday and also has been back to Missouri on a visit and
attended a meeting of my Lodge.

SANCTITY OF THE TEMPLE
Pennsylvania, 1948 (Grand Master) :
There are times when we cannot but feel that there are those in our
Fraternity who have forgotten that our Temples and Lodge Rooms are
consecrated to the teaching of the great and important Principles of
Freemasonry, and therefore are not places for frivolity or fun. Our
solemn ceremonies are not intended to be just a matter of entertainment
for the Brethren in attendance. Rather every effort should be made to
create an atmosphere of dignity and reverence, and the conduct of all
present should be commensurate with, and exemplify the Sublime Truths
of the Great Light upon our Altar, and which Truths we seek to teach.
Iowa, 1948 (Board of Custodians):
Report of the Board of Custodians: "The Third Degree is not intended to be a comedy, nor should it be given for the purpose of providing amusement to those on the sidelines. Clowns in a circus are fine, and
we all enjoy them: but clownish work in conferring a degree is out of
place. Brethren, let us not debase the dignity of our profession. Let us
not convert a sublime degree into a burlesque."
Georgia, 1947 (Jurisprudence Committee):
.
WHEREAS, the Grand Master has called to our attention that
certain groups, teams and clubs have engaged in the dramatization of the

NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED by the Grand Lodge of

disapproved and condemned and ·the Board of Custodians of Uniform

North Carolina, 1947 (Grand Master):
PROFICIENCY IN THE THIRD DEGREE
I have given much thought to the matter of requiring candidates to
become proficient in the Third Degree, and I have come to the conclusion
that a candidate should be examined in and made proficient in the Third
Degree in like manner as in the First and Second Degrees. The Mason
will find such proficiency to be of much benefit to him should he visit
other lodges. As a matter of logic and as a matter of Masonic knowledge,
a Mason should know the Third Degree as he is required to know the
First and Second Degrees. I can see no reason to the contrary. I therefore recommend the adoption of the followi~ Regulation, which is patterned after that of the Grand Lodge of Iowa: "A Master Mason must
become proficient in the Third Degree before he can vote, hold office,
serve on committee, demit from his lodge or petition for degrees or membership in any Masonic Body of the York Rite or Scottish Rite."
Indiana, 1948 (Grand Lodge) :
Number of Candidates-Presentations

"All the ceremonies of initation in the Entered Apprentice, Fellowcraft and Master Mason degrees contemplate the introduction of only
one candidate at one time.
"Each degree shall be conferred in its entirety, including all ceremonies and lectures provided in the official authorized ritual of this
•r Grand Lodge, and all of the same shall be given and conferred in the
same session of the Lodge.
"Under no conditions or circumstances may the first section of the
Entered Apprentice degree or the second section of the Master Mason
,kgree, be conferred upon more than one candidate at the same time.
"No presentation to a candidate of any nature, except a presentation,
on behalf of the Lodge, of an apron or of a Bible, may be made until all
ritualistic work of a degree, including the lectures thereof, has been completed."

Adopted.

ROCK QUARRY MEETING
On Friday evening, August 27th, the 14th Masonic District held its
9th annual meeting in Wings Rock Quarry near Travelers Rest. Several thousand Masons from South Carolina and adjoining states gathered for this meeting. A rustic Lodge was arranged on the floor of this
abandoned quarry with seating arrangements for several thousand.
The significance of this meeting lies not only in the very efficient
ritualistic work which took place and inspiring addresses given, but in
its peculiar setting. One was constantly reminded of that time when
Masons were forced to meet in the lowest valleys and on the highest
hills to escape persecution and even death. Sitting in the dim light cast
by flares arranged and looking up at the starry decked canopy of heaven
one was made to feel that he need only reach out a hand to touch the
face of the Eternal.

As to the occupancy of Masonic halls by ·boys and girls organizations, there has always been much difference of opinion and in some
instances considerable friction. The great danger has been that the
sponsoring body has failed to provide proper supervision, in which instance such occupancy proves to be a liability, not only to that organization but also to the sponsoring body. It would seem that some statement
should be made as to the Grand Lodge attitude on this whole matter of
occupancy. So far as I am aware there has never been any complaint as
to the occupancy of Masonic halls by those groups generally regarded
as Masonic, and which include Chapters of Royal Arch Masons, Councils of Royal and Select Masters, and Commanderies of Knights Templar, and in most instances it has been found that these bodies pay a
proportionate part of the upkeep and maintenance of buildings, and very
often are owners of considerable stock in Masonic Temple associations.

Connecticut, 1948 (Grand Master) :
DECISIONS AND RULINGS
'

Question: Manker Grotto has a Blue Lodge Degree Team and has
conferred the Entered Apprentice and Master Mason Degrees in various
Lodges in this vicinity. The practice when attending Lodge to confer a
degree has been to enter the Lodge-Room upon invitation of the Warshipful Master in single file wearing white aprons, also the Fezzes, advance to the Altar, remove Fezzes and salute the Worshipful Master.
After introduction the visiting team assume the stations upon the request
of the Worshipful Master. Are we acting in violation of Masonic Law
and Jurisprudence?
Ruling: I cannot see that there is any violation of Masonic Law and
Jurisprudence providing the procedure followed is specifically as outlined
in your letter. In my opinion the Fez is a part of the uniform of a member
of the Grotto and it is not a mark of discourtesy to wear that part of the
uniform on being received into a Masonic Lodge, provided that the
Fezzes are removed before salutation and that they are not worn during
the business meeting or during the conferring of the degrees.

A Masonic Lodge Room should be a place of peace and harmony,
and primarily for the use of the lodge which may own, rent or occupy
it. Anything which might create friction, or where there is any appreciable objection to a joint occupancy is not a proper 'question to inject
into a lodge.

Delaware, 1948 (Grand Master) :
LODGE MEMBERSHIP
According to the annual reports of the subordinate lodges. the membership in our jurisdiction is higher this year than in any year of our history. The total number of Master Masons is 6,463, or 309 higher than in
1930, our previous high. While we rejoice in our numbers. we must remember that the increase is due, in part, to the economic conditions that
now prevail. Therefore, we should make plans to hold our membership
when harder times arrive. One way to do this is to prevent our lodges
from becoming too large. The record shows that during the last depression lodges with 250 members or less showed a loss of 14%, while lodges
with over 250 members had a loss of 21 %. Our Masonic forebears of the
Nineteenth Century were truly builders. We have constituted only one
lodge this century. Our last lodge was established in 1902 and at that
time we had approximately 2,500 Master Masons. Today the same number of lodges is serving an increased membership of 148%.

Wisconsin, 1948 (Grand Master) :
Our one great need in this state is more lodges, particularly in our
larger centers where lodges have grown beyond one thousand in membership and the amount of degree work is becoming a task on the officers.
It is a proven fact that more lodges of smaller size enhance the real value
of Masonry, rather than allowing the lodges we now have to grow cumbersome in number.

for more new Lodges, especially suburban Lodges in our larger communities. During the past few years a large number of the residents of
our cities have been moving to suburban districts. Lodges now located
in such districts show a splendid average attendance and a larger number of candidates.

Missouri, 1948 (Grand Master) :
Large lodges necessarily have large classes of candidates, and busy
men are unable to spare time from their work to meet night after night
and day after day conferring degrees, with the consequent result of loss
of active and virile leadership. The only advantage set forth in having a
large lodge is that such organizations are enabled to have substantial
and attractive Masonic Temples, but this advantage must be disregarded
in view of the usual mortgage which hangs over such properties and
which destroys the charity of any lodge, for the money which should go
to helpless and indigent brethren is being used to pay off mortgages on
temple properties.
I would recommend that some thought be given to these large lodges
so that all Freemasons may have a chance to take part in the conferring
of degrees and bringing to the organization such leadership ?S will enable us to go forward and to accomplish the great purpose for which we
exist.
It would seem that we might well frame a law providing for the
limitation of membershp and follow out the custom of our English
Brethren, where, whenever a lodge becomes too large, a new lodge is
organized and the average lodge membership kept at a minimum figure. It has also occurred to me that there would be some value in a waiting list of petitioners, that when a lodge had reached its full quota of
membership, no further petitions would be received until such a time as
there happened to be a vacancy. Let us make the organization something
that men actually want to join, and an organization in which they will
desire to retain membership.

North Carolina, 1947 (Correspondence Report) :
"In devising a new and better method Dr. Anderson included in his
first Constitution only such of the physical qualifications required in the
Operative Manuscripts as would be necessary in the work of Speculative
Masonry. He did not include the terms 'have his limbs whole' or 'be of
able body' found in the old Manuscripts. Article IV simply provides that
an apprentice have 'No Maim or Defect in his body that may render him
uncapable of learning the Art', and then states the reason why a candidate should possess such physical qualifications, in these words: 'that
so, when otherwise qualified he may arrive to the Honour of being the
Warden, and then the Master of the Lodge, the Grand Warden, and at
length the Grand Master of all the Lodges, according to his Merit'.
Since it is the duty of a Master of a Lodge to set the Craft to work and
give them proper instruction, it would seem that Article IV clearly contemplates that a candidate shall not be so maimed or deformed in body
that he cannot learn, practice and teach the Ritual of Masonry. Article
IV contemplates also the equal right of all to advancement, according
to merit."

(Italics ours.)
New York, 1947 (Grand Master):
Eligibility of Disabled Veteran to Election as Master.
The question was presented as to the eligibility for the office of Master of a disabled war veteran, who had lost his right hand at the Battle
of Guadalcanal and had served acceptably as a Junior Officer of his
Lodge. The ruling on this question pointed out that under the recent
amendment to Section 346 of the Constitutions, disability to conform to
the ritual was no longer necessarily a bar to admission to the Fraternity,
that under Section 304, every member of a Lodge is eligible to every
office except that of Master, and that the only additional requirement for
eligibility to the Mastership, contained in Section 305, is that the Brother
shall have served as a Master or Warden. In holding that this disabled
veteran would be eligible to the office of Master if he had previously
served as a Warden, the opinion reads: "This is precisely what was determined by the Committee on the Condition of Masonry. * * * Any
other result in the present case would be unthinkable, since it would
amount to a negation of the principle underlying the new legislation of
Grand Lodge which, in effect, enacts that for Masonic membership and
perferment stress is to be placed on mental and spiritual qualifications
and not on mere physical."

THEODORE ROOSEVELT SAID ...

l

It seems to me that what this country needs more than anything else,
is to practice-not to preach only-but to practice the virtues realized
in the career of the greatest Mason that ever lived-Washington-and
pay to his memory the homage of deeds, not merely words.
One of the things that attracted me so greatly in Masonry, that I
hailed the chance of becoming a Mason, was that it did really act up to
what we, as a people, are pledged to-to treating each man on his merits
as a man. When Brother George Washington went into a Lodge of the
Fraternity,, he went into the one place in the United States where he
stood below or above his fellows according to their position in the Lodge.
He went into the place where the idea of our government was realized
as far as it is humanly possible for mankind to realize a lofty ideal. And
I know that you will not only understand me, but sympatnize with me,
when I say that my pleasure is even greater when going into some little
Lodge where I meet the plain, hard-working men-men who work with
their hands-and meet them on a footing of genuine equality, not false
equality, of genuine equality conditioned upon each man being a decent
man, a fair-dealing man.
Masonry should make, and must make, each man who conscientiously and understandingly takes its obligations, a fine type of American
citizenship, because Masonry teaches him his obligations to his fellows
in a practical fashion. It is a good thing to read the Declaration of Independence every Fourth of July; it is a good thing to talk of what
Washington and his fellows did for us. But what counts is how we live
up to the lessons that we read of. that we speak of. The lesson of
Brotherhood, first and foremost, is to learn that lesson with a full heart
on the one hand and without a weak head on the other.-/ndiana Freemason.

EAVESDROPPERS
Masonic tradition tells us of a punishment inflicted on members of
the Craft in the Middle Ages, when Masonry was purely Operative.
The Masons in those days, as at the present, were careful to take every
precaution to prevent their secrets becoming known to outsiders, and,
if anyone was caught listening, he was punished by being held under
the eaves of a house in rainy weather, while the rain went in at his
shoulders and out at his heels. From their punishment of the old ·
Masons, listeners have long been called "eavesdroppers."

and did not have nunrbers for the days: instead they thought of the year
as a succession of periods, most of them of a religious character, such
as Lent, and each day of the whole year had a name of its own-this
was one of the reasons why the Middle Ages needed so many saints:
they had to have enough saints to give each of 365 days a name.
Each gild or fraternity in the Middle Ages was required by law to
have a Patron Saint, which meant that on that Saint's day the gild
would take a holiday (holy day) and go in a body and in public procession to some chapel or altar dedicated to that Saint. The Freemasons of
those early times had a number of different Patron Saints, depending
on the place and the period of time, but apparently· they had St. Thomas
a Becket oftener than any other. Nobody knows when or why they settled down finally on the days belonging to the two Sts. John, but when
they did it was for calendar reasons, not for theological reasons. The
Baptist's day is the longest in the year in the sense of the most number of
hours of daylight: the Evangelist's day was not only the shortest in that
sense but was the turning point of the year when the days began to become longer, and for that reason everybody was happy to see it come.
-Iowa Grand Lodge Bulletin

"IN GOD WE TRUST"
Notwithstanding this government's continuing recognition of Divine
Providence in the affairs of the nation, as evidenced by the symbolism
appearing on its Great Seal and currency, there was no direct or im# ·
mediate reference to the Deity on any of the coins of his country prior to
the year 1864. On November 13, 1861. the Reverend M. R. Watkinson,
a Presbyterian minister of Ridleyville, Pa., addressed a communication to
Hon. Salmon P. Chase, then Secretary of the U. S. Treasury Depart#
ment, calling his attention to the fact that there was no mention of God
on any of our coins. In his letter he expressed grave concern about the
outcome of the Civil War and said : "If the Republic should be shattered
beyond recognition, the antiquaries of succeeding centuries would rightly
conclude that America had been a heathen nation." He suggested as a
suitable motto for the purposes desired that of "God, Liberty, Law".
In pursuance of this suggestion, and presumably after conferring
with President Lincoln, the Secretary of the Treasury addressed a letter
to James Pollock, Esq., Director of the Mint, at Philadelphia, in which
he stated: "No nation can be strong except in the strength of God, or
safe except in His defense. The trust of our people in God should be
declared on our national coins.'' He requested the Director of the Mint
to prepare a device "with· a motto expressing in the fewest and tersest
words possible this national recognition.'' However, a law had been pass#
ed by the Congress in 1837 prescribing in detail the mottoes and devices
which must appear on subsequent coinage and consequently this faw
had to be amended before the Secretary's request could be put into ef#
feet. But on April 22. 1864, the law of 1837 was amended so as to author#
ize the coinage of two cent pieces and to place upon such coins the
motto: "In God We Trust.'' Accordingly, this motto first appeared
upon the bronze two cent pieces which were coined during the Civil
War. Thereafter, two separate acts 9£ Congress, passed on March 5,
1865, and February 12, 1875, authorized the placing of the same motto
on all such coins as admit of its inscription, with the result that this motto
has been inscribed since that time on all coinage of sufficient size to admit
of such inscription.-Texas Grand Lodge, 1948

TO LEARN AND TO DO
This is the soul's work here below. The soul grows, as truly as an
oak grows. As the tree takes the air and the particles that float in the air,
the dew and the rain, and the food that in the earth lies piled around its
roots; and by its mysterious chemistry transmutes them into sap and fiber,
into wood and leaf, and flower and fruit, and taste, and color, and per~
fume; so the soul drinks in knowledge, and by a divine alchemy changes
what it learns into its own substance and develops itself from within,
outwardly, and grows, with an inherent force and power like those
which lie hid in the small germ of the acorn.
-Grand Master, Missouri, 1948
MASONIC FRAUDS
During the days of the war the Masonic deadbeat disappeared from
the scene, but he has made his appearance again in recent days. The
story is always plausible till investigated. The proceedings of the
Masonic Relief Association of the United States and Canada are at
hand and in a thoughtful paper entitled, "The Schemes and Subter~
fuges of the Unworthy to Work Freemasonry," Brother Don D. Kuem~
merling, Secretary of the Masonic Relief Association of Cincinnati tells
that only ten per cent of applicants for relief are unworthy. That is
cheering news, but ten per cent can be quite a few in number and they
can defraud the fraternity from coast to coast apart from the vigilance
of Relief Boards, the prompt reports of lodge secretaries to the Grand
Secretary, and. the work of M.R.A. in exposing their schemes. A few
of them are women who have learned that Masons can be generous
to the womenfolk of deceased or unfortunate brethren. All of this is
not news to well informed Masons, but as ·searching investigation
becomes common by city boards of Masonic relief, the deadbeat alters
his tactics and preys on the lodges located in smaller towns. It would
pay lodge secretaries and others to take a hint from the Red Cross
practice and "Verify, Verify, Verify."
--South Dakota, Correspondence Report, 1948.

Ray Denslow orMissouri makes some very pertinent remarks about

to consider that the newspapers are not always to blame for such char~

in each jurisdiction as the only high ranking Mason, Ray continues
in the following happy vein: "And in our own way of thinking there
is nothing higher in Freemasonry than that brother who throughout
a long and useful life has lived according to the teachings of the fra~
ternity: who may not have ·held a position of responsibility, yet who
has made it a part of his life to feed the hungry, clothe the naked, bind
up the wounds of the afflicted. Upon his breast may hang no jewel fit
to grace the diadem of Eastern Potentate, around his form may hang
the simple unspotted apron of the fraternity, yet the life he has lived,
his treatment of a brother, the widow, and the orphan, may have been
such as to write his name on the topmost round of the ladder. • . Such
a man has the true word of a Master Mason."
MASONIC BEQUESTS
By the will of the late Alice Mabel Steinbicker, of Wheeling, West
Virginia, the Masonic Home was made the residuary legatee for the
purpose of building a swimming pool in memory of Brother Edward L.
Steinbicker and their son, Edward Melvin Steinbicker.
After a suit in chancery instituted by the executor in the Circuit
Court of Ohio County, and after the sale of the properties under decrees
of the Court and the payment of specific bequests, there was paid to
your Board of Trustees the new sum of $23,030.55, which was accepted
subject to the provisions of said will and is now held .by the Treasurer
of the Board in a special fund for the purpose stipulated in said will.
-Grand Master, West Virginia, 1948.
LARGEST ORIENTAL RUG ONE MAN'S GIFT TO
TO MASONRY'S WASHINGTON SHRINE
On February 22, 1948, Mr. Sarkis H. Nahigian, a prominent Mason
of Chicago, presented the George Washington Masonic Memorial
Temple at Alexandria, Virginia, a priceless Persian Meshed Shrine rug,
with the prominent Masons from 48 States present to pay tribute to the
Father of our country.
Mr. Nahigian said in part:
" It gives me pleasure to donate to our beloved George Washington
Memorial Building, the largest Persian Royal Meshed carpet I have ever

536

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

known. It is one of the largest hand~made oriental rugs ever shipped
out of the Persian Empire, as it is approximately 50 feet long and 30
feed wide, containing over 54 million hand-tied knots.

Gift of Appreciation
"As to texture and workmanship, it would be impossible to reproduce
such a carpet under present economic conditions, just as it would be
impossible to secure master weavers to weave such rugs as you have now
in this shrine. I donate this carpet in grateful appreciation of all the
unlimited privileges and friendship and support I have enjoyed in this
blessed United States of America, and not among the least of these is
my privilege of being a Mason. It is also an expression of what George
Washington, and what he stands for, mean to me personally."
Rug 30 by 50 Feet
As indicated by Mr. Nahigian in his speech, the dimensions of this
rug are approximately 50 feet long and 30 feet wide, containing over 54
million hand~tied knots of the finest spun wool yarn. To weave a rug
like this would require years of careful and patient work by 12 artisans,
sitting side by side, along the width of a mammoth hand loom, tying
knot after knot on the warp threads with the various colored yarns in
the hands of the weavers under the direction of a master artisan, so that
not a single knot is misplaced. Thus they weave on, a line at a time, day
after day, which turns into months, and months become years until the
creative work is completed. This Meshed rug of untold beauty and imposing grandeur, displays a magnificent medallion in the center of a
luscious rose field. In the four corners of the field are placed outstanding
decorations complementary to the impressive medallion which has classic
ornamentations of scrolls, lotus and other flowers. The many wide and
narrow borders give to the entirety of the rug a majestic air of splendor
which overwhelms the observer's aesthetic senses.
About Mr. Nahigian
Harpoot, Armenia, was the birthplace of Mr. Sarkis H. Nahigian.
In 1890 he left his beloved Harpoot as a young man and set foot in the
United States penniless, but possessing a stout heart, together with an
admirable determination to make the most of himself in a land of plenty.
The young man landed on the east coast and for a few years labored
in a shop in Providence, Rhode Island, until the West lured him.
-Armenian Mirror-Spectator, 1948.
36 Acres of Ground
The George Washington Masonic Memorial Temple was completed
in 1925 at a cost of 4Yz million dollars. It is nine stories high and with
its beautiful geographic surroundings covering 36 acres, makes a very

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

537

imposing picture at the top of historic Shooters Hill. It is only six miles
distant from the Capitol City and the Washington Monument, Lincoln
Memorial. Capitol Building, Jefferson Memorial and other buildings of
distinction can be seen clearly on a pleasant day. Mount Vernon, the
historic home of the first President of the United States, is twelve miles
distant and it was in Alexandri_a that he spent most of his lifetime. A
temporary statue of George Washington stands in the niche of the
Memorial Hall and some day soon will be replaced by a beautiful marble
one, depicting him presiding at a meeting, with Apron intact and Gavel
in hand.

MASONIC LIBRARIES

An illuminated sign indicating the location of the library was in·
stalled recently.

Librarian's Report, 1948
A Mile of Books
The Iowa Masonic Library fills the four floors of one building and
the two floors of another and yet is everywhere crowded for space. If
these books were placed on one shelf, it would be 60,000 inches long,
or 5,000 feet, which is only 280 feet less than a mile.
If this mile of books went past your own front door, you could find
in it the answer to almost any question that could be asked about Freemasonry. You would find some of the answers in English, French,
German, Spanish, Hebrew, Latin, Greek, Dutch. Italian, Russian,
Arabic, and, in a few instances, in little-known tongues of the Far East,
because during the past two centuries our Craft has established itself
almost everywhere: and wherever it has been, Masons have written
books, or booklets, or magazines about it.
But even if that mile of books passed within three feet of your door,
it would do you little good, because you would not be able to find anything in it. How could you? Even if you knew the title and author of a
book, it would take you a long time to hunt it down; usually you would
not know the title and author but would have only some question or
subject in mind. The information would be there, within view, inside
of some book, but what book? Book titles themselves tell little about
the contents of a book.

Rhode Island, 1948
We now have a library of which we are very proud. All of the books
have been arranged in due form according to the modern method of
library cataloguing and have been placed in the room adjoining the
Grand Secretary's office. A card index has been typed, is ready for use,
and as every book has been numbered, it now becomes much easier
for one to obtain the book or information he wishes,

Utah, 1948
The library, located on the ground floor of the Masonic Temple,
adjacent to the office of the Grand Secretary, is accessible to all members during the week and its cases and shelves are well filled with
excellent books and current publications from many parts of the United
States and some foreign countries. Many valuable volumes of Masonic
history and writings of Masonic Historians and Students are to be
found. There are also many volumes of periodicals containing articles
of value and interest that have been fabric bound to better preserve them.

.,I

Massachusetts, 1947
I should like to take this opportunity to inform the Brethren in
Massachusetts that the Grand Lodge maintains an up-to-date Library
for their use and pleasure and that it ranks as one of the four or five
outstanding Masonic Libraries in the United States. There are approximately 45,000 volumes in the Library on all phases of Masonry and
related subjects, and they are arranged and classified in such a way
that any volume can be readily located. Many volumes are available
for circulation. Some of the more valuable books are accessible for use
only in the building. These include the rare books, reference works,
such as Proceedings and periodicals, and other books which can not
be replaced.
Early in the summer we were asked by the Navy Department in
Washington, and also the First Naval District in Boston, if we would
be willing to exhibit some of our John Paul Jones memorabilia during
the period when the bicentennial of his birth was to be observed throughout the country.
The following are a few of the items which were chosen for display:
Flint-Lock Pistol carried by Jones during the American Revolution.
Illuminated .Water-Color Coat-of-Arms used by John Paul Jones.
(Of particular interest to Masons as it contains the square and compass.)
Facsimile of Application of John Paul Jones for Degrees in Freemasonry in Scotland.
Copy of Miniature Portrait of John Paul Jones in color, on porcelain or metal.
Log-Book containing Memos of Correspondence between Jones and
others.

Grand Master, 1948: The Lodge Library
There should be a permanent Committee on Masonic Library and
Museum in every lodge of import, charged with the responsibility of
intelligently building a library which would be of benefit to the Masons
of North Carolina. They should be further charged with the duty of
preserving priceless relics and documents pertaining to the Craft.
A Department of Archives in Grand Lodge should also be established for the many valuable Masonic documents and records in the
possession of our lodges. They are vulnerable to varied means of destruction. I frankly think that most of our lodges possessing such documents and records would welcome a safe place in which they might be

540

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

preserved-a repository, so to speak. Title to such items would not
vest in Grand Lodge. They would remain the property of the lodge
depositing them. The ravages of time have taken a heavy toll of our
Masonic records. We should do all within our power to preserve them.

New Mexico Freemason

tions of the Grand Lodge. but because I doubted the wisdom of such
procedure. And especially, in view of the increased cost of running
the Grand Lodge. the Masonic Home. and our other activities.
A magazine is an expensive thing. It requires payment of salaries.
It requires the service of skilled employees. It requires an editor.
There are few competent Masonic editors. I am sure the Grand Lodge
does not desire to go into the publishing business for the sole purpose
of providing jobs. and especially when it would mean an increase of
$1 in per capita tax. Commercialism has no place in Freemasonry;
to print a magazine without advertising would mean additional expense. Whenever the Grand Lodge engages in solicitation of advertisements we are on the road to commercialism.

Reception of Veteran Masons
The Grand Master asked the Grand Marshal to introduce and welcome veteran Masons. Veterans of sixty, fifty and forty years were
escorted to the East, and the Grand Master first addressed them as
follows:
THE GRAND MASTER: Brethren, I remove my hat, because I
stand before the veterans of this institution.
Brother J. H. Repass, I understand you have come a long way to
receive a designation which the Grand Lodge of Montana has voted
for every veteran Mason in its jurisdiction. It is a great pleasure for
me, as Grand Mastei;, to place upon your lapel this little button which
signifies that you are a veteran Mason, and I trust that through the
years you will not forget this ceremony. In addition to this little
insignia, it is my pleasure also to present to you this certificate, which
alleges that you are a veteran of Montana. God bless you.
I will ask our Grand Marshal to welcome you.
THE GRAND MARSHAL: M. W. Grand Master, distinguished
visitors, members of the Grand Lodge, and you well beloved veterans:
I deem it a great privilege indeed to be asked to extend a welcome to
you, as well as the greetings and felicitations of the Grand Lodge of
Montana. We are certainly happy to' have you all here. We love and
respect you. All the younger Masons look to you for information, for
education. Your long experience as Masons is worth a lot to the
younger Masons. Your knowledge of the landmarks of Masonry, the
history of Masonry, the standards of Masonry, everything that goes
to make our fraternity great, is of mighty value to all of our younger
members. Masonry is a progressive science. We have our eyes fixed
on tomorrow. Tomorrow to all of us is the most important thing in the
world after today, and we are indeed looking to the future. But let us
not forget the importance of the past. Everything that we are, everything that we enjoy materially, everything in our lives, our liberties, our

Texas, 1947 (Committee Masonic Education):
"Turning to the newly made Brethren, if a man is good enough to
be made a Mason then certainly he should be made a 'good Mason..
The making of a good Mason does not stop with the conferring of the
Master's degree. It is only the beginning of a good Mason, and to
these newly made Brethren we owe the responsibility of properly
instructing them as to the designs that are and have been drawn on
the trestleboard. He should be. and it is our responsibility and duty to
see that he is truly and correctly informed as to the proper use of the
Square, the Compass, the Level. the Plumb Line, and the Trowel. If
we fail in this respect, we not only do an injury to the newly made
Brother, but we are injuring ourselves."

District of Columbia, 1949 (Grand Master) :
We shall ask for greater masonic education in our lodges. It should
not be enough that a candidate travels through the degrees towards
the light. He should be back attending the lodge on succeeding communications for a review and explanation of the work, a historical
background of masonry and a working knowledge of our Code.
In fact it is a wholesome thing for all members to receive a periodic
review of the landmarks of masonry. It will have a more binding
effect on each one.
Masters of lodges are accountable for the attendance not only of
their officers but · for the individual members of their lodges at the
Grand Lodge School of Instruction, especially on occasion of the exemplification of the degrees.

North Carolina, 1947 {Grand Master}:
District Meetings
A District Meeting was held in each of the forty Districts by the
Grand Master and the Grand Secretary. A conference was held in
the aftP.moon with the officers of lodges. Such conferences were well
attended and of considerable benefit. These conferences were devoted
in general to Masonic law and procedure, rules and regulations and
matters which the Grand Master and Grand Secretary thought necessary to be called to the attention of the Craft. The time at these officers'

purposes. I spoke at evening sessions of each of the District Meetings.

A survey of the types of programs had in the Lodges during the
past year indicates that exactly 50% consisted of papers or talks by
Lodge members on Masonic subjects as compared with only 5 % of
such talks or papers by visiting brothers. The reading of talks and
papers sent out by the Grand Lodge Committee comprised 20% while

O~r Grand Lodge is the oldest independent Grand Lodge in
America and holds a high and honorable position among the Grand
Lodges of the world. The Grand Master's jewel, as you know, was
originally offered as the badge of office to Brother George Washington,
who declined the office on the grounds that his duties in the Continental Army at that time would not permit him to carry out the duties
of the office. Most Worshipful John Blair became our first Grand
Master, followed in office by James Mercer, Edmund Randolph, John
Marshall, and a host of other brethren who have handed down to u~
a great heritage.

Iowa, 1948 (Grand Master, Missouri}:
One hundred years ago we sent a Charter to the Pacific Coast, to
what was then known as Oregon Territory, but the Charter now rests
in Bellingham, Washington. Also the same year we sent a Charter
into California, to a little place known then as Benton City, now Shasta,

Washington, 1948 {Grand Master) :
It is interesting to note from whence Masonry came, and how it
came into the Northwest. We, of course, trace our Masonry back to
Missouri, because the first charter was brought from there. Nevertheless two of the Lodges in Oregon received their charters from California. Willamette Number 2, and Lafayette Number 3. California
received its first charter from Missouri, she also received charters
from the district of Columbia, Connecticut, Virginia, Ohio and
Illinois.
The first Lodge that was chartered in Missouri received its charter
from Pennsylvania. Owing to transportation difficulties Missouri turned
to the southeast by way of Tennessee and thence to North Carolina.
So we today trace our Masonry back to North Carolina.

District of Columbia, 1948 (Grand Lodge Report) :
Washington Monument Centennial Celebration
Just 100 years ago, Benjamin B. French, the Grand Master of
Masons in the District of Columbia, stood on yonder hill, surrounded
by his Grand Lodge, and in the midst of many other patriotic groups
laid, in full Masonic ritual form, the cornerstone of that Monument.
At that time he used this gavel-The Washington Gavel. This
gavel, I now hold before you, was used by General George Washington himself, when as the Acting Grand Master of Masons he laid the
cornerstone of the United States Capitol.
This gavel is brought here today by and through the courtesy of
Potomac Lodge No. 5, FAAM. The Gavel had been placed in the
keeping of Potomac Lodge by General Washing ton. It has been
guarded by that Lodge ever since.
The other working tools used by Most Worshipful Brother French,
and his aides, were handed to Roberts Mills (A Freemason) with
instructions to look well to the erection of this national monument.
The Washington Gavel again appeared in the hands of Past Grand
Master Myron M. Parker when, on February 21, 1885, he applied the
Square, the Level and the Plumb to the completed monument and
found it to be well laid, true, and trustworthy.
So we see that this historic edifice is surrounded with deep masonic
significance.
George Washington was a Mason, who loved to meet his brethren
on the level and part with them upo~ the square. An Acting Grand

North Dakota, 1947 {Grand Historian):
Lodge Histories
I join in the recommendation of the Grand Master that a Lodge
Historian be appointed for the research on and writing of a history or a
continuation of the history of each lodge. I think these lodge histories
are very important. That is the only way of preserving the splendid
work of the pioneers who founded our lodges and of those who have
continued their splendid work down to date. That will also serve as an
inspiration and incentive to our younger members.

Iowa, 1948 (Grand Master) :
Charter Anniversaries
The celebration of the issuance of their Charter continues to have
a strong appeal to a large number of lodges.
The original suggestion that a Charter anniversary be held at
appropriate periods (ordinarily for lodges 50 or more years old) was
made by this Committee fully ten years ago; and each year the attention of lodges whose Charters were issued from 50 to 100 years before,
(selecting them at five year intervals) is called to the desirability of
recognizing the fact.
For those lodges less than 50 years old, we remind them of the
interest and value of Founders Night, furnishing an outline for this
type of meeting. In their case, it is easily possible that some, at least,
of their Charter members still survive, and can be fittingly honored.

the years 1866-1867 in an attic, buried in a bushel of old Brother Johnson's shoe pegs. That bushel of shoe pegs still remains unmolested.
A non-Mason found the old records of Blandford Bute Lodge. He
_spent the better part of the night reading them, and the next day
(This was about 1912) he called this writer and told him about them.
He made a proposition on this wise. He took the oldest of the books
and pointed carefully to one page. "Read that," he said. That which
was at his finger's end was the following: "Resolved, that Jethro
Sumner be instructed to buy a pair of striped drawers for the use of the
Lodge for two shillings." And earnestly he said, "If you will tell me
what they bought those drawers for, I will give you all of these books!"
We told him, just as vividly as if we had been on the spot when they
were purchased, and we got the books.

Colorado, 1948 {Soldiers' and Sailors' Welfare Committee) :
Our committee is charged with the duty of extending relief and
comfort to Masons who were in the military or naval service of the
United States in any war, and to their families. To better carry out

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

557

this duty committee members have been appointed so that one resides
near Fitzsimons General Hospital, one near the Veterans Administration hospital now under construction at Grand Junction, and the
third member at Ft. Lyon.
There have been no ·calls for relief or financial assistance during
the year. The work of the committee, therefore has consisted of visiting
Masons and relatives of Masons in hospitals and elsewhere, extending
words of cheer, and offering to perform any of those small services
which tend to make the days more pleasant, and which the brother is
unable to attend to personally.
Many of the cases coming to the attention of our committee are
those of Masons from other grand jurisdictions. In such cases the
brother's lodge is sent a report of the visit, together with an offer of
service in case the lodge should wish the brother to have some special
attention. These visits and reports are always appreciated.

JOHN JOSEPH PERSHING
John Joseph Pershing, Honorary Member, died.July 15, 1948, in his
87th year. He was elected Honorary Member of the Grand Lodge of
Missouri, September 30, 1941. In all the history of the Grand Lodge of
Missouri, there have been but six Honorary Members, Brother Pershing
being the last.
He was born September 13, 1860, near Laclede, Missouri. After
getting the foundation of an education in the common schools, which
was followed by several years spent in teaching, he entered the U. S.
Military Academy at West Point, from which he was graduated in
1886,, as a second lieutenant of cavalry.
After years spent in Indian fighting in the West, and in the SpanishAmerican War, he was sent to the Philippines to quell the insurrection
there. He was then a captain-two promoti,0ns were open-to major or
to brigadier-general, and he received the latter.
He led the punitive expedition into Mexico in 1915-16. following
Pancho Villa's raid in Texas, and on the outbreak of World War I,
was chosen by President Wilson to lead the American Expeditionary
Force, and he sailed for France, May 28, 1917.
Following the close of the war, by special Act of Congress, he wu
made General of the Armies-a title held by only one other-George
Washing ton.
He was made a Freemason in December, 1888, in Lincoln Lodge
No. 19, Lincoln, Nebraska. while stationed at Lincoln as Commandant
of Cadets at Nebraska University. In the Scottish Rite, he was coro-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

559

neted 33• Inspector General Honorary, January 6, 1930. On May 2,
1936, he returned to Laclede, his old home town, and participated in
laying the cornerstone of the public school building.
Following a severe illness in 1938, from which it was feared at the
time he would not recover, he made his home in the Walter Reed Hospital at Washington. After elaborate ceremonies, scarcely equaled in
this country, on July 19, he was laid to rest in Arlington Cemetery, in
a spot which he had selected among the dead of World War I. "A
great soldier and patriot has passed from the American scene." Eisenhower.
-Committee on Necrology: Missouri. 1948.

"The Crisis"
These are the times that try men's souls. The summer soldier and the
sunshine patriot, will in this crisis s.hrink from the service of their coun~
try: but he that stands it NOW deserves the thanks of man and woman.
Tyranny, like hell, is not easily conquered: yet we have this consolation

Ohio, 1948 (Grand Master}:
Communism as we see it in action today has no honor. It glorifies
itself in its 1 ability to break its word, whether verbal or written. It
glorifies expediency. It cares not for principle. It places forward the
mailed fist and dares those who disagree with it to approach.
We must go forward against the power and the forces of Com~
munism. not only to protect and save our Masonry; but also for the
larger issues which are at stake. We must go forward if we are to
preserve our religion, our churches, our schools. our democratic and
representatiTe forms of government and our American way of life.
Masonry always has been a society of leaders. Leadership is
needed now as it never has been before. Let us, therefore, my Brethren,
march on.

Maine, 1949 (Grand Master} :
We are living in a time of change and stress; when groups, factions,
minorities, blocs and nations strive to gain advantage to themselves by
a constant flow of propaganda. charge and counter charge. against their
opponents. These conditions have resulted in world wide confusion,
nervous tension and distrust.
In these surroundings Masonry has thus far stood unfalteringly by
the traditions upon which it was founded. These traditions distinguish
us from the uninitiated. We must not deviate in the least from our old
customs, usages and teachings. To do so is to invite into our Order the
same state of confusion and uncertainty which exists around us.
If Masonry is to retain its present honored position in the world we
must stand united against aggression in every form, and against any
movement which ignores or deprecates the dignity of Man. This is not
all. We must constantly strive for the betterment of mankind through
knowledge and understanding. We must constantly practice the great
teachings of Masonry to the end that an honorable and lasting peace
may be achieved among all the peoples of the earth.

New York, 1948 (Grand Master}:
We of the Masonic Fraternity are prone to eulogize the early Ma~
sonic forebears of this country and boast of what they accomplished in
setting up this great republic. They were brave men; they were outspoken
men: they were instrumental in giving us the Declaration of Independ~
ence, the Constitution and the Bill of Rights. Are we to be less brave and

be counted? We do not discuss in our Lodge room partisan politics,
