Democracy. I believe that Masons today are animated no less than in
former years by the love for Liberty and Freedom. Masonry is a peace~
ful organization, but supporters of regimentation. whether in govern~
ment or church, are deluding themselves if they believe the Masons of
the United States are not willing and eager to stand up and support
Liberty-civil. religious and intellectual-for which our forefathers
fought and won.

Today there are forty#eight states and within them over three
million Masons. If the three hundred intelligent and whole#souled
Masons of that day could create such a government, cannot three
million of us save it?
What about us? What are we to do? Do we believe that no country
can exist as a free government unless its people are also free? A:re
these things real enough to us that we could not only die to preserve
them, but to do what is more important at present, live for them? And
live as if we believe them.
The first thing is the formation of an aroused public opinion, and
perhaps the first step in public opinion is to feel deeply. God grant
that we may be brought to feel deeply about the future of America.
Feeling the need for action in America, talk about it. Talk on
the street, among your families, in your churches, in your Lodges;
in your service clubs, at your barber shop, anywhere, everywhere,
when you can secure a hearing. Talk with the earnestness which
comes from a deep love for a thing you are striving for. Talk intelli#
gently. Learn to talk more and more convincingly as time goes on, and
as you get a greater following. After all, it is easier to speak for your
country than to die for it.
As Masons of old were ready to give all to the formation of a

Freemasonry and Communism
Every Mason, as a citizen, should be informed as to the deadly
threat of Communism to our Fraternity, our country and the institu#
tions which we love and under which we have built this great nation.
. What he learns in his Masonic Lodge he is to take with him into his
daily life, guiding himself by the principles we teach-the simple prin#
ciples of right living and decent manhood.
The discussion of the so-called political parties is not a controversial subject. It is partisan politics that is forbidden. A man may be
a Mason and a member of any political party of his choosing; a man
may be a Mason and worship his God in any church he desires. be he
Hebrew, Roman Catholic, or Protestant: but no ~an may be a Mason
and a Communist, for a Communist is an avowed atheist, a follower
of the teachings of Dr. Karl Marx, who expressed himself that "reli#
gion was the opiate of the masses." You cannot be a Communist and
a Mason any more than you can be a George Washing ton and a Benedict Arnold.
Communism is not only incompatible with the tenets of Masonry,
but the Masonic Lodge system, along with the church, must cease to
exist where Communism governs. Russia today tolerates a restricted
church only as a temporary expedient, and is looking to the ultimate
extermination of all forms of worship of Deity. Masons cannot dismiss
the subject for it is not controversial in the Masonic sense. The first
law of nature is that of self preservation, and the first duty of Masonry
is to defend Masonry. To do' that Masons must be able to recognize
the danger of Communism, both in its outward and in its con#
cealed form.
Communism will never prosper in America if its purpose and its .
methods are known and understood. Ignorance of the subject has
has produced a corresponding apathy toward any need for combating
communistic activity.
A Citizen of the Soviet Socialist Republic may not own land, may
not strike, may not picket, may not travel, may not own jewelry, may
not be tried by jury, may not choose his job, may not absent himself
from work, may not ring a church bell, may not be a fried of a foreigner,
is forbidden freedom of speech, freedom of assembly, freedom of
religion, freedom of soul.

Contrast this with our beloved country where the dignity of the
individual is safeguarded and preserved. His home is his castle and
may not be invaded without due process of law. His personal effects
are protecte from unwarranted search and seizure. He may not be

DOMINION OF CANADA

WHAT ARE THE RESPONSIBILITIES AND PLACE OF
THE PAST MASTERS IN THE ACTIVITIES OF A LODGE

E~cerpts from Addresses Delivered at the

SEVENTH ANNUAL INTER-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
of the Officers of the Western Grand Lodges, A. F. & A. M.
Banff, Alberta, September, 1947.
THE DIGNITY OF CONFERING OUR DEGREES

M:.W:.Bro. Hector Mackay, Grand Master of Saskatchewan
"I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending" saith the
Lord, "In the beginning, God.'' In the ending, the resurrection to be
with God. The interim period-"life on earth".
Life in Masonic parlance comprises the Initiation, Passing and
Raising of the Candidate.
If all Masons could and would be brought to understand that brief,
concise comprehensive and all inclusive idea of what Masonry is there
would be no problem of "The Dignity of Conferring our Degrees".
The land marks of the Craft include the fundamental thought of the
belief in God. In fact, many writers maintain that belief in God is the
sole dogma and the fundamental land mark of Free Masonry.
The Officers themselves must come well trained, rehearsed, thoroughly prepared and ready and able to do their parts. They should
carry themselves erect with honest pride in what they are doing. Their
voices should be firm and the words distinct so that all may hear. The
knowledge to be imparted is not a secret to be whispered to the candidates. The members may have heard the work a thousand times. It is
still the drama of life and they are all deeply interested. They still want
to hear it, and it is their right and prerogative to have it distinctly
spoken so that all may hear.
Next in importance is the matter of prompting. No prompting
should be necessary, but when such is required it should be by some
one appointed by the Master. Let no one else interfere. Nothing can be
more disturbing nor lacking in dignity than for several to be trying
to help some hesitant, stumbling person stuttering and muttering
incoherently.
Combined with these would be the matter of deportment of all. As
stated before, the Officers should carry themselves erect and speak
distinctly. Those who remain sitting should sit up with proper
attention. There should be no slouchiness but a full, calm attentive
expectancy.
The whole will then blend into that which we have spoken of as
the dignified atmosphere. With this sort of atmosphere there can be
no room for buffoonry or horse play, no whispering among the Past
Masters in the East or from anyone else anywhere in the Lodge.

571

Rt. W. Bros. Wm. A. Henry, Deputy Grand Master of Alberta
It is in the province of the Past Master to recommend a definite line
of reading and study for members of a lodge if they appear interested
or if they can be diplomatically led to an interest in Education and
Research. It is his responsibility that he do this in response to a request
from those members rather than he be guilty of trying to force something on them. If his is a true knowledge his brethren will call upon him.
One of the most important duties of a Past Master, is to help
develop within the Lodge a proper atmosphere for the various occasions. This cannot be done by sitting in the anteroom smoking, and
then skipping into Lodge when the degree work starts. It is not a good
example to talk while the work is being put on, but this is too often
done by a couple of Past Masters. This only detracts from the solemn
occasion. It is his responsibility to see that he does nothing which is
not proper within the lodge.
It is his duty to assist the Worshipful Master, on request.
It is the Past Master's responsibility to see that everything he does
is done corerctly according to the best Masonic Procedure. He should
beware of doing anything that is different from the usual manner, just
because he did so when he was Master. Much better he do it the
correct way, because he knows the Masonic authority for thus acting,
and in this way improving the work and also increasing peace and
harmony in his Lodge.
The Past Master should readily see it is his duty to fraternize with
the new members. In this manner he could do much to encourage them
in Freemasonry. They may not at first regard him with the respect
his rank should warrant, because they do not know him, but if he
conducts himself right, his place in their affections will be secure and
much good will come to all.
· In those lodges where peace and harmony prevail. it is because of
the efficient leading of the rulers of the craft, not only present.but past.
A responsibility of the Past Master is attendance at Lodge meetings,
not just from a sense of duty, but because of the love he has for the
craft, the good he derives from the work, and the hope he can be of
assistance to the present officers and members. Too often the Past
Master drifts from his usual habit of attending lodge. This is usually
an admission on his part that all he wanted was to be a master for
twelve months. What vanity--or maybe a genuine disuse of Freemasonry. I am sure if one faithfully serves in the various offices and as
Master, he will not find it within him to drop from regular attendance.

THE REFRESHMENT PERIOD AND ITS VALUE

R. W. Bro. D. McGugan, Sr. Grand Warden of British Columbia

ALBERTA

The term "refreshment" has come to convey a double meaning in
Masonic parlance. Albert G. Mackay 33° in his encyclopaedia of
Freemasonry writes, in part, under "refreshment".

To the searchers after Masonic Truth, no other book or manual
offers greater scope than that of reviewing Grand Lodge Proceedings,
for there he will find the plan of the operations of each Jurisdiction by
means o~ Reports and discussions, the pith of Freemasonry as seen
h} them is unfolded.-Committee on Foreign Affairs. 1948.

"In Masonic language, refreshment is opposed in a peculiar sense
to labour. While a lodge is in activity it must be either at labour or at
refreshment. If a lodge is permanently closed until its next communication, the intervening period is one of abeyance, its activity for masonic
duty having for the time been suspended, although its powers and
privileges as a lodge still exist, and may at any time be resumed. But
where it is only temporarily closed, with the intention of soon again,
resuming labour, the intermediate period is called a time of re~resh­
ment, and the lodge is said not to be closed, but to be called from
labour to refreshment."
A lodge meeting is of necessity serious and solemn-and relaxation
thereafter furnishes a pleasant ending to a perfect evening.
With that sentiment in mind I believe it is wise to provide entertainment of a lighter vein as part of the program of the refreshment
period. This can be done with propriety as the lodge is closed but all
proceedings must be conducted with dignity and decorum and nothing
approaching the vulgar tolerated. "A little nonsense now and then is
relished by the wisest men."

It is beyond the scope of this paper to attempt to state exactly what_
form a refreshment period should take. It is impossible to provide a
standard formula as circumstances will distate each individual case.
With careful planning ahead a suitable and appropriate program could
be furnished for each occasion. Likewise I say nothing as to the nature
of the material refreshments served. These will vary according to
location, season and occasion.
To sum up I would say that the refreshment period forms an important and integral part of our Masonic life. if carefully planned and
properly conducted. It provides the opportunity to make friends, to
become better acquainted with the brethren, to become better educated
in all phases of Freemasonry. It further affords an opportunity to give
the brethren and particularly the younger members some duty to be
performed and to be noticed, whieh in the final analysis does more
than anything to interest a brother. It gives the opportunity to send
the brethren home rejoicing with a moral uplift that will remain with
them for a long time. In short it provides the opportunity to be "happy
ourselves and communicate that happiness to others".

Today, for present conditions, the great difficulty is the apathy
shown by most of us. Apathy of course means indifference and is a
s?rt of device and a device which compels us simply not to pay attention nor do anything hut just to drift. But the people who have evil
causes to promote are not afflicted with apathy. They never cease
promoting whatever it is they have to promote. There is an old story
hut it illustrates this difficulty. Away back before the dawn of history
man lived with the other animals. They greatly deplored the fact that
man never lived more than 40 years. They held a meeting one day to
s~e ':hat they could do. The horse said he would give man l O years of
his hfe and the dog and the monkey said they would each give ten
years of their lives. So the result is now that from 40 to 50 man works
~ike a horse, from 50 to 60 he leads a dog's life, and from 60 to 70 he
JUSt monkeys along.
I am inclined to think a good many of us who should know better
just monkey along at all ages.
-Grand Lodge, 1948; M. W. Bro. W. J. Dunlop,
G.M. of the Grand Lodge of Canada in Ontario.

GRAND LODGE OF CANADA, ONTARIO
Non ..Resident Masters of Lodges
The Worshipful Master and officers of a Masonic Lodge should.
during their term of office, reside within the jurisdiction of their lodge
or close to it if the work of the lodge is to be properly carried on. How..
ever, there are cases where an officer may be obliged to move from
the community during his term of office and through no fault of his.
Having served as an officer and being interested in Masonry he
naturally does not wish to lose his position in the line of officers. There
has been a large number of instances in which the Worshipful Master..
elect has not been a resident of his community, in fact in some cases
he has resided as much as 75 to 100 miles away. In such cases the per.. •
mission of the Grand Master is required to enable him to assume
office. Where such a situation arises the prosperity of the lodge is of
paramount importance and must have first consideration. I have granted
such permissions but have insisted upon an undertaking from the
Master.-elect that he will attend all meetings of his lodge and also that
he will resign office at the end of six months if it is found the lodge
is suffering. If the officer wishes to continue in line under such cir..
cumi.otances he should realize his responsibility to the lodge and to the
Craft and be prepared to make extra sacrifices for the benefit of
the lodge.

A successful lodge should have annual dues of sufficient amount to

The English District Grand Lodge in Newfoundland celebrated
the Centenary of its oldest lodge, St. Johns' Lodge, No. 579, E. C.
As part of this observance, an historical record, entitled "Freemasonry
in Newfoundland," was prepared by Wor. Bro. Kenneth C. Skuce,
O .B. E. A copy of this interesting work reached our desk with the
compliments of the District Grand Lodge.
The first Masonic lodge in Newfoundland was establi~hed in 1746,
by authority of R. W. Thomas Oxnard, Provincial Grand Master for
North America. During the next century, other lodges, civil and
military, also existed in the Colony for varying periods of time. The
oldest surviving lodge was instituted under dispensation from R. W.
Alexander Keith, Provincial Grand Master for Nova Scotia, in 1848,
and was chartered by the United Grand Lodge of England in 1850.
Today, the Grand Lodges of England and Scotland each maintain
a District Grand Lodge in Newfoundland. Under the English Constitution, there are fifteen lodges. There are eight Scottish lodges.

Masonic Lodges Compared with Service Clubs
Of one Lodge, a D.D.G.M. remarked that "This Lodge has a number of young members who do not feel that the Lodge is active .enough.
They want it more like a service club. They need to have the difference
between a Lodge and a service club explained by a well-skilled Brother."
Many members of our Craft are members of service clubs. The program
of a service club does undoubtedly make a strong appeal to business
and professional men because of the informal and friendly atmosphere
surrounding it, and the apparent difficulty of obtaining a membership,
restricted as it is to certain classifications. But is there any reason why
a service club should be better able than a Masonic Lodge to provide
friendliness and good feJlowship? We know of none.
We owe an obligation to our Youth to accept responsibility on our
school boards, our municipal, state, provincial and national bodies. If
we do not become members of any of these bodies we owe it to ourselves and to all in our District. lt is a duty to get out to vote. We
should strive to see that the members we elect are upright, honorable
and the best obtainable and that these bodies do not pinch pennies. On
the contrary, see that they make due allowance and ample provision
for supervised, recreational facilities and occupational guidance. There
is much that can be done but it must be done intelligently.

-Gfand Master, 1948.

The Figure Three-By W. Bro. ]. E. Campbell

In a lecture entitled "An Exposition of the Third Degree' delivered
by W. Brother C. T. F. Goy and printed in the October 1946 issue of
the Victorian Craftsman the speaker pointed out the prominent place
in the religious and moral history of man occupied by the sacred figure
three.

In the Old Testament it is very prominent. Three elements-earth,
water, air. Three illuminations-sun, moon, stars. Three great Patriarchs-Abraham, Isaac, Jacob. Three divisions of the Book-the Law,
the Prophets, the Sacred Writings.
Three famous names given to the Eternal. What were they?
In the New Testament the figure is frequently used.
Jesus lived three decades and three single years. His ministry
lasted three years. Three persons were involved in the Transfiguration.
He was tried before three men. The three crosses. He remained three
days in the tomb. Three great attributes-Faith, Hope, Charity. The
Trinity-Father, Son, Holy Ghost.
In the realm of Masonry:
The primary degrees, three knocks, three steps, three-fold sign,
three signs, three great lights, three lesser lights, three G.M.'s, three
principal officers, three W.T.'s in each D., three perambulations, three
steps in approach to A, three entrances to the T, three weapons, three
men, three Lodges sent out to search, three methods were tried.

EUROPEAN COUNTRIES
A REVIEW
The Masonic W arid today is in a state of uncertainty and it is
difficult to forecast the future. Conditions are settled only in the British
Commonwealth of Nations and in the United States. of America. There
are however some Grand Lodges in Europe which api)ear to be emerging from a state of confusion. In Norway there has been recovery and
the Grand Lodge is functioning despite the fact that Masonic Temples
were destroyed: even the Grand Lodge Temple in Oslo was ruined
by the invaders who tore down the decorations and were converting
it into what was planned to be a restaurant. The National Grand
Lodge of Denmark during the last year has become active and relations
with it have been renewed by several Grand Lodges. In Germany it is
reported that lodges in the American Military Zone are being organized
with the consent of the local military authority; it will however be · a
long time before conditions are stable and official recognition will undoubtedly be delayed. In the Russian-controlled zone all Masonic
activity is strictly prohibited. The Grand Orient of Belgium does not
require a declaration of a belief in God from its members and until a
change takes place no recognition can be made by the regular Grand
Lodges of the world. The Grand Lodge of the Netherlands is gradually recovering from disaster notwithstanding the destruction of its
buildings and libraries, the dispersion of its membership and the death
of the Grand Master in Buchenwald Camp. In France whete there
are three Grand Lodges, only one of which is recognized by the Grand
Lodge of England, all appear to be recovering .b ut conditions there
are in such an uncertain condition that it is impossible to say what the
future holds. In Switzerland the Grand Lodge Alpina which functioned during the war, recently held its 94th annual meeting and is
widely recognized. In Austria where Masonry was suppressed, there
is activity. The Grand Lodge has been re-opened and three lodges have
been reformed and are apparently recognized by the Government of
Austria. In Hungary it is reported that the government has recently
repealed a decree in force for 25 years which prohibited Freemasonry:
meanwhile buildings and property were destroyed and the lodges dissolved. In Italy there are two Grand Lodges, each of which has been
recognized by some Grand Lodges in the United States, and at present
they are being investigated by a delegation from the Masonic Service
Association. In Greece there are reports to the effect that Masonry
is being revived but conditions there are in a most unsettled condition.
The Masonic Temple in Athens is at present occupied by homeless
refugees. As to conditions in South America there is difficulty in de-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

termining whether or not recognition should be extended. Several
Grand Lodges there are widely recognized but in the case of some,
regularity of origin and adherence to the established standards are
doubtful. - W. M. Martin, Chairman, Correspondence Committee.
Saskatchewan, 1948.

Italy
The Grand Orient of Italy (National Grand Lodge)
Freemasonry in Italy has a glorious history. Dating from 1733, it
is filled with sufferings, battles and martyrs. The story of the devotion, of such great Italian Masons as Garibaldi, Mazzini and Cavour
to the cause of Liberty reads like an epic. Unfortunately, many years
ago a sharp division occurred between the Grand Orient and the Grand
Lodge, but a union was effected in November, 1945, following the
renaissance of Freemasonry which came as a result of the downfall of
the Mussolini regime.
For 20 long years the Masonic Brethren of Italy were subjected to
the most hideous atrocities. The Lodges were plundered and destroyed,
leaders of the Craft were imprisoned, tortured and slaughtered, and
great numbers of the Brethren were driven underground. In effect,
however, Masonry was never dissolved. It continued through its
Bre~hren the fight against Facism-so much so that the more influential
Masons were often arrested and deported. The infinite heroism of
those who were faithful to their trust has added one more glorious
chapter to an already proud history.
The Grand Orient is composed of more than 400 Lodges and has
a membership in excess of 15,000 under the leadership of Dr. Guido
Laj. Grand Master. The Constitution requires a belief in God and the
Holy Bible on the Altar. It is sovereign and independent, follows the
Ancient Landmarks and recognizes all the customs and usages of regular Freemasonry of the Grand Lodges of the United States. It does
not permit religious or political discussions within its constituted Lodges.
-Indiaria, Correspondence Committee, 1948.
. A letter from W. Bro. Cortini, who conducts the foreign correspondence of the Grand Orient, contains some language so important
that we quote it, as follows:
What we are actually looking for. over any material help, is esteem
and the full certitude that our American brethren consider us as the
proper fighters for liberty and democracy, the two ideals for which
we fought since our childhood and especially during the Facist period.
During this long period we accustomed our souls to the sufferings and
our body to the sacrifice, but now that we come back to liberty and
democracy, our only wish is to feel ourselves free men in a free country.
This is our real banner and our only aim.

Report of the Board of General Purpose
Visitors to Lodges
The President of the Board of General Purpose: M.W. Grand
Master and Brethren, before I put the Report for your confirmation,
I should like to say that it has been suggested, and I consider the suggestion quite apt, that I should amplify that paragraph of the Board's
Report which refers to "Visitors to Lodges." That paragraph deals
with visitors emanating from unauthoried Jurisdictions. It does not
mention the possibility of unquali.6ed visitors who have been initiated
in our own Jurisdiction or in one recognized by the Grand Lodge of
England. It would 'be well that Masters of Lodges, and indeed that
every Brother, should make themselves familiar with Rules 125 and
127 of the Book of Constitutions. which deal with this point. It is laid
down in Rule 125 that any visitor, if required, shall produce proof of
good standing in his Lodge or Lodges, and it is laid down in Rule 127
that any Brother who has been excluded from a Lodge is not permitted
to attend any Lodge until he again becomes a subscribing member. I
trust that I have said sufficient to impress on each member of the Craft
his responsibility. for our privileges are precious, and should be guarded
jealously.

SCOTLAND

political, the literary, or the commercial annals of its country, has become of great importance in the estimation of the Masonic antiquary
from its intimate· connexion with the history of the institution.
The abbey of Kilwinning is situated in the bailiwick of Cunningh~m, about three miles north of the royal burgh of Irving, near the
Irish sea. The abbey was founded in the year 1140, by Hugh Morville,
Constable of Scotland, and dedicated to St. Winning, being intended
for a company of monks of the Tyronesian order, who had been brought
from ~elso. The edifice must have been constructed at great expense,
and with much magnificence, since it is said to- have occupied several
acres of ground in its whole extent.
Laurie says, that, by authentic documents as well as by other
collateral arguments which amount almost to a demonstration, the
existence of the Kilwinning Lodge has been traced back as far as the
end of the fifteenth century, but we know that the body of architects
who perambulated the continent of Europe, under the name of "Travelling Freemasons," and the account of whom has been given in some
of the former numbers of this work, flourished at a much earlier period:
and we learn, also, from Laurie himself. that several of these Masons
traveled into Scotland, about the ·beginning of the twelfth century.
( History of Freemasonry. p. 89). Hence, we have every reason to
sup~s~ th~t these men were the architects who constructed the abbe}'
at Kilwmnmg, and who first established the institution of Freemasonry
in Scot~and. If such be the fact, we must place the origin of the first
lodge in that kingdom at an earlier date, by three centuries, than that
clai~ed for it by Laurie, which would bring it much nearer, in point
of time, to the great Masonic Assembly, convened in the year 926, by
Prince Edwin, at York, in England.
-North Carolina, 1948 (Foreign Correspondent Report).

Quarterly meetings were held in Edinburgh in February, May,

The approval of the report of the Board of General Purposes

revert to the provisions of Rule 173 of the Book of Constitutions, so

Kil winning

ascribed are around 1140 A. D.. about two hundred years after the
great Masonic Assembly which is said to have been called by order
of Prince Edwin at York, in England.

Belfast-1948
Many of our lodges, especially those in Belfast, have had a strenuous year's working as almost another thousand new members have
been added to our roll. Since the beginning of the late World War
the increase has been phenomenal and an easement of the pressure
is now anticipated. Through friendly agreement many city lodges
limit their membership to existing accommodation and this arrangement leads to understanding and closer friendship which is practically
impossible when lodge numbers become too large.

Excerpts from the Address of the Grand Master, 1949
The vitality of masonry withstood the vicissitudes of time. · It had
seen persecutions in Europe and elsewhere all the world over. In recent
time, right within our midst during enemy occupation, we witnessed
members tortured, incarcerated or murdered: yet the light of masonic
principles did not Bicker here or anywhere, whenever tyranny rules
temporarily. Indeed, wherever free men live. masonry will survive. For
men may die; institutions may perish; mighty edifices crumble to the
dusts. but the underlying principles under which free men live and die
shall survive through eternity.
New Dormitory and Bowling Alleys ·
Our Dormitory and Bowling Alleys were inaugurated last February, 1948. Partly out of the earnings of these enterprises, the
mortgage entered into between the Grand Lodge and the Philippine
Bodies A. & A. S. R. is now fully paid. Part of the earnings of the
Dormitory and Bowling Alleys were made available in the construction
of two tennis Courts and a Basketball Court.
Plaridel Masonic Temple
The seat of government of this Grand Lodge and your Masonic
Home in Manila is the Plaridel Masonic Temple.
Provincial Masonic Temples
Our provincial brethren are very determined and enthusiastic in
the rebuilding of their Masonic Homes. There are many in the process
of construction and several Lodges are now devising means with which
to start the erection of their lost ones.
Bulletins are a very important means of keeping the brethren posted
on all Lodge activities and disseminating Masonic knowledge and I
highly commend these Lodges for these publications. and hope that
in the future more of our Lodges will find themselves in a position to
publish similar bulletins.

Past Grand Masters' Gallery

In view of these pronouncements and our unequivocal stand, it
behooves us as Masons to arrest the rising tide of Communism as
effectively as we can. We will fight it. We will face it not only by
familarizing ourselves with its theories and dissecting its revolutionary
methods but also-and this is the important thing-by leaving no doubt
in the minds of our people through our througllts and deeds, that
Democracy is more preferable and dependable.

We have been able to re~establish our PAST GRAND MASTERS'

graphs have been enlarged and are now exhibited in the FOYER of

Grand Orator: The Common Enemy, Communism.
A more dangerous adversary, however, is becoming very aggressive
every day. This foe is Communism. Its poisonous tentacles have
reached far and wide. It can not be checked by an individual nor by
many persons. Men and nations must band themselves securely as a
bulwark against this menace if they expect to continue living under a
regime of justice, liberty, and democracy.
The Qriginal Communist Manifesto, among other things, provides
for "the overthrow of the burgeioisie, the dominion of the ploretariat,
•.. and the introduction of an economic and social order without
private property ... " Note the words used: "overthrow", "dominion'',
and "social order without private property".
Communism wherever found is working according to plan. It
preaches discontent, resorts to revolutions, and fosters domination. Its
influence has been felt here to such an extent that the Congress of the
Philippines as in other countries' congresses and legislatures, has created
the corresponding investigating body called the Special Committees on
Un~Filipino Activities. And because Communism runs counter to our
republican form of government, it is undemocratic; because its doctrines
are the anthithesis of ours, it is un~Filipino.
The Philippine Constitution is a Masonic document embodying
Masonic experiences and ideals. Among those who took a leading part
in its preparation and adoption are Masons themselves. It is not
surprising therefore, that Masonry and Democracy are on the same
side on the question of Communism.
Masonry is the great Peace Society on earth. It stands for orderly
government not anarchy; for the dissemination of truth not propaganda.
Its members are expected to abide by the laws and be loyal to their
country. To accept another ideology is disloyalty to their Republic
and disservice to the Fraternity.

Grand Lodge F. 8 A. M. of China
Masonic history was written at the Masonic Convention held on
January 15th and 16th, 1949, at the Masonic Temple in Shanghai,
China, when the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of China
was solemnly and unanimously organized. The convention was composed of four delegates from each of the six Lodges operating in China
under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of the Philippines, delegates
from the three Massachusetts Lodges working in Shanghai, and observers from the sister constitutions with daughter Lodges in China:
to wit-United Grand Lodge of England, the Grand Lodge of Scotland,
the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, and the Grand Lodge of Ireland.
A most cordial atmosphere of fraternal harmony and good will prevaded the convention of about one hundred Masons.
The following officers were elected to serve for the ensuing Masonic
year: Brother David W. K. Au, Grand Master: Brother Luther M.
Jee, Deputy Grand Master: Brother T. F. Wei, Senior Grand Warden:
Rt. Rev. Brother Ralph A. Ward, Junior Grand Warden: Brother
T. T. Zee, Grand Treasurer: Brother Alfred S. Lee, Grand Secretary.
-New Age, March, 1949.

Reports of Proceedings of Grand Lodge

Fifty-Years' Veterans

Notwithstanding the directions printed on the inside front cover of
the annual printed Proceedings of Grand Lodge, it would appear from
correspondence and enquiries reaching the Grand Secretary, that many
Lodges fail to receive information on matters of importance which arise
out of the business conducted in Grand Lodge. The Board desires to
emphasize that it is the duty of every Master, to whom, together with
the Wardens and Secretary of his Lodge, a copy of the Proceedings
of Grand Lodge is sent, to see that the members of his Lodge are informed, at the next regular meeting following the receipt of the Proceedings, of any matters affecting Lodges or Masons generally which
arise out of the business of Grand Lodge, inclusive of the Grand
Master's address. The Board hopes that every Master will make a
point of seeing that such information is communicated at the appropriate stage, also that the volumes of Proceedings shall be preserved
among the Lodge records for future reference.

Lodge Secretaries are reminded of the necessity to advise the Grand
Secretary of any members on their registers who are qualified for
recognition as brethren whose association with the Craft as members
of a Lodge has extended over a period of fifty years. A brother who
has served for an aggregate period of fifty years in good standing in
Freemasonry, although such service may not have been continuous, and
although portion of such service may have been served in another Jurisdiction, may, with the approval of the Board, be accorded recognition
as a fifty-years' Veteran and receive the prescribed jewel and bound
illuminated address.

Port Darwin Visit

Dear Sir and Bro.,
You are hereby invited to attend a Special Communication of the
Grand Lodge to be held at the TOWN HALL, HAY STREET,
PERTH, on Monday, 12th April, 1948, at 7:30 p. m. To commemorate the 50th Anniersary of the Initiation into Freemasonry of our Grand
Master.-Grand Secretary.

The highlight of my Masonic activity during the past six months
was the Grand Lodge visitation to Alice Springs and Port Darwin.
The Deputy Grand Master, accompanied by the Grand Director, led the
delegation to Alice Springs. Seventeen other Grand Lodge Officers
from all over the State formed themselves into a Bond's Touring Party
and joined the Deputy Grand Master. They conducted the Alice
Springs Installation and then proceeded by road to Darwin, where I
was able to join them to conduct the first Installation after the resusciation of the Darwin Lodge, which had to suspend its activities when the
Japanese attacked Darwin in February, 1942. The ceremony of Installation with the festive board which followed was a memorable
function. The enthusiasm among the Darwin brethren is amazing, and
the Lodge is overwhelmed by propositions for initiation, joining and
affiliation.
-Grand Master: 1948.

Re California
The building of a new Masonic Temple is under consideration. It
is astonishing to read the reports and the financial statements of the
Grand Lodge of California and to visualise the immense amount of work
entailed in compiling the records. Also the great amount of supervision necessary to ensure effective working of such a huge organization. Many inspectors are appointed and elected and the final report
of the Grand Lodge shows how efficiently these officers perform their
duties.

Communication From the M. W. Grand Master

It is my great privilege agaiii to extend to you a sincere welcome to
this annual Communication. It is the twelfth annual Communication
over which I have had the privilege of presiding, and I have to thank
you all, brethren, for your continued confidence in me, as shown by reelecting me to the position of Grand Master for a further term.
Brethren, as a whole, only see the result of that work as it comes
before Grand Lodge for report and recommendation. They are not
all aware of the earnest and lengthy consideration given to every question that affects the good of Freemasonry in this State.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

"Masonic Lodges and Communism"
I must say that I was surprised to hear over the air some two or
three weeks ago, in a religious session statement which associated
Freemasonry with Communism. It came from a Priest of the Church,
who apparently was interested in decrying the Craft. I have, for some
time, admired the attitude of the Roman Catholic Church towards
Communism and have had a very definite opinion that that Church and
Freemasonry are possibly the most forthright opponents of that subersive ideology. I felt compelled when, later, I read the address in print
to regard it as being based upon antipathy towards the Craft, and for
that reason its presumed association with Communism was only another
example of that old adage that "any stick is good enough with which
to beat a dog."
I have lived a fairly long life in this community and have been closely
identified with the work of my own church and with Freemasonry, as
well as with many other public services. I have repeatedly criticised
Communism because, in the words of the broadcast, "of my deep
philosophical disagreement.'' I have never considered it from a standpoint that it threatens the Capitalists' pocket. I do not think that the
protection of Capitalism enters into the question from the standpoint of
Freemasonry any more than it does from the standpoint of the Catholic
Church.
In conclusion, I am pleased to note that true Freemasonry is not
atheistic and that "individual Masons are often enough good men and
our brothers.'" From the Masonic standpoint we can sincerely say the
same of our Catholic brethren.

Re California
The address of Grand Orator William B. McKesson was scholarly,
eloquent, and long. It will be enjoyed by the student with leisure.

Irregular Bodies
"I desire to draw the attention of the Brethren to the existence of
certain irregular bodies and adopting, as far as possible, the phraseology
used by regularly established and properly constituted Masonic
Institutions.
"Such irregular bodies, for example, are the Orders known by the
name of 'The Star of the East,' 'The Eastern Star' and 'Co-Masonry.'
· "The Brethren are distinctly warned against having any connection or association in any way whatever with such irregular organisations, which have been formed without the sanction or approval of
this Grand Lodge.
"The Brethren should clearly recognise that the visitation to, or
the recognition of such irregular bodies would be an absolute breach
of their Masonic Obligations, and any Brother acting contrary to this
Pronouncement must expect Masonic punishment.''

Fifty Year Commemorative Jewel
During the year Commemorative Jewels have been presented to 16
Brethren, who have subscribed continuously to Freemasonry for the
past fifty years.
When we tum our eyes to the wider field, the outlook is not so
reassuring. We find there on every hand, strife and danger and
suspicion. I believe these are apparent in the outside world because
so many men have not been inspired with the principles of Freemasonry.
They have no belief in God, no loyalty to King or to country. I believe
we as Freemasons will, sooner or later, have to accept this challenge
that has been thrown down to us as Freemasons and decent living
people. Because if we do not take up and accept this challenge we
may lose those privileges which we value very highly-the right to
worship according to our beliefs, loyalty to our King and faithfulness to
our Country. I would ask all Freemasons to be worthy, so to live and
act that they may exemplify the principles ~f Freemasonry in their
daily workaday lives.

Report of the Grand Inspector of Workings
Unfortunately, it has been reported that in some Lodges more than
two candidates are being admitted prior to the Obligation, this of
course is wrong. In another Lodge the method adopted in closing a
Lodge working in the Third Degree, to resume in the First Degree, is
not in accordance with the instructions as laid down. Such cases are
few and far between, and I need only to draw the attention of the Wor.
Masters concerned, to have the error rectified.
Following the recent Pronouncement relating to Masonic Dress,
I would suggest to Assistant Inspectors of Workings, that they see

I pause for a moment to ask, and try to answer the question: Whom
should we admit among us as brethren? There are certain necessary
qualifications for all candidates. First. belief in God. Such belief is too
often taken for granted and treatly lightly. It is true that it must be
stated openly in our lodges, but such statement should not be a matter of
routine, and should be definite and sincere. and, before either ballot or
initiation, the Master should be satisfied of the candidate's faith in a
Supreme Being. The second qualification is good character, to which I
have referred already, and which I need not define, because the conscience of all brethren will show them in what it consists. Third, the
candidate should be in such a position that he is not likely to become
a ·b urden on our funds. Fourth, he must be one whom we can welcome
to our assemblies, who will not cause lack of harmony in the lodge or
discomfort to any of its members. one with whom we can associate
freely as a friend and a brother.

Tasmania (1948)
"As your Grand Master. may I ask you:
1. To be generous in your thoughts. 2. To be jealous of our
privileges. 3. Give serious consideration to your responsibilities-Live
into your life the teachings of Freemasonry. And, 4. Do not be afraid
to acknowledge yourself as a Freemason. Freemasonry stands for all
that is just, noble and good. Please do not misunderstand me--the
Wor. Masters of this jurisdiction will remember those antient charges
and regulations which they subscribed to at their installation.
Evening dress which is the correct Masonic dress is difficult to
procure at present, the dinner dress is gradually coming back. It is not
our desire that members absent themselves on that account, but we do
strongly suggest that. failing either of these. a dark morning dress be
worn. Brethren still have a vivid recollection of Masonic gatherings
prior to the war. The general opinion is that· much has been taken
from the impressiveness of our beautiful ritual by the relaxation of the
correct dress producing an atmosphere not conducive to our sublime
teaching. To the Masters present I make an earnest appeal to rectify
this mistake at their earliest opportunity. May I suggest also that the
Grand Inspectors when replying to the Toast of G.L.• if not unduly
upset by the warmth of their reception, make this subject one of their
main points.
·
God does not want us to do extraordinary things--He asks us to
do ordinary things extraordinarily well. It is not the primary function
of a Lodge to initiate candidates or to look for a record membership.
Our first call should be to grasp the fact that they possess a knowledge
of Masonic Truth.
